Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty to table two sets of petitions this morning.
The first petition is from residents from the Upsala area in northwestern Ontario who continue to object to the goods and services tax and call on the government to implement real tax fairness in this country.

The second petition, appropriately processed through the Clerk of Petitions, is signed by residents of Thunder Bay who are concerned about the fallout from events in what used to be the Soviet Union. Your petitioners call upon Parliament to ascertain the specific requirements for medical aid in Lithuania, allocate funds for the acquisition of required medical supplies, and expedite the shipment of these supplies to the Government of Lithuania.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to present two petitions to the House. Both concern the government's back to work legislation. The petitions are signed by Canadians resident in the Northwest Territories, the Ottawa area, Moose Factory, Ontario, Baker Lake in the Northwest Territories and in Iqaluit.
These Canadians are appalled at the government's insensitivity to the needs of its public servants and they call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and to reaffirm our support as a Parliament for the collective bargaining process in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I too am honoured and privileged to stand in this House pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present to this House a petition certified correct by the Clerk of Petitions. The constituents are from Hamilton, Stoney Creek, Burlington and Brantford. This is only one of many petitions that have come the government's way.
Your petitioners state that the Conservative government's high interest rate, high dollar policies and 33 new tax increases since September 1984 are the source of inflationary pressures. They go on to state many other examples and wrap up with a conclusion as follows: Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and reaffirm support for free collective bargaining for Canadians workers.

Mr. Speaker, I too stand pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present petitions in the House of Commons on behalf of people from Indian Head, Saskatchewan, Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, Quebec, St. Catharines, Deleage, Cap Rouge and many many towns and small villages in the province of Quebec.
These people are also very concerned about the number of taxes and the high interest rates that this government has imposed upon Canadians, taking away their purchasing power. They are concerned that this will only deepen the recession in this country. The petitioners are also very concerned about the wage limits that have been imposed upon public servants within Canada.
They call upon Parliament and pray that we will reject the imposition of wage controls and reaffirm our support for the free collective bargaining rights.

October 1, 1991
Routine Proceedings

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour today to submit some petitions that were signed by residents from the province of Quebec. These petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and re-affirm support for free collective bargaining for Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present a petition on behalf of my constituents in the city of New Westminster, British Columbia.
These petitioners state that their post office in New Westminster on Columbia Street is a vital part of their community. They say that closing this post office and replacing it with a commercial service centre for services to businesses will only establish two classes of Canadians.
This arbitrary decision was made without any consultation with the residents in New Westminister who will be affected by this decision.
Therefore, the petitioners are calling on Parliament to halt the plan to close the New Westminster post office and replace it with a commercial service centre.
The petition has been signed by hundreds of residents of the city of New Westminister.

Mr. Speaker, I too have the privilege of presenting petitions on behalf of people objecting to the fact that the government's high interest rate, high dollar policies and new taxes or tax increases-33 since September 1984-are the source of inflationary pressures and not wage demands by workers of Canada.
The petitioners are from Brampton, Ontario; Wood-bridge, Weston, Ontario; Etobicoke, Ontario; Toronto, Mississauga and Sydney Mines, Glace Bay and from Thompson, Winnipeg and numerous other smaller communities throughout Manitoba.
On the petitioners' behalf, I present this petition asking Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and reaffirm support for free collective bargaining for Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to present three petitions from Canadians in and around the metropolitan Toronto area.
These electors recite the decision of the government to impose wage controls on the federal civil service. There is significant damage perpetrated by the government's policy and the collective bargaining process for our Public Service.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and reaffirm support for free collective bargaining for all Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to submit today, pursuant to Standing Order 36, a petition which states that the Conservative government's high interest rate and high dollar policies and 33 new tax increases since September, 1984, are the source of inflationary pressures.
Of course, the petition says that wage control in the public sector has indeed a negative impact on all Canadian workers' wages, that no flexibility is possible when you restrict everybody's salaries without distinction, that the federal Conservative government is willing to deprive workers throughout Canada of their right to collective bargaining, to threaten them with lay-offs, especially because of contracting out, to interfere with the conciliation and arbitration process and to legislate employees back to work.
Therefore, the undersigned, your petitioners humbly call upon Parliament to reject the imposition of wage controls and to reaffirm its support for the free exercise by all Canadian workers of their right to collective bargaining.
Mr. Speaker, I ask that all questions be allowed to stand.
Shall all questions stand?
Agreed.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands on a point of order, and then we will hear the hon. member for Winnipeg-'Transcona.

Point of order Mr. Speaker. My question No. 17 on the Order Paper is still sitting there. It is dated May 13. That does not sound that old although I did ask for a 45 day reply. In fact it is the same question I put on on February 25 in the last session. It is still not answered. This is an outrageous delay.
I know why the government does not want to release the information. It will be humiliated and embarrassed by the result of the release. I submit that it is not proper for this government to sit twiddling its thumbs instead of providing answers to questions in this House which of course it is obliged to do. They are answerable to the people in this House. These questions are put by members of Parliament for good reason and we are entitled to replies.
I request Your Honour to impress upon the government the need for dealing with this in an expeditious way. My question is not the only one from May 13 but it dates from February 25 and this reply has been forthcoming for far too long.

Mr. Speaker, I have two points of order, the first of which has to do with the fact that yesterday during Question Period a question was asked by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Finance and Privatization.
I understand that this is the second time in recent weeks that a parliamentary secretary has asked a question.
I am sure you will know, Mr. Speaker, that the asking of questions by parliamentary secretaries is not established or accepted practice in the Canadian House of Commons. It may come to be at some point, but I am sure you are also aware that we are engaged in a process of reviewing the format and the nature of Question Period. A subcommittee of the Standing Committee on
Points of Order
House Management has been struck to do this and this work will be ongoing as part of the work of that committee and as part of the intention of the government to review the format and the nature of Question Period.
It seems to me that that work should not be preempted or anticipated or in any way affected by ad hoc changes to Question Period such as are constituted by this repetition of permitting a parliamentary secretary to ask a question in the House of Commons.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this is an oversight, a second oversight. I hope that you will be able to tell us that this was so, that we will not have to worry about this again, and that the process of reviewing and reforming Question Period can carry on without the anxiety of thinking there is some kind of process happening extraneous to what the committee is doing.

I want to respond immediately to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Transcona. He raises a point and he is correct that twice within the last couple of weeks a parliamentary secretary has been recognized.
I want to say first of all to the hon. member and to the House that that was an inadvertence and an oversight on my part for which I apologize if it has caused any anxiety.
I want to make it very clear that the sixth edition of Beauchesne's, citation 413, deals with questions by parliamentary secretaries and I read the section:
Those such as Parliamentary Secretaries who are clothed with the
responsibility of answering for the Government ought not to use the
time of the Question Period for the privilege of asking questions of
the Government.
It cites Debates, November 5, 1974, pages 1059-64.
That practice has been adhered to and there may have been a slippage out of inadvertence, but that practice has been adhered to and I want to assure the House that I am not unilaterally changing the practice.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Transcona on another point.

On another point of order, Mr. Speaker. Thank you for your response to my first point of order.

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
My next point of order has to do with the language being employed by Journals in the title of notices going out with respect to the special joint committee which is considering the government's constitutional proposals.
In the order setting up the committee, it is referred to as the special joint committee and then there is a rather lengthy description of what the committee will be considering. But in the Journals titling of the notices, we find this special joint committee referred to as the Special Joint Committee on a Renewed Canada.
There has been no decision taken or no process followed by which to arrive at a description of this committee as the Special Joint Committee on a Renewed Canada. The purpose of the committee is to consider whether or not these proposals will in fact lead to a renewed Canada and whether the judgment of Canadians will be similar to that of the government, that these proposals will lead to a renewed Canada. It may be unintentional, I am sure it is, but there is an element of presumption, almost of propaganda to put it pejoratively-but I don't mean it quite that way-in the title of the committee. I think this kind of liberty should not be taken by whoever has taken this liberty of describing the committee in this way, and I would hope that more technical and objective and non-loaded ways of titling committees could be formed. Again, this is a new practice, in my experience, that this way of describing committees might be employed.
I would ask you to look into it and perhaps to report back to the House as to what could be done to prevent this sort of thing in the future and to do something about the naming of this specific committee.

I can assure the hon. member that I will look at the matter immediately. If it is appropriate to stay with the more technical name, that will be done; in the meantime, I will consider the situation. I think it should also be clear, of course, that the committee could, if it wished I suppose, and if that was done in the appropriate way within the committee, come up with a name which met the approval of the committee.
However, I accept what the hon. member has said, that that has not yet been done and I will look into it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
moved that Bill C-29, an Act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada and to amend another Act in relation thereto, be read the third time and passed.
-He said: Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of third reading of Bill C-29, an Act respecting compensation in the public sector, I would ask all members of the House to debate this bill as quickly as possible, so that it can be considered and passed by the Senate. Thus Canadians will again be able to receive essential services and everything will go back to normal.

Picketing by the Public Service Alliance has become more violent and aggressive each day. Services to Canadians are being increasingly disrupted and Canada's international reputation as a reliable supplier of grain to the rest of the world is again being threatened. But Public Service Alliance picket captains and some members continue to disregard a ruling made on September 23 by the Public Service Staff Relations Board to, and I quote:
-stop from interfering with, impeding or preventing designated employees from reporting to work.
It appears that alliance leaders have very little respect or regard for the law. Having been told to stop illegal strike activity by this agent of Parliament, the alliance has chosen to ignore the ruling and to embark on still more illegal activities.
I wonder if alliance members are really proud that they have been able to shut down of the port of Vancouver. I wonder how many alliance members are proud that the union has been able to prevent nurses from entering the veterans' hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue to care for their patients, many of whom are seniors.
The union leadership does not seem to mind that the livelihood of many of our farm producers is being threatened by their strike activities. I would like to remind hon. members that the plight of these same farmers was described in desperate terms by opposition
October 1, 1991

members during Question Period in this very Chamber only yesterday.
If the welfare of Canadians and the faith of the economic recovery do not concern the PSAC leadership, they concern me greatly. Commuters and ordinary Canadians living in the national capital region had this brought home to them this morning.
PSAC picketing has become disruptive without regard to the law or the rights and livelihood of members of the public to get to and from work on public transit.

The union has increasingly resorted to insults and intimidation, even going so far as to call some of its own members good for nothing. Yesterday, Alliance strikers threw eggs and tomatoes at nursing staff of the Ste. Anne-de-Bellevue hospital, although, Mr. Speaker, these designated employees had to report to work because public safety requires it. They are not even in the same union.
Mr. Speaker, it is most regrettable that many Alliance members who have chosen to continue to work, as is their right, have been harassed and threatened by their own union which, lacking logical means of persuasion, has tried desperately in this way to rally their support for a futile strike.
Many employees, Mr. Speaker, understand the justification of the government's salary policy because they see it in the broader economic context and realize that it is useless to lose several weeks of pay. I am convinced that most Alliance members, who are law-abiding citizens, will want to put these points of view across to their union leaders.
Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, I think that it is in the interest of all public servants, including members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, for members of all parties to recognize that this important bill must be passed as soon as possible, if we want to end the strike once and for all.

I would now like to summarize some of the principal elements of this bill and to briefly go over the rationale
Government Orders
as to why this government feels the wage restraint must play its part in securing and enduring economic recovery.
Anyone who has followed this issue over the last several weeks will attest that the government has taken the more difficult path to achieve wage restraint. Expediency has not driven this government. Why is that?
It is because, despite the commentary of some opposition members to the contrary, this government respects the collective bargaining process and respects as well the rights and views of union members.
It would have been so easy to have chosen the simple way and legislated the wage restraint program immediately after it was announced as previous federal and some provincial governments have done.
Needless to say, the government's legal advisers examined jurisprudence in this respect to determine whether the legislative method of securing wage restraint was a viable course to take and could be justified and defended as an approach given.
I am assured that it is and that it can be given the economic conditions that have given rise to the decision.
Before resorting to legislation, I was determined to appeal to the unions to think through and come to understand the government's reasoning in limiting wage increases. I wanted to communicate to them how wage restraint can eliminate the principal fuel of inflation and reduce the incentive for price increases. I wanted an opportunity to demonstrate to union leadership that they and their members were not being singled out for harsh treatment by the government. I told them, I know, that zero and 3 per cent would be hard to accept and was not a true reflection of what their members' contribution to Canada was worth.
Nevertheless, I wanted them to understand that hundreds of thousands of Canadians have paid a far higher price during the recent recession. They had lost their jobs or they had taken big pay cuts and given back benefits in an effort to keep their employer afloat and maintain jobs.
I wanted to persuade union leaders that every sector, every Canadian had a part to play in the economic recovery and every Canadian would benefit because of it.

October 1, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, since it took power in September 1984, inheriting an enormous debt, the government has adopted more of a private-sector management style. Nevertheless, we note that although the government has greatly improved its efficiency, it is still running a deficit.
Had we granted a pay increase to our employees this year, we would have faced the following choice: either we would have had to eliminate jobs to pay for this increase, which would have reduced services to the public; or we would have had to borrow more, which would have added to the deficit.

This government chose the best interests of Canada over the immediate financial interests of its employees, but not without giving it a great deal of consideration. If this had been almost any other employer, you can bet that many employees now facing zero and three would have suffered the same fate as their counterparts in industry.
I must remind hon. members that over the entire course of the recent five-year downsizing program, our employees enjoyed a 99.5 per cent rate of job security within the Public Service. Public Service employees enjoy an invaluable job protection package and their total benefits package is comparable to that of good employers in the private sectors
While zero per cent this year and a 3 per cent raise next year may sound harsh to those who now have a job, our employees should remind themselves that there are approximately 40,000 candidates prequalified and interested in being hired for jobs in the federal Public Service. There were 236,000 applications for Pubic Service jobs last year alone, a number equal to the size of the entire Public Service itself.
Clearly, there are a great number of Canadians who would like to have a chance to have a Public Service job, even with no wage increase this year.
They should remind themselves, as well, that Pubic Service managers by losing their performance pay this year, will suffer an actual pay cut rather than just a freeze. This comes at a time when their ranks are already undergoing a 10 per cent cut over two years, proportionately a far more severe downsizing than employees in general went through over the past several years.

I must admit that many of our employees, in particular those who have the legal right to strike, do not earn big salaries. Many of them have significant family responsibilities and have already been sorely tested. Unfortunately, the strike will only cost them more, but I think that the time for reconciliation has come.
I therefore ordered my officials at the bargaining table to make every possible effort to reach a negotiated settlement with the Alliance, one that would strengthen or improve existing benefits while respecting the overall program of salary restrictions.
Mr. Speaker, I think that what we agreed on was in keeping with our ability to pay. Furthermore, we did all we could to follow up their other concerns: pay equity and issues related to job security. We offered a lumpsum payment to employees whose income was less than the average salary in Canada. We increased the number of day care centres in the work place by 50 per cent. We also improved other benefits.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, four other unions have already reached agreements with our negotiators and these agreements comply with the salary policy of 0 and 3 per cent, which clearly shows that a settlement was possible.
Mr. Speaker, in the end, we were unable to reach a negotiated settlement with the leaders of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. They left the bargaining table and broke an agreement I had made with the President of the Alliance whereby members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada would remain at work while negotiations continued. The Alliance leaders rejected the improvements contained in the offer I just described and did not submit it to their members. Instead, they chose to send their members back out on the picket lines, which in many regions has disrupted the access to work of must public servants.
The disruptions caused by the picketing are again threatening the safety of all Canadians. The Alliance's activities are endangering the safety of our own employees on the picket lines-not only Alliance members but also members of other unions, managers, customers

and ordinary citizens who are trying to go to work or use government services to which they are entitled.

It is time these picket lines, disruptive and dangerous as they have become, were ended and our employees came back to work. It is time that Bill C-29 was passed so that the zero and three wage policy can be extended to all of the other groups that it encompasses: to the Prime Minister, the federal cabinet, and all members of this House, to the Senate and the employees of Parliament, to the members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP, and to heads and employees of other government bodies that are non-commercial and not normally selffinancing.
Bill C-29 would extend 0 and 3 to a total of 378,000 federal public sector employees and officials and not only to the 156,000 PSAC members.
It is time that the benefits of Bill C-29 were brought home to all taxpayers and that any uncertainty be put to rest that the government might waiver from the economic recovery plan announced in the budget. That recovery plan is working. Make no mistake about it. That is why I commend this bill to all hon. members for passage.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to comment on the bill one last time and to highlight the fact that this bill does something very serious, not only for the specific employees that it affects but for all Canadians.
It removes a fundamental democratic right to collective bargaining. This is a right that Canada has accepted in international conventions that it has signed. It was implemented for workers across Canada in legislation. It was implemented under the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson for employees of the Public Service in 1967 and that has never been abrogated as it is being abrogated today.
It is not coincidental that objections to this bill have come from unions in other public sectors such as provincial and municipal, from the Federation of Teachers and numerous unions that represent teachers and from private sector unions.
People who have any knowledge about the history of labour relations know it is only the actions of workers that stopped 10-year old children from being sent down to the mines, that allowed people to work a reasonable number of hours a day and still have some time for a personal life and for family, that allowed workers to
Government Orders
attain decent, safe, healthy working conditions instead of being required to put their lives at risk just to have a job, and that allowed workers to use their labour in exchange for a decent living which at least allowed them to survive on the money they were earning with their labour.
Collective bargaining rights allow an ordinary worker, who is dependent on somebody else for the very food with which they feed their families and for the money to pay for shelter and buy clothes, some small measure of power to balance off the tremendous economic power that an employer has over the life of that worker and the lives of his or her family.
All Canadians need to be concerned when the government can cavalierly cancel any basic democratic right as it is doing with this bill for a period of two years.
The government did that the night it announced its budget on February 26. It said there will be no collective bargaining. It said this government was not interested even in bringing in a third party mediator, arbitrator or conciliator who might possibly bring some objective evaluation to whether the government is acting responsibly and fairly.
The government rejected, as of February 26, all possibility of a peaceful, reasonable settlement between it and its employees. I want to make clear that the employees have never said they were not willing to live with the economic policies of the government. They have just said that there are other things to be negotiated and they want to be able to sit down at the bargaining table and negotiate those other things.
The minister referred to a number of the effects of the strike. What the minister refuses to do is to take responsibility for that strike. There is not a Canadian who does not understand that this government is lower in the polls than any other government in the history of Canada has ever been. It is desperate to hang on to the shreds of popularity that remain to it and to do whatever it can to build those up. It really does not care who it hurts in the process.
Who it has hurt in the process is not only its own employees but small businesses that are dependent on the delivery of goods and services and people who travel whether on business or to visit family. It has hurt people, as the minister said, our veterans in hospital. It is jeopardizing a large portion of our grain harvest. It is jeopardizing our international trade. It is jeopardizing our reputation as a nation that works co-operatively among the different sectors in society and can be relied

Government Orders
on in international markets to deliver what it says it is going to deliver.
This has been the pattern of the government. It has very carefully selected vulnerable targets. It has used the elderly. It has used the unemployed. It has used seniors. It has used aboriginal Canadians. It has selected those people in society who have the least power to defend themselves and has systematically sought to turn the anger of the Canadian public away from the government, against its own fellow citizens.
A government that should be building a nation, that should be solving problems instead of creating them, that should be building co-operation and collaboration for the many challenges we face for the future instead has chosen to pit one Canadian against the other, to persuade Canadians that their prosperity depends on somebody else suffering. That is a cruel, destructive, vicious approach to trying to protect its own political popularity, and fortunately the polls are saying to everybody that it is not working.
I want to address some specific points the minister made. The minister talked about nurses being prevented from entering hospitals. I want to remind the minister of approximately a year and a half ago when again this government forced the lowest paid of its workers on to strike, the hospital services workers who serve those same veterans, who serve aboriginal communities and deliver health prevention programs. Those very same strikers, at their own expense, continued to provide essential services in those hospitals.
This gallery was full during that strike. While this government was forcing those people back to work because it had refused to negotiate a settlement with them, this gallery was full of nurses and dietitians from Ste. Anne de Bellevue, the same hospital the minister just mentioned. The nurses, the dietitians and the doctors who were filling these galleries in support of those workers know that without those people who are earning a miserly $17,000 a year, they cannot do their professional jobs of looking after the sick, the elderly, and those who have suffered and are disabled because they have fought for this country. Those same workers who earn only $17,000 a year, were never treated fairly by this government, but provided those services even while they were legally out on strike.
The government did exactly the same thing to the ships' crew workers. It failed to designate people who go out to sea at risk to their own lives to save others as essential workers, so we had a strike of the ships' crew workers in December 1989. Again the government did not heed the calls from this side of the House for four months to get back to the bargaining table and negotiate a settlement, and the strike happened. It disrupted transportation in the Great Lakes-seaway system at a cost of a million dollars a day. This government ignored every warning that that was exactly what would happen in December if it did not reach a solution before then.
What did the ships' crews workers do? Did they do what the government had planned for them to do: withdraw essential services? No, they did not. At their own cost of half a million dollars and at inconvenience they left their own families. They stayed in hotels to be available should any emergency arise and were able on a couple of occasions during that strike to put out to sea to save lives. In a crisis which this government had created they set aside their own right to be on strike and at their own expense made sure they kept doing their jobs. This government should do the same.
The minister has referred to the disruption in the grain trade right now. This is a very serious situation, and we are well aware of this serious situation. Back in February when the government decided not to negotiate with its employees, one thing it knew with absolute surety was that the grain elevators would be full of wheat in September. Did this government designate those grain workers as essential when it had the opportunity to do so? No, it did not. Did this government deliberately want to create a crisis in the transport of grain in this country and our shipments to the Soviet Union, and create a crisis in the destruction of a crop for our western farmers? That is the only explanation I can think of as to why it did not designate grain workers as essential workers.
This government thrives on creating crises. It has created a crisis in our economy. We are seeing jobs leaving the most prosperous parts of our country. They are jobs that are going and not coming back. It is creating a crisis in employment. One and a half million people, on this very day, are unemployed in this country. The total throughout this year of how many people have been unemployed is going to be many, many million. How
October 1, 1991

many families does that touch, across the country, during the year with crisis?
It has created a crisis in the very continuance of this country. I almost hate to talk about it at this point because it is so fragile. A government that only knows how to create crises is not a government that can build a strong nation ready for the next century.
Because it has created this economic turmoil, it is trying to persuade people that they are lucky to have any job at any salary. That is back to the old days of the robber barons, when if you owned a business, and if you were bigger than the little business beside you, you just put them out of business. You put their employees out of work and you did not care about that.
That is the kind of country this government would like us to go back to where only those who are rich and powerful can hope for a decent life in this country. That is not the Canadian dream. That is not the country that the people who have sat in these seats for generations before us planned for our children and our grandchildren.
The government has created economic turmoil since co-operative relationships between business and labour, management and labour, at all levels are absolutely essential to progress and prosperity for any nation.
The minister has talked about violence. The minister has said: "We are not to blame. It is those poor people out there on the picket lines who earn $20,000 a year. They're to blame." We had the minister again yesterday in the House saying: "We are not guilty of bad faith bargaining," and trying to mislead Canadians about what the Public Service Staff Relations Board actually ruled.
I want to read this because honesty has become a real issue in this whole debate. I want to read what the Public Service Staff Relations Board said, having heard from government lawyers, having heard from union lawyers, having heard all the evidence. We will know who is responsible for what is going on right now. "This board, in general, shares the views expressed in the cases cited above: The obligation provided under the Public Service Staff Relations Act to bargain in good faith, and make every reasonable effort to conclude a collective agree-
Govemment Orders
ment, is not substantially different for this employer than it is for any other employer in any jurisdiction in Canada. The insistence on conditions precedent to negotiating terms and conditions of employment at the bargaining table is incompatible with the requirement to make every reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement. Accordingly, the board finds that the employer has acted contrary to section 51 of the act and orders the employer to comply with section 51 of the act."
The minister tried to pretend in this House yesterday that being in violation of section 51 was not a condemnation of bad faith bargaining. Let me read into the record, and let me read for Canadians who would like to know whether they can ever believe the government, what section 51 states: "Where notice to bargain collectively has been given the bargaining agent and the officers designated to represent the employer shall, without delay, but in any case within 20 days after the notice is given, or within such further times as the parties may agree, meet and commence to bargain collectively in good faith and make every reasonable effort to conclude a collective agreement." Section 51 is the section of which this government is in violation and has been in violation since last spring. That is the section that imposes a duty on both parties to bargain collectively in good faith. This government has violated that section no matter what the minister stands up and says in this House to try and pretend it has not.
The issue is not who has started the fight. I think the evidence is pretty clear that this government, since February 26, had no intention of reaching a conclusion or settlement with its employees. It was obviously prepared to jeopardize the economy of this country, the transportation system, services to Canadians, anything that Canadians are paying for, to impose its own particular agenda and to find whatever victim, whatever scapegoat, it could find to deflect attention from its many failings.
The issue now is how it can be solved. How can we return services to Canadians, how we can return the employees, who want to be back at work, to their jobs? We should not do it with this legislation. If we send people back to work under this legislation, we send people back in an atmosphere of bitterness and total loss of self respect. We send them back with even more worries about how they are going to pay the rent and how they are going to feed their children because this bill represents a loss of income to people, a serious loss of

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
income. People who are worried, people who lack self respect, people who lack confidence in their employer, people who feel bitterness toward their employer are not productive and efficient workers, no matter how hard they try.
This government has stored up problems for the Public Service of Canada for a long time to come. It is a terrible thing to do to Canadians who pay for services through their taxes and to people who, for a long time, have been proud of serving the people of Canada. These people are defending rights that are important, not only to them, but to all Canadians. A government that can remove rights from one group of Canadians can remove rights from many groups of Canadians.
We have seen it do that already with old age security. People who have saved and worked all their lives are now being told that what they saved and worked for, in true conservative principle, is going to be taken away from them.
The government has done it to the unemployed. There is an unemployment insurance scheme, but the government is going to make sure that a lot of people who most need it, in the areas that most need it, and I think particularly of Atlantic Canada, are not going to be able to qualify for unemployment insurance. They are going to have to pay into it, but they are never going to be able to benefit from it.
This issue has become an issue of honesty. We have seen how the minister, on the floor of this House, denied that the government was guilty of bad faith bargaining, despite a ruling by the Public Service Staff Relations Board whose purpose is to ensure that collective bargaining operates fairly for both sides. We have seen ads placed by this government saying that its budgetary guidelines apply to the Armed Forces and the RCMP. That is simply not true.
The budget of this government did not apply wage restraint to the Armed Forces, did not apply wage restraint to the RCMP. As of the date of publication of that ad, that was an untrue statement. That is an untrue statement today, that will be an untrue statement tomorrow, and it will be an untrue statement until this
Parliament passes this savage piece of legislation that the government has put before us.
It has become a question of honesty. Again, the government said that this applies to all members of Parliament. Well, it is really easy this year. When inflation is 6 per cent, we are going to get our nice healthy 3 per cent raise. Next year, when we go into a year where we are going to a get zero increase, we will still have that nice, healthy nearly 4 per cent raise that we got this year.
That is not fair. That is just not fair, and it is not honest to tell Canadians that we are taking the same punishment everybody else is.
That is nonsense. It has become a question of honesty. The ad placed by the government said that other agreements and other unions have accepted 0, 3. What the government forgot to say was that, for much better paid groups of employees, it has reached settlements that are very generous in fact.
It has done them in other ways other than by increasing wage rates. It has improved classifications. It has given people bonuses. It has given them extra premiums for various kinds of things, but it has meant that employees earning say $50,000, $70,000, such as engineers, translators, air traffic controllers, have got in fact substantial increases in income this year.
For this government to pretend that those people are getting nothing, and therefore the lowest paid should be getting nothing, is absolutely incredible.
It will not tell Canadians the truth. It will not even tell this House the truth about those other agreements, and about how much extra income those other people are earning because of special deals made by this government. To not even tell the truth about that at this point in time, when all we are doing is looking for a solution to it, is unconscionable.
It has also become a question of fairness. One message that has got through to the public is that we have a lot of people working for the Public Service who are not earning very much money.
What has also got through to the public is that, disproportionately, a lot of those people are women. Mr. Capello said that 35,000 people would be getting this bonus because they earn under $27,000, and that 25,000
October 1, 1991

of them are women. That is a record that this government should be ashamed of, the fact that the vast majority of its lowest paid employees are women.
We moved an amendment yesterday to ask the government to make sure that it implemented pay equity rather than treating it as something to be negotiated at the bargaining table. It is the law of Canada, after all and any other employer would have to live with it.
This government refused to consider that amendment. We did not say: "Add more money to employment equity." We just said: "Stop paying these phoney token payments to people, as if they do not deserve them as part of their salary, but make these payments part of the salary so that they fully qualify for other benefits such as pensions".
No wonder most of the elderly poor in this country are women, when they cannot even earn wages that reflect the value of the work they do. This government refuses to implement pay equity.
The Human Rights Commissioner has slammed this government for its refusal to implement pay equity. The minister can stand up all he wants, such as yesterday, and talk about how much money the government is putting into pay equity. He knows that that is one-third of what is needed to give groups of employees in the government, who are primarily women, equal pay for similar work being performed by groups, who are primarily men, and who are much higher paid.
He knows that that should be incorporated into salaries. That is the only thing that is true pay equity, and he has consistently refused to it. He has consistently insisted on fighting the Human Rights Commission when it tries to make a decision that will introduce pay equity into the Public Service.
I challenge the minister to explain why this government wants to talk about pay equity but not implement it.
Bonuses is another issue of fairness. The minister has been waffling all over the place on that in the last week. I want to point out to Canadians that whatever the minister has said in the media, whatever the minister has said in the House, again we have to look at the facts. The facts are that in the legislation before the House today,
Government Orders
this government intends to implement bonuses which are specifically exempted from any controls.
An amendment was introduced in the House yesterday to take out that exemption so that bonuses would be included in the freeze on increases. The government did not accept that amendment. This government, despite the minister saying in the House and in the media that there would be no bonuses, has insisted on bringing forward a law that exempts bonuses from any limits.
This government has brought forward a bill that allows it to exempt any employee or any group of employees from any of the provisions of this act, giving it full freedom to play favouritism as it has done up until now, with contracts to those who are doing well already and to bring down the hammer on those who are not.
The government published an ad that said it has offered pay equity. It has offered to incorporate pay equity into salaries. The government is very clever about not telling the truth. What it did not tell people is that it is only a small portion of what those groups of employees are due, and that it does not intend to do it tomorrow, but to do it some time in the future.
If the government is going to be spending my money and the money of the taxpayers of Canada to put out advertisements, those advertisements had better tell the truth, and this one did not.
I challenge the minister or one of the speakers from the government side to say how this government is going to implement, in legislation, the promises the minister has made in the media, that there will be no bonuses. Not that I agree with that. Not that I think it is fair. I do not think this whole piece of legislation is fair. I think everybody should be treated the same. I think that what applies to one should apply to all. The minister cannot simply stand up in this House and say he is going to do something and then go to the media and say he is going to do something and then refuse to put it in this piece of legislation before us.
The minister has talked about economic recovery. This kind of turmoil does more damage to economic recovery than any amount of fair negotiation might do. I want to touch on one more point.
In the last few years the government has insisted on firing people and contracting out a lot of work. The minister said that not many people have been touched by the downsizing lay-off program. He is wrong. He is totally ignoring the tens of thousands of people who have

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
been forced to take early retirement, forced to take reduced pensions because this government wanted to get rid of their jobs and give them to somebody else who could be brought in on a contract at a much higher price to reward friends.
The whole compensation package of the Public Service Alliance of Canada is less than the cost of contracting out by this government-$5 billion minimum in contracting out and that does not count all the little bits and pieces here and there throughout the departments. That is only the tip of the iceberg of contracting.
This government brings in somebody to work beside a government employee, but one is on a contract and one works for the government. Is the one on contract subject to this limit on compensation? No. If you are a friend of the government and you have a nice contract, you can get an increase and there is no limit on it. It is just the whim of how well they want to reward this person.
This government has tried to say it is being fair and that this applies to everybody. That is nonsense. This government specifically rejected an amendment last night that would have included independent contractors in the same compensation package that is being applied to all government employees.
When the price of contractors is $5 billion and the price of the whole Public Service Alliance is $4.7 billion, how can the government pretend its agenda is really fiscal restraint when it is refusing to apply the same limits to its independent contractors that it does to its own employees?
I think Canadians have learned in the last few weeks that the mistrust they have for this government has been demonstrated again in its dealings with this strike. The Public Service is not a group of lazy, over-paid people that the government has every right to want to be rid of and to punish. Public Service workers are just like the factory workers in Ontario who are losing their jobs, just like the farmers who are losing their farms, just like the small businesses that are suffering because of the policies of this government, just like the middle income families who are paying more than their fair share of taxes while those in the upper income brackets are paying less, just like the poor who are being told that the Government of Canada is no longer interested in paying
its share of the social safety net in this country, and just like every other segment of society, except the rich and powerful, who have somehow become victims of this government.
People have come to see over the past couple of weeks that this is just one more target for a government that cannot manage and cannot run the economy and we are all suffering from it.
This has been a difficult issue. It is one we should never have had to face and it is one from which we will be feeling the repercussions for many months and perhaps for years to come. You cannot run a country without a good Public Service. This government has systematically undermined the Public Service and made it more difficult for Canadians to get value for the money they pay in taxes. It is an approach that is not helping reduce the debt and the deficit, they keep going up, but it is hurting services to Canadians. Canadians are tired of paying more and getting less. They have been doing it for too long. They do not mind if it is going to solve problems, but it is not.
This bill should never have come before this House. It was unnecessary. The turmoil in the country for the last few weeks has been unnecessary, but it is the kind of thing that this government likes to do. It gets some kind of perverse pleasure out of pitting Canadians against Canadians and causing disruption to their basic services.
Mr. Speaker, we will be voting against this bill, of course, later today. We urge the government to take one last chance to avoid this kind of divisiveness and reach a solution with its employees. That is still possible. It owes that to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start today by quoting some words that were written seven years ago: "Economic equality is the vehicle through which women will come to full partnership and participation with men in our society. Parliament has committed the federal jurisdiction to equal pay for work of equal value. My government agrees that this concept is one of the keys to the achievement of economic equality for women."
Mr. Speaker, those words were written in the Conservative government's throne speech, its promise to Canadians in 1984. It is 1991 and we see a government that is

legislating people back to work instead of negotiating pay equity.
Lower wages for women developed a long, long time ago. It is based on assumptions, assumptions that women have no dependents, are supported by someone else and are inferior to men.
We know this was never really the reality, let alone today. Yet these are the assumptions that this government is entrenching when it insists on paying women less for work that is just as skilled, for working conditions that are just as hard or just as difficult, for work that requires the same amount of responsibility as that work that is traditionally performed by men.
A study that rated thousands of Public Service jobs found that community health nurses, mostly women, were making far less than pesticide officers, mostly men. They found that chiefs of library services, mostly women, were making $6,000 less than other government managers. It found that processing clerks, again mostly women, were making thousands of dollars less than labourers.
Since 1978, it has been illegal in this country to pay unequal wages for work of equal value. There have been pay equity complaints filed against the federal government with the Canadian Human Rights Commission over the past 10 years. They began under the Liberal administration and they have continued under this Tory administration. It can take years before a complaint is heard.
The Human Rights Commission is not equipped to solve and enforce the vast number of pay equity complaints it receives. It now has some 68,000 pay equity complaints that have been lodged against this federal government, 68,000 to examine.
The Public Service Alliance of Canada is a union which represents many low-wage women, clerks, secretaries, in the Public Service.
In 1985, all 13 Public Service unions agreed to work with management to achieve pay equity. Some 4,300 employees filled out lengthy and detailed questionnaires, but in 1990 the alliance pulled out of the five-year joint union/management study of pay equity because the government refused to budge.
Government Orders
Federal clerks earn between $16,500 a year and $40,000 a year. The majority of them earn between $19,000 and $26,000 a year. These are the people we are talking about. The President of the Treasury Board has said that Public Service employees have to accept no wage increase, even after years of increases that have been lower than other workers in Canada and, in fact, lower than the rates of inflation in the country. He keeps saying we are living beyond our means. I wonder what means he is talking about. Clerks, who are also mostly women, earn $19,000 to $26,000 a year. A federal hospital worker, again a female dominated job ghetto, earns about $18,000 a year.
I wonder if the minister has ever tried to raise a family alone on a gross wage of $18,000 a year. The minister's salaries and benefits have gone up by $15,000 a year since last year. The money he is receiving has increased by almost the entire amount of the salary of some of these female employees whom he says will get no raise at all.
Is that fair? Is that just? Senior public servants, those making $80,000 or $100,000 or $120,000 a year got a 4.2 per cent increase. But a single parent earning $19,000 a year is to get zero per cent. When you factor in inflation, this person is earning less and less and less every year.
I read a media report recently about a Public Service clerk, a single parent, who has to go to the food bank by the end of each month to feed her family.
It seems to be the government and its friends who are living beyond our means, certainly not low wage Public Service sector employees.
Low wage Public Service employees do not have the means with which to live beyond their means, in fact. So why is the government not cutting the salaries of the people at the top, the fat cats, instead of eroding those of low and middle-income workers and their families.
This government's idea of pay equity is very bizarre. Women are being given one-quarter of what they are owed for work they have already performed and were underpaid for in relation to men. Now these women must pay higher taxes on this income than their male counterparts paid years previously. The annual salary equalization adjustments represent only one-third of what these women should receive.

Government Orders
The Canadian Human Rights Commissioner, the chief of equal pay, confirmed that this government's idea of pay equity contributions are half the rate that other major public employers in Canadian and American jurisdictions are granting.
Since 1990 this government has twice attempted to block in the federal courts the Canadian Human Rights Commission from investigating the pay equity situation. Twice it has tried to block it.
Commissioner Max Yalden said last month that the federal government is not playing fair with striking Public Service employees. He found it, and I quote, "very strange that the government is still trying to kill a human rights tribunal set up to resolve the pay equity issue", while at the same time he is telling striking employees that this issue should be dealt with by the tribunal and not at the bargaining table.
Just what is the government playing at and why is it playing with the lives, the health and the incomes of low wage earners and their families?
In early 1990 the Thsk Force on Barriers to Women in the Public Service, which was chaired by Senator Pat Carney, released a report. Among the documentation that it presented, it showed that 75 per cent of all women in the Public Service are concentrated in four fairly low paying job groups: secretarial, clerical, administrative and program management. It also found that women tend to be compressed at the lower echelon of even these classifications. In other words, they are not even the heads of their own job ghettos.
Job security is a big issue for women in the Public Service. Twenty per cent of all women Public Service employees are in term positions, 60 per cent of all the term positions are held by women. This makes them more vulnerable to lay-offs and less likely to receive benefits.
The data show that the federal government is an extremely poor employer of women. It has taken advantage of women employees over years and years and done very little to advance equality of any kind.
We have seen this government pull stunts like this before. It imposed back to work legislation on female
federal hospital workers in 1989 instead of negotiating pay equity with them. This was in spite of a 1987 Canadian Human Rights decision in favour of the female dominated hospital service workers.
I want to return to some other lovely words that were said by the Prime Minister during the 1988 election campaign, during the leaders' debate that was televised across the country and I quote: "We are agreeing on a policy of pay equity for women. We are budgeting for the funds required on an ongoing basis to make sure that they are available so that this money will be given to those women who have been deprived of the degree of equality that we seek. The money is being budgeted so that when the agreement is reached it will be there to close the gap. The commitment is there and the money is there. We are beginning at home. We are getting our own shop in order", he said, "I think that this would be, once it is done, an excellent model for the public sector. I think we have to do it properly ourselves and then see if and how we can work it out with the private sector".
Where is that money now, that money that was budgeted for, that money that was set aside? Where is that commitment now? How many more years will it take before the government gets its own shop in order?
We have seen governments that deal with this issue fairly. The Ontario New Democrat government extended pay equity to groups of women in female job ghettos who were excluded from the previous government's policy. One of the very first actions of the Ontario government was to drop the previous government's pay equity court case against nurses and guarantee pay equity for the nurses. It is meeting its pay equity adjustments for public sector workers. Ontario in fact has the most far-reaching pay equity system in North America.
It does not just cover the cost of the public sector, but the private sector under provincial jurisdiction as well.
This government cannot even handle its own public sector. It refuses to negotiate pay equity with its workers. This government should follow the example that has already been set out for it by the government in Ontario.
Pay equity is an issue that affects every woman in Canada. Every battle that is fought brings the reality of pay equity for work of equal value just a little closer for
October 1, 1991

all women in our society. Equal pay is the law, and it is a law that is being ignored by this government.
One document puts the situation very clearly, and I quote:
What would your reaction be if you were told that you had just lost thousands of dollars? Anger or shock, sadness that such a thing could happen.
Well, there are millions of women in Canada who are being robbed of thousands of dollars each and every year. It is a fact that women earn less than men for performing work of the same value. Often women earn much, much less; 10 per cent; 20 percent and sometimes even 40 per cent.
We have a law that forbids the employer from discriminating between men and women and paying wages for work of equal value. This government is ignoring that law.
There is a binding Public Service Staff Relations Board ruling that the government must negotiate with its workers, not force them to accept a zero per cent increase and no pay equity, without even talking. This government is breaking that as well.
I wonder how the government can expect and hope for Canadians to respect the laws that are passed here in this House of Commons when the government itself ignores them.
The government has shown over and over again that it has no respect for Canadians, especially low income women working for low wages, and that it has no respect for the democratic process.
A strong economy and a stable society cannot be built by undercutting more than 50 per cent of the population of Canada, by undercutting women. This is a terrible kind of role model for other Canadians.
Women and all workers are simply not going to take this any more. I often question the government on issues of concern to women. Many times, over and over again, the Prime Minister or other government ministers stand in this House and talk about equality and about how they have appointed a woman to this board or they have appointed two women to another government function or another government board. They speak with such bravado and such boasting tones about how they have appointed more women to positions in government.
It is not good enough for the Prime Minister and the members of cabinet to simply tell us that they have appointed another woman here or there, or that they support the issue of equality for women in our society.
Government Orders
This government has an opportunity right now to put its money where its mouth is, to show that it has a firm commitment to equality for women within its own Public Service. We have had enough talk about equality for women. It is not good enough anymore for the government to say equity, they must pay equity.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments on the speech by the member of the New Democratic party. I may remind her that in 1967, it was a Liberal government that introduced collective bargaining in the Public Service and that the present Tory government is destroying our public service by using strategies like today's back-to-work legislation, contracting out and bonuses as incentives for senior, in fact, very senior public servants. I may remind the NDP hon. member that this government has ignored women as far as wages are concerned. Many women in my riding earn very low salaries as a result of this government's policies. These women, in many cases single parents, have to pay taxes, including federal and provincial income tax, municipal taxes and school taxes. Because of this government's economic restraint policy, there has been a flow of fiscal responsibility from the federal government to the provinces and subsequently to municipalities and school boards, which has engulfed low-income earners, most of whom are women responsible for raising a family. I say women, because all too often, women are at the bottom of the wage scale although they have the same responsibilities, the same duties and the same tasks as men.
This government has ruined the relationship between employees and employer, the employer being the present government. How will these employees feel, now that they are being forced back to work? It's almost like seeing a film on slavery. You see the employer taking employees by the scruff of their necks and saying: You are going to work today and tomorrow, otherwise you will be fined $500 per day. And on top of that, your salary increase will be zero per cent. Either you toe the line or you might lose your job. That is the kind of employer we have today.
Mr. Speaker, at the same time these employees have to cope with tax increases at all the levels I just mentioned. I think that with its economic restraint policy, this government is dividing the country into

different sectors and pitting those sectors against each other-
