I would be happy to oblige, Mr. Speaker. If I could, before my time is up, I would like to get some clarification. During this period, are we not entitled to make some remarks or comments and to ask questions? Surely, during this five minute period, hon. members can choose between these three options, right?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member asked this question. The philosophy behind the question and comment period is to give as many members as possible the opportunity to comment briefly or to ask a question of the previous speaker. This is not a period when you can rise and make a new speech. The objective of the Speaker is to recognize as many members as possible. Therefore, when an hon. member takes ten minutes to make a comment, it goes against this philosophy, as was stated by one of my predecessors in the Chair, Mrs. Jeanne Sauve.
So, I would ask the hon. member to cooperate and complete his comments or ask a question.

Mr. Speaker, surely you know I come from a riding where there are between 24,000 and 25,000 civil servants. So, of course, I stand up for them. Consequently, I would like to ask the hon. member from the NDP if she agrees with me that this government is wrecking labour relations between employees and employers?

Mr. Speaker, I would agree that labour relations between the government and its own employers have certainly hit a new low, but there have been times under previous Liberal administrations where the relationship has been very testy also, to say the least, and some of the legislation that previous Liberal governments brought to Public Service workers was not well received by the workers either. I think back to the six and five legislation not so many years ago.
It is true that the relationship has hit a new low and new depths with this Conservative government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the speech made by the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby and I paid particular attention to what she said regarding pay equity in the Public Service. Her remarks suggested that this government did not do anything about pay equity.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the hon. member that this government's commitment to pay equity goes back to 1984 and that, after the election that year, when we came into office, a study was conducted within the Public Service in order to determine how many employees could be eligible for a pay equity program. That study indicated that 79,400 public servants could be subject to a pay equity program or policy.
I would also like to remind the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, that, up until now, this government has paid $317 million to 79,400 Public Service employees to meet its commitments with respect to pay equity.
I would also like to point out to her, Mr. Speaker, that $81 million will be paid during the next fiscal year under the pay equity policy.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby if she knows of any businesses in the private sector or any provincial or municipal governments in Canada that have a pay equity policy as generous or should I say as fair as the one that applies to federal Public Service employees.

Mr. Speaker, the member opposite certainly does not have to remind me of the commitments that were made by members of his government in 1984. In fact, they made up a great deal of the comments that I made today to remind them of the commitments that they made to Canadian women, the commitments that they made to Canadian women in the Public Service, and the commitments that they failed to uphold. He certainly does not need to remind me of that.

My question is: Where is the money that was promised? It is not being paid. Only one-third has been committed to pay equity of what is just and fair. His government continues to fight decisions of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, to fight them in the federal courts of this land, fight in opposition to pay equity trying to stop fair and just settlements on pay equity. That is the Conservative government record.
When he asked me if there had been a jurisdiction, yes, and I pointed it out in my remarks today. The government in Ontario has expanded the pay equity, has dropped the court actions that were started by the previous Liberal administration against public health nurses, and has set a great example for all of North America on the issue of pay equity.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every time I have spoken in this House since 1988,1 did so eagerly, of course, and with the desire to contribute positively to the issue or bill being debated.
Is a parliamentarian's first responsibility not to give his opinion on the subject of the debate, Mr. Speaker? When he takes part in the debate, should he not seek to protect and defend the nation's higher interests, while respecting individual freedoms and society's welfare?
Mr. Speaker, I will try to reconcile these great objectives as I participate in the debate on Bill C-29 today. As the Treasury Board President said, this bill was not tabled with a glad heart and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I will not be glad to vote for Bill C-29.
Bill C-29 temporarily suspends the legal right to strike for members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, extends the collective agreement for two years and sets salary conditions for the same period. Mr. Speaker, I must regretfully note that this bill, while pursuing objectives in the public interest, temporarily suspends the legal right to strike for employees who belong to the Alliance.
Moreover, the bill, by setting salary conditions for public servants for the next few years, suspends their
Government Orders
ability to negotiate pay increases. Mr. Speaker, that is why I had reservations about the bill when it was tabled.
That is also why I always hoped that the government would not have to bring in such a bill. I always believed it was possible for the Alliance to accept the salary conditions proposed in the Government of Canada's most recent budget. An agreement with the Alliance would have made it possible to continue discussions on all working conditions and clauses related to them in the collective agreement, except of course for the salary clauses.
It would have been far better for the two parties to agree and reach a negotiated settlement. Until last week, as I said before and say again, I had serious reservations about the negotiating process. I wondered whether both parties had exhausted every avenue of bargaining as should be done when a collective agreement is renewed. Mr. Speaker, I was under the wrong impression that additional efforts could have been made by both parties to reach a negotiated settlement.
When I became aware of the number of meetings, the number of days and hours Treasury Board negotiators had spent at the table, I realized that a big effort, and major attempt had been made to come to a negotiated settlement. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, I had been particularly happy two weeks ago to see the progress that allowed public servants to go back to work and the negotiations to resume.
All last week, like many Canadians and like a very large majority of the people in my riding, I cherished the hope that those discussions would lead to a negotiated settlement that would be in keeping with the budget restrictions of the federal government and at the same time help improve the working conditions of the employees of the federal government and members of the Public Service.
Obviously, it is with great regret and surprise that I saw the union negotiators leave the table last Friday, following the tabling of specific proposals made by the Treasury Board representatives. Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to list the offers made last Friday to the union representatives at the negotiating table.
First, the government, through its negotiators, was maintaining its position of zero per cent increase for this year and 3 per cent for the following year.

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
The government, through its negotiators, offered a $500 lump sum payment for the 35,200 indeterminate employees with salaries under $27,000. It should be noted that a previous proposal calling for a lump sum payment for those earning up to $25,000 would have benefited only 14,000 civil servants. That is to say that there has been a major improvement at that level.
There was a proposal to guarantee employment to those whose jobs would cease as a result of contracting out or privatization, a unique advantage indeed granted to the public servants belonging to PSAC. Such an advantage is nowhere to be found in collective agreements signed in the private sector, Mr. Speaker. It is a definite advantage.
We are also proposing to guarantee reasonable job offers to all other employees affected by a work force adjustment. We proposed improvements to fringe benefits, including the dental plan, health care, disability insurance, annual leave, shift premiums, day care, meal allowances and much more, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada find hard to understand because such advantages are a rarity in the private sector.
Of course, our proposals include provisions for pay equity, as I told my hon. colleague from New-Westmin-ster-Burnaby earlier, amounting to $81 billion. Once these proposals were on the table, the president of PSAC left without even responding to these proposals. Instead, he chose to make his union's response known through the media and to order his members to resume their national strike.
Normally, in the bargaining process, when the employer tables a proposal affecting or improving previous proposals or working conditions, it is only natural, and the right thing to do for the union to consider these offers and to get back to the employer with comments whether all or part of proposals are rejected but, in any event, to pursue the bargaining process.
What is abnormal and regrettable in this case, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the PSAC negotiators left the bargaining table, did not submit the latest offers to their members and decided to go back on strike.
Mr. Speaker, it is essential that this government continue to strive to reduce government spending and the national deficit, because Canadian men and women cannot bear any further tax increases. The wage policy
set out in the last budget is an integral part and an important aspect of the objectives identified by the Government of Canada.
The Alliance should have recognized how important it is for our country to attain these objectives. The Government had and still has no other choice but to ask all its partners to join in an effort to reduce the deficit and put the economy back on track. The PSAC obviously refuses to take part in that effort which has already been accepted by many groups of employees from other jurisdictions.
Instead the Alliance has chosen to attack the Government's objectives and of course to resume its strike. Even though it is a legal strike, Mr. Speaker, the Alliance has overstepped its authority in preventing essential services employees from going to work. In so doing, the Alliance has caused severe harm to large groups of citizens by depriving them of services neccesa-ry for their safety and their well-being. It has caused irretrievable damage to vital sectors of our economy.
Mr. Speaker, this strike is not driven by economics, it is political, and this is a direct quote from the President of the Alliance. Just remember what he said in front of the Parliament Buildings a few days ago, and also the speech where he said that this government had to be defeated.
I would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that the Alliance was calling for a strike in the interest of its members. It is my opinion that leaders of the union should have listened to their members and should have directed their efforts toward bargaining, with a view to securing better working conditions while waiting until for the government's finances to improve and allow it to grant better pay conditions to its employees.
By so doing, the leaders of the Alliance would have contributed to the improvement of the financial situation of the country. They would have supported the economic recovery efforts by the government and the private sector and they would have, in my opinion, really promoted the long term interest of their members.
The government for its part is proposing a pay policy which will allow keeping the number of positions at its present level for Alliance members. I consider that a very reasonable policy which confirms the government's
October 1, 1991

intention to grant its employees the best working conditions possible under the current financial situation.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that Bill C-29 allows for negotiations between the government and the Alliance on a large number of non-monetary and monetary clauses included in the present contract.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that both parties will take this opportunity to resume talks as soon as possible. Once again, I regret that Bill C-29 removes, even temporarily, the right to strike, but the objectives of this bill are to ensure the continuation of services which the government has the duty to provide, to protect the economic recovery and to further the efforts undertaken by the government to reduce the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, the last point I would like to mention is the feeling that there are far too many union negotiators. Not only do we see the Alliance leaders, Mr. Bean and Mrs. Hurens, on television almost every day, but we also see some of our NDP colleagues literally holding hands with them. Is it not normal to believe, Mr. Speaker, that the PSAC works out its negotiation strategy in the offices of NDP members? Moreover, we all heard the member for Mission-Coquitlam say that on Friday Mr. Bean, while in her office, tried to contact the President of the Treasury Board. I would have thought that the President of the PSAC would have an office of his own and facilities provided for him by the Alliance to make his own calls and contacts. Why use the offices of NDP members? Listen, this proves that what we are having here is a political strike.
Mr. Speaker, I regret the inconveniences caused by bill C-29, and I still have the same reservations to make on the principle of such a bill. I believe that in the case of a labour conflict, the balance of power should lead to a negotiated settlement, but I am also convinced that the circumstances surrounding this conflict and the difficulties it is causing to the country truly justify the bill. I hope it will be adopted as fast as possible.

A very brief question, Mr. Speaker. While the hon. member for Manicouagan deplores the strike but is in favour of the back-to-work legislation, he seems to be suggesting at the beginning of his speech that he believes in salary negotiations. My question to him is this: Is it possible to
Government Orders
negotiate salaries when one of the parties, namely the employer, offers a 0 per cent increase or the door?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
It is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that a government sets its objectives through the budgetary process.
It is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that a government makes decisions on the compensation of its emplooyees.
I remember well to have experimented the adverse effects of a legislation passed by a previous liberal government where we were directed not to exceed some increase percentages within collective agreements that I had negotiated myself for the employer and where the salary increases were cancelled by that legislation, while that legislation also applied to the then employees of the Public Service of Canada. That is when the Liberals were in power.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing unusual in the fact that a government sets its salary policies through the budgetary process in order to make all people concerned aware of its objectives.
Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet, I would like to go back to what the hon. member for Ottawa West stated earlier when she said that a number of groups in the federal government are not covered by the salary policy. She mentioned among others the National Defence and the RCMP. I would like to tell her that under Appendix I of the bill both the National Defence and the Department of the Solicitor General are subject to this legislation.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that this be mentioned and I thank you.

Mr. Speaker, the situation today is really a tragic one for the Public Service Alliance workers.
A group of women workers are at the Status of Women office here in Ottawa right now. They are asking for a meeting with this government on the issue of pay equity. They simply want to discuss the issue. They have asked that the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women meet with them and listen to their concerns. They have been refused that hearing.
I want to ask the government side whether or not they would agree that these women have a right to speak to their minister responsible for the status of women about

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
an issue that is of such critical concern, not simply to these women but to all the women of Canada. I ask the minister to make a commitment on behalf of the government to begin the process of talking about this issue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague for New Westminster-Burnaby is forgetting that the pay equity situation has been referred, at the request of the union, to the Human Rights Commission. The government has agreed to that and it is trying to address the situation in a fair and reasonable manner, fulfilling its commitment and at the same time complying with decisions that have been made. The government will keep on doing this.
I talked about the amount of money that has been put into pay equity just a few minutes ago and I can assure my colleague that this government is committed to pay equity and everything will be done to achieve that goal.

Mr. Speaker, if that is true, can the member opposite please tell me why, in the offer that was made to the Public Service Alliance of Canada, there was a small token toward pay equity and even that small token was not incorporated in this bill? Can the member explain why his government refuses to incorporate pay equity into salary so that it is subject to all the other privileges of money that is earned as salary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does my hon. colleague from Ottawa West consider that $317 million is a token? Does she consider that $81 million budgeted for the coming year for pay equity is a small token? I would like to suggest to her that we are talking about enormous amounts of money and we are just trying to address that situation with the money and the finances available to the federal government.
If we manage to control the deficit, put the economy of the country back on track, this government is committed to do more. I can assure my hon. colleague that what she calls a token for a great majority of Canadian taxpayers is a great amount of money which people in my riding would look at with much envy. My hon. colleague talked about poor people on picket lines earning $20,000 a year. I can talk to her about poor people not on picket lines, minding their home with revenues of $5,000, $6,000, or
$7,000 a year. That is what I call a token, not $317 million and not $81 million.

Mr. Speaker, you sometimes must have patience in this House in awaiting your turn to speak. While the member for Manicouagan is here I would like to comment on the $317 million that he is talking about. It is a significant amount as is the $81 million a year that he is putting into pay equity.
He talks about it being a considerable amount of money. It is absolutely a considerable amount of money. Yet the government has just recently thrown away $267 million to the KAON project in B.C. It has sent the National Energy Board to Calgary when it could have been left here in Ottawa at no cost. It has sent the Farm Credit Corporation to Saskatchewan when it could have been left here in Ottawa at no cost. It has been the multi-million dollar government which Canada has never seen the likes of before.
Of course $81 million is a lot of money, but let us not throw these figures around unless we put them in perspective. From 1984 to 1988 this government made the largest amount of revenue over anticipated revenue that any government in this country has ever produced, and it has never put one cent of it against the debt. It has never put one cent of it toward pay equity. I am a little bit sick and tired of hearing how great this government is with regard to pay equity.
That was not intended to be part of my speech, but I had to throw it in because I really felt that the hon. member was over-stating his case.
Getting back to my speech, I am delighted to stand here and speak to Bill C-29, an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada, but this bill is just another example of the government's continuing oppressive autocratic style.
The government continues to flip-flop. First it would not negotiate, then it will negotiate, and now it will not negotiate any more. I do not think this government has a clue as to what it is doing.
For a fleeting moment about 10 days ago, I really thought the government had its act together when it announced it would suspend the legislation, which it is now going to implement, and return to the bargaining table. In fact I was so pleased with the minister's acceptance of going back to the bargaining table I even
October 1, 1991

sent him a note thanking him on behalf of the public servants of Canada for being a considerate, kind and warm-hearted minister.
It was a sham.

It was a sham. It was a charade. It was the biggest charade. I hope he frames my note.
Two weeks ago during the first strike action I received a copy of a letter which was sent to the President of the Treasury Board by Glen Whalley, a Nepean constituent. He does not mind my giving his name. He sent a copy to me and I really felt that his comments were noteworthy because what he said in that letter I believe effectively described the feelings of the average public servant, not only that but the feelings of the average Canadian.
I am going to quote this letter:
I am a family man, with bills to pay, who takes pride in my job and I am a member of PSAC. You seem to have a misguided view of the labour force that is working for the Government of Canada. I can understand that, what with all the opinions and accusations flying around Parliament Hill, the bargaining tables and the media. So I would like to offer a point of view from one of the common folk.
Your government has been in power for seven years and yet you still try to blame your financial situation on previous governments. It was your government that perpetuated this recent economic disaster with your lack of foresight and sensitivity. It was your government that provided the catalyst for our dilemma by shoving, amongst other things, Free Trade and the GST down our throats.
The cost of our goods are not going down, the cost of living is still going up and we watch our industries moving south. We see our families, friends and neighbours being laid off or losing their businesses to bankruptcy.
Now you come to us and expect us to accept your offer. In fact, you almost act surprised that we do not want to seal our financial future for the next three years and put our faith in your unpredictable budgetary mismanagement. You also want us to blindly agree to this offer before knowing if you will negotiate in good faith on the remainder of our concerns. Let us face it, sir, your track record so far is not very favourable. I ask you as a businessman, would you accept these terms in your employment contract?
In turn, I have a proposition to offer you.
And this gentleman says to the minister:
If you can convince the working people in the private sector of Canada, who receive pay increases this year to donate their new income to help pay off the national debt, that is after paying for increases in utilities, food and clothing, after paying federal and provincial income taxes, federal GST and provincial sales taxes,
Government Orders
municipal and property taxes, gas taxes, car taxes, tire taxes, liquor taxes, cigarette taxes, restaurant food taxes and on and on.
If you convince those working Canadians of the private sector still bargaining for wage settlements to donate any future increases this year to help pay off the deficit.
And if you can convince your fellow MPs, Senators and any other senior management staff to give up the tax-free portion of their income and donate the applicable taxes that the rest of us are forced to pay;
If you can do this, then I will try to convince my co-workers that your zero, three and three offer is a good deal.
I will set aside further arguments concerning your party's disregard for past promises for such things as pay equity. Their deceptions about the effectiveness of contracting out. The blunders, the questionable antics and budget expenses of senior management and ministers that cost taxpayers millions of dollars every year. Sneaky manoeuvres, like rushing through pay increases for the elite few at the top just before introducing wage controls on lower level employees. The fact that you have no respect for the collective bargaining process, the conciliators you agreed to work with or your own rules of fair play in negotiations; and finally, your government's obnoxious attitude that it can do whatever it pleases because it has a majority in the House of Commons, even though it is now backed by less than 16 per cent of the population.
Please, people of Canada, don't be angry with us for trying to maintain our standard of living. We did not increase your taxes. We did not break political promises or create an economic environment where farmers and fishermen are unable to support their families and where single parent families are forced on to welfare to survive.
We did not introduce taxes to send truck drivers and small businesses into financial ruin. Most of all, we are not responsible for this government and its policies.
I had to read that letter almost in its entirety, because I do not think that I or anyone else in this House could have said it as well and as sensitively to get the point of the average Canadian and the average public servant across.
I received another phone call this morning from Mr. Barker. He goes on to say that the government is seriously damaging and destroying the Public Service in this country, an institution with a proud history of service and one that he is most proud to have worked with.
He spoke of the hypocrisy of the government involving Canada in larger and larger trading blocks and talking about making Canadians more competitive while at the same time it is treating its own employees in total contradiction to this, through demoralizing, contracting out, cutting back, wage freezes.

Government Orders
Many, many people when they call speak of their anger toward this government and about their despair that public servants have somehow inherited the dubious position of being the government's whipping boy.
I have heard them talk about the government's deception on the effectiveness of contracting out, of the past broken promises of pay equity. I have heard first hand the outrage and cynicism of the average public servant about the patronage which this government dishes out to its own Tory cronies.
The government is running roughshod over members of the Public Service of Canada by again bringing forth this back-to-work legislation just as sure as it has run roughshod over parliamentary tradition and guidelines by bringing back this legislation.
The fact is that although this act will eventually apply to MPs, senators, presidents of Crown corporations and senior managers, this will only occur next year when inflation is expected to be much lower.
Is it any wonder that Canadians are skeptical about politicians? I would like to ask when you were at the bargaining table if consideration was given for PSAC employees to receive the increase this year, the same as I have received my increase this year and the same as all the department heads, 5,000 of them, 5,000 cabinet appointees got bonuses in the past year, some of them as high as 25 per cent of their salaries.
Can you tell me that Ron Lawless, president of the Canadian National Railway and VIA Rail who was already making in the salary range of $365,000, should receive another $30,000 bonus this year? He has already got a $30,000 bonus. That is more than these public servants' total annual salary.
Before the government brought down its measures against the Public Service in its budget, the government revealed that it would not go the route of conciliation or arbitration. It has threatened from the beginning that it would introduce legislation to bypass any settlement that did not accept the wage freeze as a given. Its whole attempt at bargaining right from the outset has been a charade of the worst kind.
My colleague from Ottawa West mentioned this in her speech. The government is in clear contravention of section 51 of the Public Service Staff Relations Board Act. The government is breaking the law. The government is clearly breaking the law.
Has this government ever made any reasonable effort to conclude a collective agreement? No. Has one word of the section of the Public Service Staff Relations Board Act been honoured by this government? No. This government has in no way acted in an honourable fashion with respect to its employees. There has been no collective bargaining, and let us make that clear.
It already has in hand no fewer than five conciliation board reports which have been unable to make any progress toward a solution. Three of these even highlighted the government's responsibility for the lack of collective bargaining.
Who is being hurt by the actions of this government? In the immediate it clearly is the little guy, the lowest paid members of the Public Service. Because the government has forced the public servants out on strike, it clearly then becomes the business community. It is the children. It is the Canadian public generally who is also being hurt, all because the government may not play by the rule book.
Does this government understand anything about the concept of worker productivity? Does it not think about how these people will function when they return to their desks after they have been told their work is worth zero per cent and after they have been bullied back to work?
It is very frustrating for me to stand here in the House to tiy to represent the public servants and try to get their point across. They do not have thousands of dollars to run these great big ads in the paper, the big ads that are not telling the truth.
Your money and mine that they are using.

Your money and mine the government is using to put a point across but it does not tell in this document that it is breaking the law, does it? It does not say that it is in contravention of section 51 of the Public Service Act, does it?
I would hope that this government could get back to the bargaining table, but the only hope that we have is
October 1, 1991

with the appointment of a mediator. I felt last week and I mentioned this earlier, 10 days ago, that the minister was sensitive and that he did care. But I look at the president of the Public Service union and I look at the minister responsible for public servants-and I don't know if this is going to be unparliamentary; you might call me on this one-but I see two blockheads who simply cannot negotiate and cannot arrive at a solution. I think that we have to put a mediator in to negotiate this solution.
Pay equity is also not negotiable. It should not be on the table. It is the right of all that pay equity be in force and that should not even be part of the bargaining tool. It should be there and it should be part of what women should expect in the work force.
This government keeps using the excuse that it has been concerned about the economy and that is why it must do this. Had it truly been concerned as I mentioned earlier, the excess revenue that it received in that period between 1984 and 1988 could probably have wiped out the debt or certainly reduced it tremendously. You know the old saying "Nero fiddled while Rome burned"? Well, I see this government fiddling while the country is being decimated.
The minister said an interesting thing in his speech yesterday. He said he was not here to win a popularity contest. Well, he sure has not won a popularity contest, nor has the government. He has played his rules right there. He is not popular.
I was speaking earlier about the amount of money the government has spent on pay equity and the amount of money the government has spent on other programs. I have never heard figures on the amount of money the House would need to approve even 3 per cent for these public servants. I have never heard that amount of money so I don't know what it is. But you know, we throw away money. Maybe it is not thrown away, maybe it is good for business. A shipbuilding company in I think it was Valleyview, Quebec, was given several hundred million to bail it out, to keep it from going bankrupt. A couple of years ago we sent the Space Agency that was situated here in the nation's capital to St. Hubert, Quebec. It is now, I might add, in the riding of a member of the Bloc Quebecois. We give $267 million to a TRIUMF KAEON project at the University of British Columbia when most of the research scientists in this
Government Orders
country will tell you that it will be the most drastic drain on the federal treasury-
Bad management, that is what she is talking about.
I am getting to bad management, that is exactly what I am getting to.
Lack of vision.

I don't know how a government can ever hope to get any loyalty from the Public Service again when we throw money away as easily as we do but will not sit down and talk about what is the value of a good employee.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of speaking here in the House on this subject. I hope there is some rationale, that someone comes to their senses.
Mr. Speaker, I move pursuant to Standing Order 26(1):
That the House sit between the hours of 1 and 2 p.m. today for the
purpose of considering Bill C-29.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the speech by the hon. member for Nepean and to the speeches by the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Carleton-Gloucester. Since the beginning of this debate Mr. Speaker, my impression has been that instead of a Canada Round or a Quebec Round, we have an Ottawa Round, because Liberal members have delegated their members from the Ottawa area where their public servants are-
You have no respect for public servants!

They say I don't respect public servants, Mr. Speaker. I listened very attentively to what the hon. member of Carleton-Gloucester had to say, and now I would also like to have a chance to express my point of view.
There are many public servants in my riding as well. However, my point is that members of this House do not represent public servants. They have a union to do that. Only a few minutes ago, the hon. member for Nepean said clearly that she felt she spoke for public servants in this House, although she represents all residents of Nepean, and above all, the national interest of this country. And Mr. Speaker, that national interest is now facing a very serious challenge.
I would like to ask her the following question: We have yet to hear a single NDP member condemn these acts of violence and intimidation against men and women who wanted to go to work and were on essential services. Not a single NDP member was willing to condemn this kind of violence.
Earlier, the hon. member for Ottawa West had an opportunity to condemn the violence against nurses at the Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue Hospital, a veterans' hospital in Quebec, and she failed to condemn at least this instance of violence.

Is there some kind of double standard at work here among Liberal members? Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand here and respond to the member across the floor. First of all I would like to say quite clearly and quite unequivocally that I represent national interests in this House of Commons. If I was a member from Atlantic Canada, do you think that I would not be on my feet talking about the fishing industry? They are representing their constituencies when they speak about the fishing industry and what you people have done to it.
I am in a riding which happens to be in the nation's capital.
Do you not think that because I have a high number of public servants that I will not represent these public servants in the House of Commons? Of course I will. That is my responsibility.
I hope so.

At the same time, I will support my colleague from the western provinces when I see the wheat farmers. They have a product but there is no money for their wheat. Do you not think that when my colleague speaks in the House of Commons on the plight of these farmers that I will not support him? Of course I will.
He mentioned the violence, some minor skirmishes on the picket lines. I deplore these skirmishes. To the many strikers I have spoken to, I have said "Please, be peaceful. The public will recognize what you are trying to do and what you are trying to achieve but they will

understand it more if it is achieved through peaceful means".

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. The hon. member from the government side of the bench has mentioned my name and I think he may have inadvertently left a totally wrong impression with the public that may be watching and with the House of Commons about people who have spoken on this debate.
I think if the hon. member looks back over the debate, over the petitions that have been presented, over the Standing Order statements in the House, over the questions and again specifically over the speakers who have spoken and will speak on this debate, he will find among those lists representatives from southern Ontario, northern Ontario, eastern Ontario, all provinces in Atlantic Canada and from western Canada as well. I think it is wrong of him to leave the impression that the 70 per cent of people-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Another question or comment?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the member for Nepean, and Nepean is the twin riding for Carleton- Gloucester, for an excellent speech and an excellent presentation. My question is this: I feel embarrassed that I am taken as being part of the employer, the federal government, because I sit in Parliament, and this year I have received a 4.3 per cent increase in my salary while the employees, our employees, are getting or will be getting zero per cent. I would prefer that if the employees, the public servants are going to get zero per cent, then I too should get zero per cent.
Unfortunately, this government is imposing two standards on an uneven playing field. I would like the member's comments.

I did mention in my comments the fact that there was no doubt on the government side when it
Government Orders
passed legislation giving us an increase for the year 1991. I think it was less than 4 per cent but it does not make any difference how much we got. Now, all of a sudden it is saying that next year we will have a zero increase.
The question I was asking was: has the minister, when sitting down at the bargaining table, said: "Okay guys, will you take your 3 per cent this year and possibly consider a zero per cent next year?" Has that ever been discussed?
I think we are setting two standards here. There seems to be one set of standards for managers, for senators, for members of Parliament, and another set of standards for the members of PSAC. I think they should be looking at that very, very closely. I do not agree with it and I thank you very much for that wonderful question.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate.
I guess the debate really started back in February when the government brought forward its budget document, and that set the policy of the Government of Canada. Somehow there is a perception that this is all a surprise and that this has only come to fruition in the last couple of weeks.
I would like, if I might, to point out some of the items that were in the budget of February, of this year. I will not read them word for word, but they can be found on page nine. That deals with the government management of a number of its affairs. The first item on that list of eight that are here relates to the fact that the ministerial pay of the Prime Minister and cabinet members will be frozen for one year. I realize that does not get a very high profile in the public debate, but that was the number one item that was mentioned.
The second item that was mentioned deals with the wage budgets of departments. In that particular clause it says that there will be no more money available, but if the Public Service wants to negotiate a salary increase that we would certainly consider up to about three per cent, but any increase would be tied directly to attrition within the Public Service. The jobs that would become vacant through attrition, or people retiring, would not be filled.

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
So there was an opportunity for salary increase if the Public Service would accept that we were going to continue to streamline some government operations.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, we were unable to negotiate that in March, April, May and finally in June. As we are well into the new budget year, we cannot go back and say: "Well we will do that now," but that was part of the management offer that was in the budget.
The next item was, of course, that we would limit the raises in years .two and three to 3 per cent.
Beyond that, it talked about the rates of salary increases for the executive members because there is this concern that the management group is being treated differently. You will see that it says here that these various public servants, deputy ministers and heads of Crown corporations will be limited to a level no higher than the average of the negotiated settlements in the Public Service. There it is, very clear and in black and white, that if we can only negotiate, for example, zero per cent with the Public Service, then that is what everybody gets. It says that right here in the document, but somehow that does not seem to be part of the public discussions.
The next item talks about the salaries for members of Parliament. It very clearly says exactly the same thing, that we will get what the Public Service gets, or the lower of inflation minus 1 per cent or what the Public Service gets. So, based on the program now, the Public Service and MPs will both get zero per cent.
What is not given a lot of profile is that in the budget there is a commitment that we were going to reduce the senior managers in the Public Service by 10 per cent this year. We are proceeding with that. So when people talk about the fact that there is really no cutback for anybody, ask those 10 per cent of the senior managers who are losing their jobs whether there is a cutback there.
Finally, there is a restriction on capital spending and it will be frozen at last year's level.
That started the process of this debate. I can tell you that in my almost three years of being a member of Parliament, I have had the privilege of talking to many of the Public Service employees who serve my constituency and look after the needs of my constituents. I would not for a moment debate the fact that they are under a
tremendous strain and that in many cases they work hard with resources that are limited. In my constituency in Ontario, they are faced with a unique challenge. Here we have the federal government restricting what we are doing with salaries, yet we see the provincial government increasing its salary or wage bill by 14 per cent while we are holding it to zero per cent. The municipalities are increasing their wage bill. The school boards are increasing their wage bill. The regional government is increasing its wage bill. So here they are working in an environment in southern Ontario where all of the other public servants are getting increases and we are not.
That is an unfortunate circumstance and I understand the difficulty that causes them. There is not a simple answer to that situation. I am certainly aware of it, and I hold extreme sympathy, but I guess I can say the same thing, members of Parliament are not getting a salary increase, so I am tying myself to the same thing. I live in the same constituency that they do, so I am faced with that same thing. That is a sacrifice that is there and we just have to carry on with it. It seems that, somehow, that side of the discussion is not as public. I understand their needs, I understand their pressures, but it seems that from the other side there is a total ignoring of the circumstances that we at the federal level find ourselves in.
We end up coming to the circumstance we are now in. We are obviously at an impasse. The Public Service is out on strike for the second time. Why are they out for the second time?
This morning there was a group of public servants who appeared at my constituency office. They were veiy polite, very well-behaved. I certainly cannot be negative about the way they visited my office and the points they made. I talked to them on the phone for about 40 minutes.
I come back to some of the original comments I made, that they are under their particular pressures. Then they throw out such comments as: "Well, the government wastes so much money." I get that comment from a lot of my constituents who really cannot do anything about it. Mr. Speaker, government members who rise keep talking about fiscal restraint. I am wondering if the member could tell us why that fiscal restraint does not apply to independent contractors working for the government who may be performing the same work and who may already be getting paid more for it, as it applies to the people working for the Public Service.

Is he aware that contracts are costing more than the entire payroll of the Pubic Service Alliance? Why does he not think the same restraint should apply to independent contractors?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what budget the member is looking at. The budget I looked at says that this year the total cost of government operations is being restricted to what it was last year.
Within that, if there are outside contractors who have contracts with the government and want to raise their prices, the contractors had to bid to get the job in the first place, which the Public Service does not have to do. Second, once they have the job and the budget says there is no more money, if they have doubled their price something else within the system of government is going to have to be given up to offset that increase in cost.
I can honestly say that in a public tendering process, at least in the part of Canada I live in, things are very competitive. I can assure him that there are no great increases in individual tenders and individual contracts. That is not to say that some are not going up. The same goes for contracting out. If the contracting out price is doubled, then there are half the contracts to issue. It is as simple as that.

The ships are backing up at the ports. There are 42 ships waiting and another 10 coming into the west coast. They cannot deliver our wheat.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association has talked to Canadians and to this government about the devastating impact on Canadian manufacturers, manufacturers who depend on imports from the United States but the bridges are being blocked, manufacturers who are dependent on air travel but cannot count on our airlines today.

Mr. John Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business states: "It is totally incomprehensible that the government would idly stand by and watch while small firms are being put at risk and in some cases thrown into bankruptcy by a breakdown of our system of government. I will just give one example. Last night I was in Willowdale. The chief executive officer of a major corporation had to be in Montreal this morning for an 11 a.m. appointment. He could not trust the airlines. He was driving from his house, leaving at 5.30 in the morning in order to ensure that he could keep that commitment.
The automobile is no substitute for secure air travel in Canada. Businesses need the assurance that they will be able to count on our transportation infrastructure.
With all of these problems that we face, why can I and my party not support this government's back to work legislation? First of all, this started out not as an attempt to deal in an equitable or fair way with our public
servants. It started out as part of the government's political agenda. They looked back to the Reaganesque approach in the United States when President Reagan became a hero among neo-conservative circles by stamping on the air traffic controllers and firing them. This government felt that we have tough times. It would not admit that they were government induced, but we all know we are facing very tough times. It was part of this government's political agenda to beat up on the public servants so they could appear tough and in the eyes of Canadians who are not public servants, gain that political credit that they thought would be theirs for dealing firmly with our public servants.
When it introduced this back to work legislation, it made the Public Service an offer it had to refuse: 0, 3 and 3. They had to refuse that. What did this government do? It brought in its back to work legislation. But we on this side of the House opposed it and Canadians everywhere did not rally to its support. The public will was not there because people across Canada realized that this government was not being fair. It was not being fair to the one group that it was trying to make the scapegoats for the failure of its economic policies.
There were alternatives. From day one, we said: "Do not deal with back to work legislation. Bring in a mediator who can deal in a fair and an objective way with the issues at stake". The government has refused that. It is still refusing it.
There was another solution it could have brought in. It could have levelled with Canadians. It could have said: "Canada, we are in a terrible economic crisis. We have lost 13 per cent of our manufacturing jobs in 2.5 years since January, 1989. Unemployment is going up, it is not going down, in spite of our consideration that the recession is over".
It could have said that we are facing extremely tough times because our ability to compete is falling. It could have said to all Canadians: "We must all cut back. We must all suffer, equitably and fairly. Every Canadian, from the Prime Minister, through the cabinet, through members of Parliament, through the public service and through the business sector and employees must suffer".

our economy. It should have called on all people to bear that burden.

We are not going to have harmony among the sectors, government, business, labour, or between the government as an employer and its own employees. We are not going to have that co-operative effort which is necessary to make us competitive on a global basis.
