Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for his very fine words that are now on the record of this Chamber.
I am particularly impressed with his reference to the state of mind, the demoralization of our public servants today by the Government of Canada.
I was listening to the President of the Treasury Board in this Chamber last night say that regional rates of pay were a good thing. Those were his exact words. That is, paying people different wages for doing the same job depending on where they were working. He made reference to the fact that about 20,000 or 24,000 of our workers in Canada in the general trades and labour end of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the pipe fitters, the plumbers, carpenters and drivers of machinery, are on different wage rates in Canada.
Here in Ontario there is one wage rate if you are working in metropolitan Toronto, and there is another wage rate if you are outside of metropolitan Toronto. If you are doing the same job for the federal government, there is one wage rate if you are working in Vancouver and another wage rate if you are working outside of metropolitan Vancouver. If you are working in Vancouver as a plumber, you get more wages than if you are living outside of Vancouver and working for the federal government as a plumber. But you make less wages if you are working for the federal government in Vancouver as a pipe fitter than you do if you are living outside of Vancouver working as a pipe fitter. The same applies to Toronto.
In other words, for some occupations you receive higher wages if you live in a metropolitan area than if you live outside, and for other occupations you receive more wages if you live outside than if you live inside. This is completely, absolutely ridiculous and does not stand up to reason at all. The minister blamed it on a former government. I have researched this thoroughly and I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the way this started back in the sixties was that it actually started with the union. It was the union that negotiated regional rates with the government of the day. It was, and I can prove it, the union and the government of the day.
What has happened since then? We have gone past the age of enlightenment. We are up to 1991. We have laws in this country on wage rates. This government certainly breaks the law. Yet the President of the Treasury Board stands up in the Chamber and says: "No, no, it is all right, it is great".
The hon. member a few moments ago-and perhaps he could comment further on it-referred to the total destruction of service to the people of Canada by the Government of Canada. In every area, from the mail service to when you walk into an office, there is the total destruction of service. We have public servants who are looking over their shoulder wondering when they are going to get laid off or when some manager way up somewhere is going to receive a bonus for getting rid of them.

The member for Gander-Grand Falls, as usual, has raised a couple of issues which are critical to our dealings with our own employees, our own public servants, and to the fabric of what Canada is about.
First of all, if an employee is always looking over his or her shoulder, worrying if the axe going to fall on their neck next, then it is inhuman to think that that person is going to be able to concentrate on the job and on service. It is just not human nature. They are more worried, and become more worried, about office politics, which is

very, seldom conducive to solid performance and competitiveness.
There is nothing wrong with giving some people some security so that they can throw themselves into their jobs, so they can feel confident about their own future, so that they can invest in their own upgrading, so that they can become part of something that is going to be there a year from now, so that they can contribute on a long term basis. It is this type of morale and spirit that we see in competitive companies around the world.
Take the Japanese, for example. They know that they have jobs for life and they are going to be trained and people are going to work with them to make them more competitive and make them the most competitive in the world. In those circumstances, they are prepared to give because they are part of something and they have security.
Rather than the fear approach in managing your own people, how about the carrot approach? How about the security approach, that we are all part of something and we can make it bigger? That is what is going to produce the high morale and the high efficiency, be it in the private sector or the public sector.
He raised another issue about differential rates of compensation for people inside and outside various geographic regions in this country. This is one of the great Canadian dilemmas. I don't have an answer to that. For example, we know that people living in the north of Canada have very much higher living costs. This is why a number of years ago we brought a northern benefits provision into our Income Tax Act, recognizing that these people living in a particular region had an unfair burden to bear in order to stay Canadian and live there, the cost of fuels and things like this. So we have, over the years, attempted to recognize that there are inequities in our country caused simply by geography, caused simply by the various costs of living.
I am not saying that we have found ways of dealing with those in an equitable and fair manner for all involved. But it is a struggle that we have to go through,
Government Orders
just as we recognize that in the regions in Canada, they may have fewer economic opportunities than in some of the central parts and we have to find ways to give those people security, dignity and meaningful lives.
In conclusion, I think that will be part of the ongoing struggle, through the millennia, of being Canadian. Because we are a sharing people and because we do believe that Canada united is stronger than Canada driven apart, we will make that commitment and that effort to ensure the equity.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls for that question on regional rates. I was most interested that it was a member from Toronto who, in the second part of his answer, gave sort of an answer but did not really come out, perhaps, as fervently for the principle as I was hoping, knowing his interesting background in national and provincial politics. I listened to his speech and have been sitting here all morning in hopes of perhaps contributing a few thoughts to this debate and add another dimension to it.
I was one of the members here when the Public Service Staff Relations Act-1966 was debated in this House of Commons and I am going to refer, if I can catch the Speaker's eye some time during the debate this afternoon, to a few remarks made about what might happen when we embarked on what, at that time, was a pretty brand new blazing precedent in terms of extending this right for public servants.
I have a question for the member who just spoke. I have listened here and have watched on television most of the debate as we have had this on-again, off-again problem, and it is an unfortunate problem. Frankly, as The Citizen said, and almost everyone else outside of Ottawa has said, both parties have tainted fingers on this.
My question is, and I have not heard very many members get into this, does the member sort of equivocate it on regional pay rates? I can understand that, although I am a little disappointed. I would like to ask him what his thought is about the right to strike in the Public Service, as compared to compulsory arbitration.

Government Orders

I don't know what the solution is. I would have to be very honest with you. We cannot afford strikes. We cannot afford strikes in the public sector, we cannot afford strikes in the private sector.
As I put on the record, our record among all those countries I mentioned is abysmal. We are far out of step with international standards in terms of days lost because of strikes and walkouts. Surely we have got to find a way to do it. If the member thinks that by eliminating the right to strike may do it, I am not sure it will.
I think it has to start right at the top, with management. I think it is an attitude. I know when I was an employer in the private sector people could have struck, people could have walked out. If they don't like what you are doing, they just do not perform up to their potential as human beings.
Management has an obligation to provide the conditions under which people can fulfil all of their potential in their work environment. That is not happening, and we have got to find a way to get rid of strikes. To me, it is not a legislative concern as much as it is one of attitude and changing the whole ethos of both the public and private sector in Canada.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Saint-Maurice.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker-

I have a quick point of order, Mr. Speaker, which is very relevant to the present discussion. I am sorry to interrupt my good friend who made an interesting contribution to this debate in second reading. I am certainly looking forward to his contribution at third reading.
Is it correct that as far as I can tell, yesterday's Hansard is not on our desks now because of the strike, that the truck with Hansard is somehow impeded in a traffic jam or is being prevented from coming to the Hill?
With respect, Mr. Speaker, if you do not know the answer, could you kindly get the answer and find out what the devil is going on here?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I understand the question of the hon. member. I have in my hand the Hansard.

I have a copy here of yesterday's Hansard, but it is not bound. We intend to check whether all members will receive copies of Hansard in its usual form. I want to thank the hon. member for drawing the attention of the House to this matter.
Resuming debate. The hon. member for Saint-Maurice.

Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned, my hon. friend from Annapolis Valley-Hants can rise at any time on a point of order because he is a good friend, and I don't mind being interrupted, especially since I had not even started.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak today on third reading of the back-to-work legislation aimed at employees who are members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. Although I have several reasons for wishing to speak to this bill, there is one important point I would like to make for the benefit of Canadians who are listening. After two and half years in the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, I realize that most of the time the House might as well be on another planet, a planet not familiar to Canadians who live on Main Street in Shawinigan, Vancouver, Smiths Falls in Ontario or Gander in Newfoundland.
This place operates on assumptions that have no application in the real world. Earlier, the hon. member for Willowdale made a veiy interesting speech. He mentioned the fact that we in Canada have the worst record for strikes in the Western world. This hardly enviable record is not necessarily the fault of the Government of Canada but of Canadian society as a whole. Consider that Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, the three provinces with the largest populations, have experienced a number of strikes with a very negative impact on the Canadian economy. These strikes were in the primary sector and, more specifically, in the pulp and paper, aluminum and forestry industries.
Our competitive position on international markets has been seriously undermined by these strikes which also occurred in the steel industry and other sectors. Mr. Speaker, I think that someday, we will have to consider doing what other countries have already done: draw up a
October 1, 1991

new social contract, signed by all three economic part-ners-govemments, unions and business.
Although his speech was most interesting, the hon. member for Willowdale finally put the blame on the Government of Canada. Of course, strikes were a serious matter and hurt the economy, but we should let the strike go on and not pass this legislation, not put an end to the strike immediately, because our competitive position- That was not the way to solve our problems.
The Liberal member talked about the concerns of the business community. The funny thing is, Mr. Speaker, the business community brought this subject up last week, when the Quebec division of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association made suggestions to the government of Canada for improving exactly what my Liberal colleague from Willowdale just mentioned, i.e. our competitiveness on the international markets. Canadian manufacturers, responsible for creating jobs in Quebec and in Canada, made a number of recommendations to the government. There are three that I would like to quote if I may, Mr. Speaker.
First, that Canadian manufacturers should continue to invest in modem technologies to increase the productivity of the labour force. I am in agreement with that. Their second recommendation-and my hon. colleague from Willowdale should listen to this-was that all levels of government without any exception-federal, provincial, municipal, school boards, Hydro-Quebec, Hydro-Ontario, B.C. Hydro-would negotiate lower wage settlements to match the overall productivity growth in Canada."
This year, Mr. Speaker, our productivity growth was not great.
The other recommendation the Canadian Manufacturers' Association made was the following: that the governments should try to eliminate the budget deficit and cut back on other funding requirements so as to reduce borrowing by the public sector on financial markets. What does that mean in layman's terms, Mr. Speaker, for the ordinary people across this country who sometimes get the feeling they have landed on another planet? It means, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian savings and foreign capital in Canada are in fact used mainly to
Government Orders
service our national debt instead of financing capital projects needed at the industrial and economic level. This has to be pointed out.
So, manufacturers tell us, and I tend to agree with them, that we have to reduce the deficit and to limit the total payroll in the federal Civil Service, in order to set an example for provinces and businesses. You know what, Mr. Speaker, it works. In four Canadian provinces, our plan for 0, 3, and 3 per cent has been applied, and in a more drastic manner too. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Quebec, unions, even the most militant of them, like the CSN with comrade Gerald Larose, and the Quebec civil servants have agreed to 0 per cent for a six-month period? There was no strike. They did not organize a political strike just to please the New Democrats or the Liberals, who want to knock down the government at any cost. Just wait until the next election, then you can do whatever you want to, but for now, Canada has to work.
Even the unions in the province of Quebec said they did not really like 0 per cent, but still, they sat down with the government and signed an agreement, giving Quebec civil servants 0 per cent.
What happened elsewhere? In some provinces, agreements were signed, then tom by the government who came back offering 0 per cent. In many sectors, Mr. Speaker, that is how things are done. Why? It is quite simple, Mr. Speaker. This year, the budget of the Canadian government will reach $192 billion. I think that is more than enough to ask from Canadian taxpayers. That is enough. I do not think we should add one more cent to federal expenses. I believe Canadian citizens consider that with this amount we should be able to manage. The majority of Canadians think like that, except members of the Liberal Party of Canada and members of the New Democratic Party of Canada.
Some people here are going to say: "You are not serious." But I do have proof of what I am saying, Mr. Speaker. Members on this side of the House had the political will-and God knows how much of it was needed over the last two years-to say no, despite the fact that everybody is asking us for something. In our offices we receive dozens and dozens of organizations asking for grants for this, or financial help for that, but

Government Orders
once in a while we have to say no. And it's not easy as a member of Parliament to have to say no.
The Liberals when they were in government, at the time of Pierre Elliott Tbudeau, said yes to everybody. And the result is the huge deficit that we must bear today and for a long time to come; my children and my grandchildren will continue paying interest on that debt, Mr. Speaker, not to mention paying back the principal.
I was going to say that on this side of the House we decided to put a stop to spending. The time has come to stop throwing money out of the window, but it's not easy to close a wide open system, a system which was spending freely taxpayers' money, and make such a system conform to more reasonable standards. That's what we have been doing for the past seven years, not perfectly, but Liberals were spending 14 per cent more each year, while we were able to limit spending growth to
3.4	per cent per year. You have to say no to thousands and thousands of Canadians, Mr. Speaker, and that is not easy.
And we want to continue on that course. Canadians want us to put a stop to public spending, but here I have, Mr. Speaker, something called the Status of Bills and Motions. For those who don't know what it is, motions are proposals made by members from any party in the House requesting the House to make a decision on a given subject.
In this book, Mr. Speaker, there are hundreds of motions. I was counting them. I think there are 500 or 600. Some are from members of this side of the House, but most come from the New Democratic Party. This is quite strange. I am counting them today, and when I have the final tally, Mr. Speaker, I will bring it to you. It will make good reading for you tonight. I believe that 200 or 300 motions have now been tabled by members of the NDP. About 200 of those motions request new expenses, the creation of new departments as well as new investigating committees, the giving of this for that, the giving of money to so and so, to a group, in short to just about everybody in Canada.
The New Democratic Party is of the opinion that 192 billion dollars a year is not enough. It has found a way to table 200 motions to tell Canadians: Ottawa does not spend enough; it should spend more. Those people have
never understood how the economy works and they want to please everybody. Yes, yes, yes. You want such and such a thing: fine, we will give it to you. We, the Government of Canada, are generous. We will empty the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers, but it is no big deal since we are in the opposition.
What is rather surprising, Mr. Speaker, is that the Liberals, who have been in power long enough, are doing the same thing. They are starting to tell us that right now they are concerned with the deficit. You have noticed that. It is the honourable member for Lasalle- Emard, who lost during the leadership convention of his party. I found that what he had to say was interesting. This is a guy who was saying: indeed, may be it is time to start cutting on the government expenditures. The Liberal grassroots rejected him and chose instead the member for Beausejour as the leader of the party, a person who knows how to spend, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday afternoon, during Oral Questions, the leader of the Opposition, the member for Beausejour, rose. You should have seen his face.
He was mad. He was tense and he was looking at the President of the Treasury Board and pointing his finger at him saying: is it not an awful thing that this government has tolerated 14 days of a strike that affected the Western grain producers and the transport of grains? As he was saying, and I quote: "We are presently losing 30 million dollars a week with this strike. Why, Mr. President of the Treasury Board, have you not included in the essential services the workers that look after the transport and the handling of grains?" Because, if you listen to him, 30 million dollars is a big loss for the economy. We on this side of the House agree that it is indeed a big loss and that is why we are tabling a special Act, because the interest of Canada comes before the right of anyone in this country to strike and that interest is in serious jeopardy.
But what is even worse, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that yesterday the leader of the Opposition had the audacity to criticize the President of the Treasury Board, to say that after two weeks of strike, the situation is now intolerable and that the Canadian economy in the West, as well as the farmers, will be ruined. It just so happens that in 1975 the leader of the Opposition was the President of the Treasury Board and do you know what happened that year Mr. Speaker? There was a strike in

the sector of handling and transport of grains in Western Canada. Look at what the leader of the Opposition did then. It just serves to show that the people across th floor say things but do the opposite. That is the recent history of Canada, the history of recent years. Do you know what he did Mr. Speaker? He tolerated the strike by western grain handlers, who are civil servants, not for a period of 14 days like us who have tabled a bill more than seven days ago, not for a week, two weeks or even three weeks, Mr. Speaker, but for 31 days!
And do you know what he did to solve the problem? He gave an additional one percent raise to the strikers, who were civil servants working in the grain sector, one percent more than what they were asking for. Do you know what these civil servants were asking then? Brace yourself. They wanted, over a period of two years, a 28.4 per cent raise Mr. Speaker. So the President of the Treasury Board said: Listen, you have been on strike for 31 days, you have lost money. It does not make sense; we will give you 29.4 per cent over a period of two years.
And do you know what the then President of the Treasury Board said at the time, that is on March 19 1975? He said, and I quote because I want it to be clear that those are not my words: "In my opinion it is a good agreement. The population will understand, I hope, that it is sometimes necessary to suffer because of a small strike that lasted 31 days." It is the leader of the Opposition who, yesterday, made a tantrum in the House to show that he, and he was talking loud, loved the Rockies and that he wanted to protect the farmers of Western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, how can we give the least bit of credibility to the people across the floor when they make such speeches? They do one thing one year and they preach exactly the opposite. They try to win on both sides.
Mr. Speaker, as is the case for the honourable member for Carleton-Gloucester, there are many civil servants in my riding. I have met them and they are not pleased with the government. They are not pleased and it is understandable. It is understandable that they are not happy given the kind of things they hear in this House and the fact that they do not get the full picture. That is the reason why an ad was published in the weekend newspapers to explain the government offers.
Government Orders
A lump sum of 500 dollars was offered to the lowest paid civil servants. Do you know what Darryl Bean said? He said: "It's a slap in the face". Mr. Speaker, some people in the riding of Saint-Maurice, who live in Saint-Mathieu du Parc, in Saint-Boniface and in Saint-Georges de Champlain, would be quite happy to get slapped in the face by the federal government with a 500 dollar cheque.
Do you see the problem, Mr. Speaker? I agree that the federal civil servants should be well treated, but I think that they should also be made aware of what the reality is. They are entitled to a free dental plan paid almost entirely by the Canadian government. They are entitled to retirement pensions that are fully indexed to the cost of living. I believe those are very important benefits in many other provincial economic sectors. I will end by talking about pay equity.
Pay equity refers, among other things, to the money that was given to women who were earning less than men last year. The NDP members tell us that we do not make any sense. Yet, to ensure fair treatment to the women that are in the public service, last year the federal government took money in the pockets of Canadian taxpayers-it took 317 million dollars-and redistributed that money to ensure pay equity for women. This year, we are adding another 81 million dollars. The people across the floor are still complaining. When are we going to stop, Mr. Speaker?
In my riding, there are people-Revenue Canada employees-who, last year, received 2,000 dollar cheques at Christmas. They got a 2,000 dollar cheque because of pay equity. Yet, those people are still not happy. The NDP members are telling us in their 200 motions:

The government should spend billions and billions and billions of dollars more money, more taxes for Canadians. The Liberals are saying the same thing.

I will conclude on that note. It is urgent, in the national interest, to stop making great patriotic speeches about the country and to act in the interest of Canada. We must pass this legislation. We must give leadership to Canadians and make sure that the Public Service of Canada is at the service of all Canadians.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, in his speech the member spoke about the motions and the fact that there were a number of motions from the New Democratic Party. He said that these are the types of motions that would cost the taxpayers money. However he did not refer to some of the motions that I have put.
One of mine calls for a prohibition of promises during election campaigns. I wonder, if the government is so concerned about saving money, would it stop making promises just prior to Saskatchewan and B.C. elections? I wonder if the member from the province of Quebec who has been in the House for a while now can explain exactly how much his government spent trying to secure the by-election in Lac-Saint-Jean.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, the promises made during an election campaign and the reality of a government are not always to our liking. The NDP cannot use that technique since Bob Rae has become the Premier of Ontario. The NDP can no longer tell us what to do.
You talk about the honourable member for Lac-Saint-Jean and that is another matter. The money that was spent in that riding has been increased. That could be re-evaluated.
This could lead to a lengthy debate and I am prepared to get to the bottom of this with my hon. colleague from Churchill. We should also refrain from constant suggestions that something always happens at election time, whether provincial or by-elections.
What is important today is that the Canadian economy as well as the economic recovery are threatened by the federal public service strike now entering its third week. Yesterday, activities in the port of Vancouver were at a standstill. In Dorval, nails were spread over the road causing hundreds of flats. Nurses at the Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue hospital, a veterans hospital, were prevented- were assaulted. They had tomatoes and I do not know what else thrown at them. Essential services regulations were violated.
I can still hear the member for Shefford talking nonsense. Maybe he should tell us what he really thinks of all this. Last week, one Bloc Quebecois member was for it and another one was against. One day, the member for Shefford-as regards the member for Hull, it is quite another matter-is a member of the Liberal Party of Canada. The next thing you know, he has made an about-turn because the wind has changed. He resigned from that party and turned sovereigntist after losing the leadership race. He actually joined the Bloc Quebecois while still a member of the Liberal Party of Canada. He then joined the Quebec Liberal Party. Tomorrow, he may join the Parti Quebecois. We have no lesson to learn from the worse political flopper in the history of the Canadian Parliament.
This government is responsible and dependable. It is not easy to act under the present circumstances but we wanted to set an example for all the people of Canada. We will continue to do so and to denounce acts of violence occurring on the picket lines. I am sure that what concerns the Canadian people is to have a government that actually takes on its responsibilities. The Canadian people know better than that. They have come to the conclusion that they will pass judgement on this government in due time, but, for the time being, they will let it govern. That is how things work. So, let it be no attempt to overthrow the government like the present one as the members of the NDP are attempting to do.

Mr. Speaker, as I listened to this muddled speech, I thought it clearly reflected the state of panic of the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. A few days before the Bloc Quebecois was established in Saint-Maurice, the hon. member panicked. He comes down hard on public servants but earlier criticized the hon. member for Beausejour for having said this or that a few years ago. At the same time he was proud of the number of public servants he had in his riding. In fact, he failed to give credit where credit is due, and although it is not my intention to defend the hon. member for Beausejour, I think the hon. member seems to have forgotten why there are so many public servants in his riding in the first place.
My point is that we have no trouble with our position. As individual members, we are free to express our views. We are not stuck with a party like his, where whenever his leader rises to support a measure, the hon. member

for Saint-Maurice, who has never shown any personal initiative, votes with his government and jumps when he is told to jump. That is what he has done so far.
They say jump, and he jumps.
We in the Bloc Quebecois can make up our own minds and make our own decisions.
Enlightened decisions.

In this instance, I can inform the hon. member that we intend to vote against his bill because it ignores collective bargaining traditions in this country. It is pure provocation, no less. This government is so panicky that, now it is down to 12 per cent in the polls, it is prepared to attack its own public servants to give the impression it is doing its job. Unfortunately, provocation is no way to run a country. The hon. member for Saint-Maurice should be ashamed to be a party to this provocation, just to score a few political points that will have no impact at all.
Today is a sad day for the labour movement. It is a sad day for government responsibility, because this government wanted to use public servants to try and score political points. Unfortunately, Canadians have seen through this ploy, and that is why the government is still down there in the polls.

As usual, the hon. member for the Bloc Quebecois did not speak to the substance of the matter. They have a one-track mind. They get up in the morning and look at the polls. They do the same when they go to bed at night. They don't do anything else.
Mr. Speaker, we ignore the polls. We run the country. It isn't easy to get along with people like that, but we will manage. What I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, is that when I rise in this House it is, unlike the hon. member for Shefford, to defend the interests of Quebec and Canada. He can no longer say that. He is trying to defend the federal public servants. What is he doing in this debate? What is he doing in the House of Commons? We can ask ourselves this question. I do know however, Mr. Speaker, that in Quebec the government has imposed a zero per cent raise for 6 months to its public servants and unions accepted it! There was a social consensus. Why don't we have that here? Why are members of the Bloc Quebecois not supporting the government? It's quite
Government Orders
simple, Mr. Speaker, it's because these people want trouble for the country, they do everything they can to make things go wrong and this is why, we have to denounce members of the Bloc Quebecois who are totally incapable of assuming their responsibilities in this House. As far as politics are concerned we will meet again in two years, we will meet in Shefford, people in Grandby will have every opportunity to reward the hon. member for Shefford.
I will conclude Mr. Speaker, if you don't mind, by saying that our wage and non-monetary offers to public servants are among the best in this country. What more do they want? They have the best pension plans there are, they have the best dental plan there is. Compare that to what the provinces have, you can't fool people all the time. They know that public servants are not about to starve, that we are not about to flog them! There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that we would like to give more to our civil servants, but there is a fiscal reality. We have $192 billion at our disposal and I don't think we can spend as much as members from the NDP or the Liberal Party of Canada are asking us to do.
It is about time we put an end to the profligacy and we ask opposition members to come back on earth and stop living with their heads in the clouds.

Mr. Speaker, I asked one of the members who spoke previously if he knew how much the government had spent in the riding of Lac-Saint-Jean just prior to the by-election which eventually elected the new leader of the Bloc Quebecois.
I think it is an interesting point because if that money had been offered to the Public Service workers who are on strike right now, there would not be a strike in Canada. All the speeches by government ministers and government members, talking about the need for restraint, ignore their own practices.
If there is a by-election it wants to win for one of the Prime Minister's former friends, then it has the money. If there is a provincial election in Saskatchewan, then it has the money. If there is an impending election in B.C., then it has the money. Prior to the 1988 election, which elected some of those members, the government had all the money it could find and tried to spend it.

If you want to talk about honesty, then give the complete picture. This government has had a terrible history. In 1985 it attacked the pensioners. It said that they were the cause of inflation, that they had to give up some of their pensions. Later it attacked those receiving the family allowance. Now it is attacking government workers.
Yet every time the Prime Minister has somebody he wants to help, some contract, then the money can be found.
We have seen so much government waste, but that is not what we are dealing with here. There are all sorts of topics and areas where there is government waste, but that is not what we are debating.
The entire cost of giving those people who are on strike a wage increase equal to the cost of inflation is about $300 million. This government makes promises of that amount without any tendering process, without any consultation, without any consideration or regional development, without any figuring out of how it affects other companies that are competing in that same field. That money is found and it is found for political reasons.
For members of the Conservative Party to get up now and say that we cannot afford to give our employees an increase equal to the cost of inflation is denying what they do on a daily basis. If the main goal of the government is to attack the deficit, then it should come forward with a package that takes away some of the arbitrary rights to mismanage our future. That is what is costing us money. To say that someone in the city of Brandon, where I was last week, earning $23,000 or $24,000, is causing the inflation in this country, that she is responsible for the debt and the deficit in this country is simply not true.
What these government members in their vehemence have ignored is that the person I am talking about in the city of Brandon was not a militant. She was not someone who said she had to stand up to this government, she was someone forced into that situation. This person listens to Conservative backbenchers and ministers get up in this House and attack her. That is what they do. They do it with vehemence. How can you expect those employees of the federal government to sit back and take it.
All of us reject the use of violence whether it is on the picket line or elsewhere. But one of the things I have noticed in this debate is that there is all sorts of concern about violence that occurs on the picket line-and I share that concern-but there is all sorts of concern about the number of days that are lost during strikes and lockouts. Let me make one point, Mr. Speaker. Those members are not concerned when five times as many people are off work because of sickness and death in the workplace every year as there is because of strikes and lockouts.
I recognize it is two o'clock and if I may, at three o'clock, finish my speech.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to rise in the House of Commons today to commemorate the 50th anniversary of Dorval Airport in my riding.

Who among us, in deed what Canadian has not heard of Dorval airport, a most important national and international centre?
This airport facility makes an invaluable contribution especially for the residents of Lachine-Lac-Saint-Louis.

Mayor Yeomans of Dorval has indicated that the economic contribution of Dorval Airport to the region is second only to the economic impact of the arrival of Jacques Cartier. For 50 years Dorval Airport has provided the Montreal community with an efficient, convenient, and accessible transport centre for all air travellers.
Congratulations, Dorval, and here's to 50 more years of growth and achievement.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no tragedy is more serious than the one that affects thousands of children every day throughout the world.
Each day, some 40,000 of them die of hunger and diseases related to adequate nutrition and a lack of hygiene. Thousands more are subjected to slavery, exploitation and prostitution at ridiculously low rates, to operate of markets and systems that can only be termed criminal.
It is a world crisis that is just as unacceptable and urgent as war and the devastation of our environment.
Last year, 71 international leaders met at the World Summit for Children. They made a commitment to cut infant mortality by one third to reduce malnutrition by 50 per cent and to provide access to drinking water for everybody by the year 2000.
Mr. Speaker, these goals are attainable, but the political will must be present. Our political leaders must take their commitments to heart. On this first anniversary of the World Summit for Children, I urge our government to keep to its promises!

Mr. Speaker, October is breast cancer awareness month in the U.S., but not in Canada. One in 10 women in this country will face breast cancer in her lifetime. Breast cancer is a disease that maims and kills women in huge numbers. Some research has been done through breast screening programs and programs to teach women selfexamination, but it is a disease for which funding for preventive research is sadly limited.
Let me give you an example. For each person who dies of AIDS, $365,000 will have been spent on preventive research. For every woman who dies of breast cancer, only $882 will have been spent on preventive research.
This is not meant to suggest that research should not be done on AIDS, but to illustrate how inadequate the funding for breast cancer research really is. Every woman is at risk and Canadian women deserve better.
Declaring October breast cancer awareness month would be one small way for this government to recognize the seriousness of breast cancer and to renew its commitment to breast cancer research.

Mr. Speaker, 102,000 British pensioners living in Canada are being discriminated against by the British Parliament to the tune of some 104 million pounds.
Britain indexes pensions owed to its former residents and workers who live in the United States and 31 other countries, but not Canada. This is like a mother disinheriting her own children by giving away the family jewels to the neighbours. Surely Britain, which played such a significant role in Canada's history, should not deny its former residents benefits they have earned.
I urge the government to encourage the British Parliament to have pity on British pensioners living in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations' survey on human development ranks Canada as the second best country in the world in which to live.
I believe we can be number one. Increased prosperity for all our citizens will become a reality as Canada becomes more competitive. Tbgether we must foster a learning culture in Canada. We must encourage and invest in research and development, in science and technology. We must invest in our country and its resources. We must promote a more competitive domestic market by reducing and eliminating provincial trade barriers. We must expand our pursuit of every available trade opportunity.
We have been blessed in this country with many competitive advantages; strategic geography, rich natural

resources and natural trade markets. Let us build on these advantages and let us make Canada number one.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the economy is taking a toll on our children. In the past year, there has been a 50 per cent increase in the number of children in this region who are on general welfare. It is estimated that 7,708 children are receiving family benefits. This is an increase of close to 17 per cent over the same period last year.
These numbers do not include the children of the working poor who, while not receiving benefits, are struggling to make ends meet.
The same report indicates that the general welfare caseload rose more than 45 per cent over the pass 12 months. The government continues to ignore the suffering. It has yet to fulfil its commitment to alleviating child poverty by bringing into force the convention on the rights of the child.
The government was quick to place a cap on its Canada Assistance Plan contributions which pay for the above mentioned welfare programs.
I ask this government; when will it finally act to end the suffering of our children?

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to inform you today of an environmental program that was launched in Repentigny, the largest municipality in my riding.
In announcing its selective garbage collection project, Repentigny set a precedent among Canadian municipalities. Mr. Speaker, under this program, a contribution of 25 cents per week per owner will create a capital fund whereby this city can initiate environmental projects- innovative and rewarding environmental protection initiatives.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to point out the work done by the mayor of Repentigny, Jacques Dupuis, the committee chairman, Florian Chartrand, and all those responsible for this program, namely the residents of Repentigny, who demonstrate in a concrete way their desire to preserve the environment. I call on all Canadian municipalities to follow the example of Repentigny, because, Mr. Speaker, the environment is everyone's business.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday over 4,000 farmers rallied in Rosetown, Saskatchewan to protest the lack of action by the government in the farm financial crisis.
Last year the government cut support programs for Canadian farmers by $1.3 billion when grain prices were falling to their lowest level in a generation. Last winter the government committed to providing over $1 billion in emergency transitional assistance to the new safety net system. However, none of this money has been paid yet.
The situation is desperate this fall because the government has not provided the cash it promised last winter and still only gives vague promises about help this winter. It is another smoke and mirrors show, just like the Minister of Agriculture's visit to the Rosetown rally yesterday. He slipped in the back door and sneaked out the side door. He did not speak to the farmers and practically no one even knew he was in the arena. Then he announced on television last night that there would be no new help for Canadian farmers, farmers losing their farms, homes and livelihood.
I call on the government to stop this smoke and mirrors show, to stop the stonewalling and to provide the emergency assistance it promised last winter.

Mr. Speaker, my statement is about the House of Commons legislative committee on Bill C-17 concerning gun control. The Conservative Whip has appointed himself to this committee. That is very unusual! On top of that, he has used his power to appoint other members who, like
October 1, 1991

him, want to weaken the proposed legislation. He has hijacked the committee.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Whip has hijacked the gun committee. The minister is going to lose her bill on arms control at a time when a majority of Canadians want effective gun control. The minister and the Prime Minister had better wake up and crack the whip on the Whip.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 7, 1991, the people of Haiti celebrated cheerfully as father Jean-Bertrand Aristide was elected president with 70 per cent of popular votes. With him a duly elected government was finally in place, following a series of dictatorial regimes, which would lead Haiti toward democracy. Seven months have gone by, during which the people of Haiti have had a taste of freedom and social justice. Now, Mr. Speaker, soldiers have broken the constitutional order by instigating a coup to overthrow the first duly elected government of that country since 1804.
As a friend of the Haitian people, I object most strongly to this coup which is likely to throw the country in complete chaos. I congratulate my government for having vigorously condemned from the very beginning this putsch which will bring nothing but tears to this noble and courageous people.

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations General Assembly has designated October 1 as the International Seniors Day. It is an opportunity for the people of Canada and other nations all over the world to reflect on the actual and potential contributions of elders to their society. It also creates an awareness of an obvious demographic phenomenon, that is population ageing.
By appointing a Minister of State for Seniors in 1987 and implementing in 1988 a strategy for seniors, this government clearly showed its commitment to the needs and concerns of seniors in Canada.

I would wish, Mr. Speaker, that all my colleagues in the House would join me in wishing our senior citizens a very happy day.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Conference Board of Canada forecast unemployment across Canada will remain above 10 per cent for the rest of 1991 and for the next year as well. Jobs are going to be hard to find over the coming year says the board.
In my province of Prince Edward Island, where unemployment is closer to 16 per cent, for some people it is impossible to find a job. Their future is bleak. There are small businesses which cannot make their bank payments. There are farmers who face bankruptcy. In fact, Statistics Canada recently reported a 14 per cent increase in bankruptcies in Atlantic Canada in August. The reason is this government's economic policies. High interest rates, high taxes, a high dollar are combining to make 1991 one of the worst years on record for Islanders.
I call on the government to bring in some economic policies that will produce some much needed prosperity. Atlantic Canadians are waiting.

Mr. Speaker, at the request of the Vancouver School Board, the B.C. ombudsman has begun an investigation into whether the rights of children, particularly the right to an education, are being denied because they are hungry.
School boards in Vancouver, Victoria, Burnaby and Surrey are being forced to feed hungry children, without the promised assistance from the provincial government of British Columbia.
The request for an investigation cites several articles from the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, including Article 27.1 which states that it is the right of every child to a standard of living adequate for the child's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development.

October 1, 1991
Oral Questions
The time has long since passed for the federal government to ratify the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and to take steps to ensure that no child in Canada is denied an education because of hunger.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intended to make a statement on Canadian unity today, but after what I said in the House last night about the Public Service strike, my riding office was besieged by more than 200 strikers who came to criticize my speech and demand the right to free bargaining and an independent mediator.
The government showed it was willing to reach an agreement last week when it improved its offer to the union. Unfortunately, the union left the bargaining table without bothering to respond. It preferred to respond by going back on strike, by preventing this country's essential services from functioning properly, by blockading bridges like they did this morning, and by preventing workers from going to work. The union is not getting the sympathy of Canadians.
What I have to say to all public servants in my riding in Laval-Est and across the country is this: Let's be realistic; the measures the government announced are not a personal attack on you as union members, because you deserve far better. The purpose of these measures is to ensure that all Canadians take part in a wage restraint program that will bring greater prosperity to this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am against violence, and I will never give in to intimidation and blackmail.

our goal, that is our objective and it is quite clear that we are on track in terms of achieving both.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Rosetown, Saskatchewan, 3,000 fanners, victims of the high dollar policy of this government, were asking for help. The Minister of Agriculture said a flat no, no emergency assistance for them at all at this moment.
Since 1986, the time that the Minister of Finance was Minister of Agriculture, in Saskatchewan alone two families leave the farm for good every day of the week. I want to know from the minister what the government intends to do. These people want to stay on the farm. They want to be productive. They want to contribute to the wealth of the country, and the government does not want to help them this time, this year when they need money.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. member that I was in Rosetown yesterday, along with my colleagues from this side of the House and along with colleagues from the other side of the House.
I think the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre would have been welcomed there. I think what my hon. colleague across the aisle should understand is that since 1984 this government has increased three times the assistance to grains and oilseeds by the administration that he was part of. He knows very well, as do members on the other side, that the problem today is the stupidity of a price war between the European community and the United States. This government has taken steps in the past to protect farmers, to maintain farmers' integrity, and we continue to do that.
There has been no Prime Minister in the country at any time who has paid more attention or contributed more to stability, and this government will continue to do it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same minister who does not appear to appreciate the frustration felt by farmers. His
stonewalling on this issue of emergency assistance adds to that frustration.
The government's own committee on third line of defence feels frustrated and has urged the government to deal with the shortfall on the last crop year.
When will the government honour its commitment to farmers and provide the emergency assistance they so badly need?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows-and I must say he was missed at Rosetown-this government put forward some $400 million last year, in 1990. It put forward some $650 million additional in the FSAM program this year.
However, I draw to the hon. member's attention that he is talking about the shortfall in 1991. I think if he reads the conclusion put forward by Prairie Pools Incorporated, he will see that this crisis has been caused not by Canadian farmers but by the unfair trading actions of the United States and the European community. The real solution to the problem lies with a GATT agreement, which will restore some order to the international market. That is not going to happen in the short term. We know that, and that is why we have been supporting farmers since 1984 and will continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, we missed the minister in Miami and in Brandon as well.
I have a question for the same minister. The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds has suggested that farmers dump their wheat at BMW dealerships in protest against what the Europeans are doing.
By the same token, why do they not do the same thing at Ford dealership or Cadillac dealership? The Americans are perhaps doing even worse to our farmers than what the Europeans have done.
Why is the minister not addressing this particular issue? The Americans are hurting our farmers.

which is also a very high quality product, at tariffs of up to 200 per cent.

Take them on, Charlie.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The Public Service strike is continuing. The anger and sense of despair at the lack of respect this government has shown its own workers are mounting.
During the 1984 election the Prime Minister made a personal commitment to the women of Canada on pay equity. He reiterated that commitment in 1988. Pay equity has been the law in Canada since 1977.
I want to ask the Prime Minister why he does not show the good faith of his government, keep his commitment to the women of Canada and enact the legislation now on pay equity.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the hon. member because indeed it is this government that has implemented pay equity, the largest pay equity settlement that has ever been made, $370 million.
If we take the example of a secretary, over the past few years as a result of that pay equity settlement she has received an additional $7,000. This year, in addition to her salary, she will receive another $1,289 and, if she still is earning less than $27,000, she will receive another $500.
This government is without comparison in terms of our commitment and our action on pay equity.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the Prime Minister. It is clear that the government and the Prime Minister do not respect the commitment made to Canadian women, because the Human Rights Commission has said that the government's action on this problem are inadequate. Therefore, I ask the Prime Minister again: Why does the government not just implement the legislation now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):

Mr. Speaker, let me again say to the hon. member that indeed this government has implemented pay equity legislation.
There are 73,400 government employees who are benefitting from that pay legislation, and $81 million will be paid out this year in pay equity payments, primarily to women in the Public Service.
We will continue to work on pay equity legislation, but to the average employee, the clerk or the secretary who has benefitted from pay equity, I think we have shown that commitment and we will continue to show that commitment.

The pay equity settlement by the government has been inadequate. The conciliation board has said that. The Human Rights Commission has said that and I am sure the Minister responsible for the Status of Women is truly aware of that as well.
It could take up to a week, since the back-to-work legislation goes to the Senate, before this dispute will be settled. In the interest of the people of Canada, in the interest of showing respect for the workers of this government, I want to say to the Prime Minister that rather than bring in the riot troops, rather than bring in helicopters, rather than bring in newspaper ads, why does the Prime Minister not-

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of External Affairs. Canadians support the government's condemnation of the coup in Haiti, but we are concerned about the violence in the capital. More than 130 people have already died in that country. What measures will the government take to ensure the safety of the thousands of Canadians in that country? Will he ask the international community to intervene in order to restore democracy in Haiti?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Canadian people, the government and all the members of this House were shocked and disappointed for the Haitian people who are once again the victims of a coup. We reacted very firmly. Yesterday, my colleague, the Secretary of State, told our permanent representative at the OAS to consider with the permanent committee the

possibility of OAS members taking action to help the people of Haiti. As well, a message was sent to the Secretary General of the United Nations, through our ambassador, asking him to see what measures could be taken by the UN to support the Haitian people.

Mr. Speaker, as I said, we support the position taken by the government as regards to the coup.

I have a question for the Prime Minister. In his speech at Stanford he said that the time has come in which the advancement and promotion of human rights must overtake considerations of national sovereignty.
In that case, should Canada now be asking the Security Council of the United Nations or the governing council of the OAS for direct intervention into Haiti to protect human rights and to restore democracy?
We are not asking for just a cancellation today, but direct intervention on the principle that the Prime Minister announced on Sunday.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister has just indicated, the illegal and undemocratic action taken in Haiti is one that the government, and I am sure Parliament of Canada, views not only with alarm but with horror. Once again the people of Haiti have been deprived of their fundamental human rights. The minister, in consequence, has announced our intention to sever all relations in terms of aid with Haiti.
Last night I received a call from President Carlos Andres Perez of Venezuela with whom we were in touch in respect of arranging for the removal of President Aristide from Haiti. We also discussed the possibility of some of the matters raised by my hon. friend.
In this hemisphere where democracy has flourished in a remarkable way particularly over the last 10 or 15 years, it has become completely unacceptable that the island of

Haiti remains an island of repression, violence and human degradation.
Canada, working through the OAS and the United Nations, has brought this to the attention of both last night and this morning. We will be asking all members of the House to support the government in an initiative to ensure the liberation of Haiti and the restoration of the duly elected, democratically elected president of the Republic of Haiti.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board.
The minister was quick to do an about-face and promised that the government's well-placed friends who earn hundreds of thousands of dollars a year would not receive an extravagant $80,000 bonus. Since the minister refused to include these bonuses in his wage-freeze bill yesterday, when will he present some document in which he keeps his promises not to give gifts to the government's highly paid friends?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)

The problem of putting such things in legislation is that we have a whole series of bonuses provided for by law. For example, the bilingual bonus-we do not want to touch that. There are bonuses for officers on ships and shift premiums.
So we preferred to make a solemn commitment and will follow it up with an order in council: no salary increase for employees, managers, the Prime Minister, heads of corporations and others, and no performance bonus is to be given this year.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question on this matter of national interest is addressed to the Prime Minister.
Canadians are proud of our history of settling issues calmly and reasonably, not by confrontation, and today is the last chance for the government to show responsible leadership and settle its disputes with the Public Service the Canadian way.
Will the Prime Minister please explain why even now his government refuses to take the chance that a clear, impartial, mediator can bring a reasonable settlement to this dispute?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Canadian truckers cannot continue to live on empty promises, endless meetings and continued studies as they have for close to two years.
Now that the minister has broken yet another promise, namely to provide an assistance package for truckers by the end of September, when will the government finally provide the necessary federal assistance package for our Canadian industry? Or is the government merely involved in a fruitless public relations exercise again?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that we have made good on our commitment to the task force members. We have met with them on a number of occasions. They have developed with us an assistance package. We took these initiatives to a meeting a couple of weeks ago with the ministers of transportation from the provinces.

Everyone understands that the major portion of the trucking problems do not rest with the Government of Canada, but rests in the provincial legislatures. The tax on fuel is enormous and the action will have to be taken in the legislatures of the provinces.

Rather than always casting the blame on the provinces and only looking at the price of fuel, which is only one factor, why will this government not modify and reform its own exclusive federal regulations which impact on trucking and therefore provide a national solution to what clearly is a national industry in need of support?

I believe the measures we have taken have helped the trucking industry considerably, and we will continue to co-operate with this sector.
The hon. member for York South- Weston.

Security Intelligence Service, the RCMP, officials at Transport Canada and ministers of the cabinet?

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my regret at the loss of one of Canada's most respected public figures, former Supreme Court of Canada Judge Jean Beetz, who died yesterday.
Born in Montreal in 1927, the Hon. Jean Beetz had a long and distinguished career in both the academic and legal worlds. He was for many years a Professor of Law at the University of Montreal where he became dean of the faculty. His expertise in constitutional law led to his appointment as Special Counsel to the Prime Minister for Constitutional Affairs, a position he held from 1968 to 1971. In this capacity he was a key player in the constitutional negotiations of those years.

His appointment as judge of the Quebec Court of Appeal was soon followed by his appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1974. In the 14 years that followed, he wrote landmark judgments that reflected his profound knowledge and experience of civil and constitutional law.

He was known and admired not only for the acumen of his judgments, but for his courteous and gentlemanly bearing. Throughout his years on the court he remained accessible and ever-ready to share with his legal and judicial colleagues, young and old, his vast fund of learning. Those who knew him will readily acknowledge his many kindnesses.
His loss will be felt deeply, not only by the legal profession but, indeed, by all Canadians.

subsubtopic: FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we cast our memories back to that day. We can recall indeed a very long day. While you were elected during the sitting of September 30, 1986, this election took 13 ballots.
Thirteen is not such an unlucky number after all. In fact you were proclaimed elected at 1.30 in the morning of October 1. That was indeed a remarkable occasion. It is the first time that this House ever elected its Speaker by secret ballot. What was more notable was the meaning of this election to you as an individual.
A little more than a year earlier you had suffered a cruel political setback. You had the courage and strength of character to look misfortune in the eye. As it happened, misfortune blinked.
In the judgment of your peers, you were found to be the one whose integrity and fortitude they considered so impeccable that they chose you as the impartial adjudicator of their proceedings and the prime protector of their rights.
Five years as Speaker is a very long time. Of the 32 Speakers since Confederation you are only the seventh to serve that long. By the end of this coming January you will be the fourth longest serving Speaker of this House.
Privilege
Mr. Speaker, there must have been times in the last five years that you wondered what you were doing in the Chair. It is a tribute, Sir, perhaps to your even-handedness, that from time to time some of the rest of us have wondered the same thing.
That of course, Mr. Speaker, is the whole point. It falls upon you to attempt to moderate a process that by its very nature must at times become extremely immoderate. You are not a judge or a magistrate; you are merely one of our peers. It is from that fact, however, that you derive your authority. You are the one in whom 294 of your colleagues have placed their trust. This is a trust that has to be renewed, not just at the beginning of a Parliament but each and every day.
Today is the 1,827th day on which that trust has been renewed and I hope there will be many more to come. The late Lester B. Pearson, in nominating a former Speaker, described his qualities in the words of Socrates, and I quote: "To hear courteously, to answer wisely, to consider soberly and to decide impartially".
For five years, Mr. Speaker, this House has benefitted from your meeting this criteria. We look forward to many more years.

Mr. Speaker, when I started my speech prior to the noon hour I had talked about the fact that this government has spent millions upon millions of dollars trying to gain political favour with Canadians. This occurs usually just prior to an election, and I gave the example of the member for Lac-Saint-Jean in a by-election where I believe the federal government committed itself to approximately $100 million in that one by-election.
I would like to point out to the people who are listening that the amount that the Prime Minister and this cabinet found in order to try and win that one by-election would have given every person on strike on Canada today a 2 per cent increase in salary.
I also pointed out other examples of how prior to elections, whether it be in Saskatchewan or B.C., or during those elections as well, the federal government has found money. In the six months prior to the 1988 federal election, this government, which was so concerned about restraint that it wanted to cut back the old age pensions and was cutting back other programs that were necessary for post-secondary education and medicare, spent hundreds upon hundreds of millions of dollars which at that time it could afford.
I reject the argument that is made by this government that it is out here to fight the deficit. It has proven time after time after time that when it comes to its own political advantage it will spend the taxpayers' money. However when it comes to those receiving the old age pension, to those receiving family allowances, to those who need to have a post-secondary education, to those who need medical assistance, this government does not have the same considerations.
I was in my own riding last week in a native community called Lac Brochet, a community for which this federal government has responsibility. The school children in that community have been waiting 19 years to have a permanent school built. They do not even have trailers but have makeshift classrooms in a part of the country where the temperature goes to 40 and 50 degrees below zero. Kids are walking outside, going from one class to the next class. That same community was told that they would have to wait another six years before they got a permanent school-in total almost 26 years before a school will be built. The government does not have money for that, but it certainly has money for its political objectives.
Today when I look at this legislation and realize how little it would cost to give these workers a reasonable pay increase, I know that this government is playing politics with the government employees. It could have paid for that increase with the promises it made in the last federal election. As I pointed out earlier, what it spent to buy one by-election would have given each and every employee a 2 per cent increase. The way it has fought against pay equity, the way it has fought against any system of classification of its employees, the way it has refused to have a mediator come in to try and resolve this dispute, the way it has rejected conciliation boards that have called upon this government to negotiate pay equity, the way it rejected negotiating anything until the

Public Service Staff Relations Board's ruling, indicates a government that did not make any serious effort to try and negotiate this settlement.
This was a politically motivated strike and it was motivated by this government.
Earlier in Question Period today, the President of the Treasury Board said that he was not going to appoint a mediator because he was not going to react to the illegal activities of some members of the Public Service Alliance.
The Public Service was asking for a mediator before this strike started. The Public Service was asking for a mediator before the government was found in contempt of its own laws by the Public Service Staff Relations Board.
The Public Service Alliance was asking for a mediator once the government was found guilty by its own quasi-judicial board. This is not a new request but the government has refused to respect the laws of this land and to negotiate fairly.
Others got up earlier and said: "There has got to be a better way of resolving disputes." There are other ways of resolving disputes but the government in its throne speech and the President of the Treasury Board in his speeches in the House in May and June indicated that they would not accept those other routes.
They said: "If there is an arbitration board that comes down and gives the workers too much, we are going to rule it back. If they negotiate a settlement which does not give the workers zero per cent, we are going to legislate that back".
They refused a mediator. They refused to listen to the conciliation board. They refused to use arbitration. They forced this strike on Canadians. It may have been done for political purposes, but it was a stupid move by this government. It was an uncaring move.
I have been on the picket lines talking to some of those people, and not just in the Ottawa region. Just last week I was in Brandon, Manitoba talking to fairly young people who had never been on strike before, people who do not earn a large salary. They have heard what government ministers and government members have said in this House of Commons. They know that they are being treated with not only words of contempt, but

contempt in the thoughts and minds of those government members.
They know that they are not given any self-respect. They know that this government has been vehement in its attack on the Public Service, individually and collectively.
Mr. Speaker, you cannot have the President of the Treasury Board and the government House leader attacking workers and expect them to sit and respect this government. You cannot have this government saying that the work that these people do is not necessary and expect those people to respect this government. You cannot have, as I heard today in Question Period when somebody was talking about the farmers-the member for Saskatoon-Humboldt was speaking- Conservative members saying: "Tell that to your friends at the alliance."
The point is that our member was talking about the fact that many, many farmers have had to seek jobs outside of farming in order to keep their farms going.
One of the people I ran into in Brandon was in exactly that situation. He said: "The farmers in my area understand why there is a strike. I need a pay increase to keep the farm going." This government has tried to pit farmers against workers just as it has tried to pit the unemployed against the employed. It has tried to pit one group of Canadians against another group of Canadians. It tried to get the pensioners upset with the postal workers in August.
It is ironic that in a time when this government is calling for a renewed federalism, a new Constitution, when people will work together, listen to each other and try to resolve the problems that this country faces, it has taken the exact opposite approach in this House and in this nation as a whole with regard to its own employees. Yesterday in debate I mentioned that this government has known since Friday that there was another offer coming from the Public Service Alliance. Various members of cabinet received calls. People in the Prime Minister's office received calls, and they were told this offer was there.
The government could have sat down and negotiated. It refused to do so. Instead, we have a Public Service strike in this country growing anger and we have to face the fact that when this legislation passes the House and Senate, as it will, that there is going to be a large number of very angry government workers, not because of the zero and three, although that is certainly upsetting to many of them. What they will be upset about is the
