callous, uncaring way that this government continuously attacked them.
This government was not concerned about its employees. This government was not concerned about fairness. This government was not concerned about trying to resolve some of the issues. This government was concerned with its own political agenda and that is obvious to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, Surrey is one of the municipalities that is hard hit because of the government's refusal to negotiate. It has one of the largest tax centres outside of Ottawa, with 1,000 permanent employees and approximately another 1,200 temporary employees. It has a large UIC office. It has an immigration office and also contains the Douglas and Pacific border crossings, which employ hundreds of people, both as immigration officers and customs officers.
At the beginning of the strike I had the opportunity walk the picket lines with the strikers in all of those locations. The first thing that struck me was that the overwhelming majority of them were women. I talked to them about why they were there. They said, first of all, their rates of pay were relatively low. They made $20,000, $23,000 or $24,000. They pointed out that their combined family income would not allow them to buy a house in Surrey.
They pointed out that in the last two years in Surrey, rents have increased on an average of 50 per cent, partially because this government has reneged on its promise to develop social and co-op housing. The only housing left is rental and that is at a premium.
They pointed out that their UIC premiums have gone up 25 per cent. That is a straight tax increase, no matter how you cut it.
They pointed out that the GST had been brought in and that the inflation rate in Vancouver was 6 per cent, which means that without a wage increase they had 6 per cent less money in their pocket, if they were in a stable rental accommodation.
If they were not in a stable rental accommodation, but in one where rents had gone up because the Socred
government has removed all rent controls in that province, and rents had gone up 25 per cent, 40 per cent, 50 per cent, they asked what they were going to do. "Where are we going to get the money to clothe our children, to ensure that our children have adequate food, to meet the necessities of life."
I am not talking about the big boys earning the $80,000. The dominant number of strikers were women.
I then talked to some of the merchants. I will just ask my friend to comment on the impact on this type of community where retail sales are sagging because a large segment of the community has been denied a cost of living increase. They have had to cut back on basic necessities and the retail industry is suffering.
I wonder if my friend would like to comment on those two things: the domination of the work force by women, and the impact of no increase on retail sales.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. I think that is one of the things the government has ignored in this back to work legislation. We think of people with fixed incomes and we have a lot of pity for them in our society with high inflation.
One of the things this government has also ignored is that a lot of people, whether they are renters or farmers with increased costs because of interest rates, who not only have stable costs, are going to have increasing costs in the coming fiscal year. These will be costs that they really have no control over such as costs that have gone up as a result of the goods and services tax and mortgages or leases that will have increased payments over the next couple of years. For people who are earning incomes in the $20,000 or $30,000 range, those increasing costs will not be met with the zero per cent salary increase. Their costs will go up, in some cases tremendously as my colleague pointed out. Yet they have been told that they are going to go home with a pay slip which may have the same amount of money but which will probably have more deductions next year.
They are going to be taking home less money. The cost of living will have gone up. In addition to that, their fixed costs will have gone up.
October 1, 1991

We are asking those people to survive with less as they try to pay out more. There is no attempt by this government to ever take that into consideration. I find it ironic, Mr. Speaker, that in this legislation they finally offer a number-I think it is 33,000 Public Service employees-a $500 lump sum payment.
If this government had been serious about negotiating, opening position could have been made last February. That could have been the position where the government was saying: "Here is our way of trying to help some of the people at the low end of the scale". No, it did not take that position, it did not take that position until there was a strike. It did not take that position until the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruled against it. Now it refuses to budge from that position.
It knows it can negotiate. It knows there are areas where the Public Service and the government could work out some of the problems that my colleague was talking about. However, This government refuses to sit down and try to resolve those problems.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member from Churchill for his insight into this debate. I would like to pose a question to him, revolving around morale in the Public Service.
I have in my constituency, as a matter of fact in the same building where my constituency office is, the Department of Citizenship. I have across the street a Canada Employment Commission. Not far from our riding we have immigration offices. In the riding we have National Health and Welfare offices. So I have many public servants affected by this strike.
These people are very conscientious. They know they are there to serve and when you serve the people, the public, you help people. You help people, you make them happy and you as a worker are also happy.
What I have noticed lately, Mr. Speaker, is that the morale of these workers has just hit rock bottom. It does not matter which department we call, these people are well-meaning but because this government has so mistreated its workers, the morale is at rock bottom.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Churchill whether he notices the same low morale in the constituency that he represents, in Churchill, or is this unique to our Toronto region?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is obvious to many people in this room and across Canada that morale will be a serious problem. It is not a new problem but I think it is going to be a vastly enhanced problem in the future.
I remember the reaction of government workers after the anti-inflation program in the 1970s, the six and five program in the 1980s and I listened to people out there last week in Brandon, Manitoba. It is obvious that you cannot keep treating people the way this government is and expect them to go back to work after and be happy.
This government has heard various government members ranting at them and just ranting and ranting and ranting at them. They are going to go in, making one-third the salary of some of these Conservative MPs who are ranting at them and be expected to do a job, knowing that the government has absolutely no appreciation whatsoever for them.

speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Portneuf.

Mr. Speaker, I rise again today concerning Bill C-29, which does not particularly please me, but which is unfortunately necessary. Why is it necessary? Because it seems to me that there are people in this country who take advantage of the powers that were given to them in good faith by the grassroots. I am referring to Mr. Bean, the president of the Public Service Alliance.
The union members have put their faith in him. Those are people with whom I work every day of the week, throughout the year, people with whom I was able to develop, over the last seven years, good working relations, as well as a better understanding of the stakeholders, through the different services that the population has set up for itself. Now, some leaders who want some form of political gain or who want to support certain political parties in Canada are using those services. I personally find this unfortunate and unacceptable.

October 1, 1991

Sometime ago I was reading an editorial in the newspaper and here is what it said about the perception of people. This editorial reflects exactly the thoughts or reactions that the people in my riding tell me every time I have the opportunity to meet them-and God knows that I see a lot of them these days. It says: "Day after day, the headlines refer to the lay-offs that the businesses in the private sector are compelled to make. In the meantime, the Federal civil servants go back on strike to protect their purchasing power, as though they lived in a glass buble. Job security has become an invaluable benefit in the last ten years, specially in the light of two recessions. Everywhere in the private sector workers deal with the stress associated with the risk of losing their jobs, temporarily or permanently, because they are aware of the problems faced by the companies for which they work. Several unions have had to show a good degree of lucidity and realism and have agreed to defend the solution based on salary freeze and work sharing in order to enable their members to maintain a decent revenue. As for the Public Service Alliance, it does not want to make any compromise."
The editorial adds that "All Canadians have suffered a loss of their purchasing power. The raising of the psychological and financial comfort of the 156,000 civil servants that are on strike would never be an objective for Canadians, quite the contrary. Wall to wall job security. Working conditions strictly monitored by governmental organizations that measure the inclination of chairs or the purety of the air in the buildings where these servants of the State work. Not to mention a pension plan that is better than what exists in the private sector. There are also benefits that, more often than not, make these Canadians, these civil servants, the spoiled children of the society in periods of recession." They say Minister Loiselle and the government should stand firm.
Why editorial writers are saying this? Simply because some union leaders probably failed to listen to the grass roots.
Another point: Mr. Bean refused a wage freeze. France Pilon, in Le Droit of April 25, 1991: "The downside of the convention came with the announcement of spending cuts totalling $1.8 million annually, which will force the union to freeze certain positions. Public servants will also have to pay 83 cents a month into the strike fund which is now at about $15 million. Union dues have been increased as well. Ms. Hurens was
not able to say exactly how much, although she said it was less than $4".
In April, Public Service union leaders had already decided there would be a strike. However, they had also decided they could not afford to increase the salaries of PSAC staff. They cut 20 positions so they could give a 3 per cent increase to the remaining staff. They said: It is too bad, but it was the best we could do.
Mr. Speaker, today and yesterday, Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition has held up debate and held up this legislation while trying to convince us and Canadians across the country that the government is coming down hard on its employees. Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that as far as the average citizen is concerned, I, as the member for Portneuf, am there to serve them. They pay me as they pay other public servants, whether they are federal, provincial or municipal. Why do they pay us? They pay us to provide the services they want, services they are paying for.
Today, Mr. Speaker, Canadians cannot afford to increase the quality or number of those services. Why? Because plants are closing, including one in Matane; 1,000 direct and indirect jobs in the Matane area. There are 100,000 jobs in Montreal or Toronto. But not a word. Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition doesn't mention this because it would jeopardize their strategy, which is to cover for Mr. Bean and urge him to keep his members on the ricket line while not giving them the whole story. Most government employees don't want a strike, and that is what causes all the violence.
Tensions are rising. All day yesterday and again today, they talked about the tension there would be in the workplace the day after the strike for which I was responsible. Mr. Speaker, neither you nor the President of the Treasury Board nor myself ordered government employees, the servants of the Canadian people, to take to the streets and take the people of this country hostage. We, here in this House, did not ask for that to happen. It was the President of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. He knew what he was going to do. He knew he would hijack our airports, harbours, railways, health services and even unemployment services- they must certainly need them at this point. We don't have many unemployed people in Canada these days: 1,200,000! How many tens of thousands of elderly people wait for their old age security pension cheque every month to be able to survive. He knew what he was doing. His purpose was not to defend his members' working
October 1, 1991

conditions, it was not to explain the basis of his demands to his members, no. It was to say, "I, Bean, will challenge the Canadian government's budget because the New Democratic Party does not agree with it and I advise the NDP." But he forgot that he was also taking some fellow workers hostage. Often when I hear Mr. Bean talk about solidarity and how important it is, can he explain to me how much he supports the unionized workers who are now laid off temporarily, waiting for parts to cross the border so that they can go back to work? Does he support them? Does Mr. Bean's behaviour show solidarity with the employees in my riding who have difficulty every day in trying to save their industries? Domtar, Donnacona.
On August 2-that is not a century ago, it is a little over a month back-we lost 135 jobs at the insulating board division of Domtar. Fifty more lay-offs were announced for the period up to January 1, in addition to the 53 that had already been announced and about thirty others were announced in early December last year for the pulp and paper mill next to Domtar.
I met representatives of the employees, I had discussions with employees at that plant, I spoke with the plant managers. They do not know whether the factory will still exist on January 1 or July 1 next year. Can you imagine the stress they are under? You think that their first thought on waking up in the morning is to worry about whether public servants will lose their job security, even though they know that public servants cannot lose their job security since the government cannot go bankrupt.
Public servants are the only ones in the country to have wall-to-wall security, because they work for an organization that cannot go broke. A provincial government cannot go broke. I have not yet seen any cities go broke. But all the rest who make the system work and who pay those salaries do not have that security. They could have a collective agreement a foot thick, but the day the factory is no longer competitive and the business can no longer sell its products, the boss is out of a job and so are the employees. Everyone is out in the street, at the unemployment office. Except that today, the office is closed.

But they paid for those services, Mr. Speaker. Those people paid for them! They agreed to give collective agreements and working conditions and salaries that are much better than those most people have. The proof, Mr. Speaker, is that an average Canadian earns $27,400 a year. An average civil servant in Canada earns $33,500. We said yes, but we provided for essential services. The idea of essential services makes me laugh. Why would a government set up services that were not essential to begin with? We must define what is really essential. Air traffic controllers are essential in a country. What constitutes essential services in air traffic navigation? Can you tell me? What is essential in meat quality control? If we only need ten inspectors to provide essential services, why have hundreds of them then? I would assume that, if there are hundreds of them, it is because they are all needed. I do not think that people are hired in the public service for the sake of it. They are hired because they are needed, to provide services which the people have to tighten their belts to get, if there are any belts left to tighten. I can tell you that where I come from, many people just lost their belts.
Yesterday's edition of Le Soleil reported 609,500 welfare recipients in Quebec. These people are no longer drawing UI benefits; they are down to the last resort. Are these the people to whom we will be asking for money to pay civil servants' wage increases? I am not quite sure they are the ones to ask.
In the same article, we could read that Ontario was headed toward having a million of these people down to the last resort: welfare. They are certainly not the ones we should be turning to for help. Can our 1,200,000 unemployed citizens on UI or waiting for the offices to reopen to be provided with the services they have been paying for all those years who can afford it?
Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition did not raise that point. They talked about how badly treated government employees are, but failed to mention the people who are being highjacked today. And that is not right!
With regard to essential services, all government services are essential, at whatever level of government. In a municipality, when there is a fire department it is because it is essential. The police department exists because it is essential. At the provincial level, hospital

Government Orders
services are essential services. Otherwise, there would not be any.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the opposition does not talk about that. It unduly extends the debate not unlike what happened last December. Thanks to the opposition and its tactics to make the debate drag on, this House ended up considering the opportunity to become involved in the Gulf War while the war was on. Thanks to the loyalty of our friends opposite, we were wondering if Canada should do its duty.
Well, today, we have to pass a special bill, an emergency bill, to stop the violence, if I may call it that, spreading on the picket lines. We are in no hurry, of course not, there is no rush. In a little while, we will send it to the other place. I do not know how long it will take-it all depends on the quality of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition over there-but there is no hurry. Some essential services are not being provided right now, because people are prevented from going to work. There is no harm done. It always falls on the poor taxpayer, who pays his taxes in good faith, in order to be able to afford these services! Some members in this House seem to forget they are here to serve the public, they have a duty to people on welfare, to the unemployed waiting for then-cheques or waiting in line to fill in some forms so they can get their benefits, the only income they will receive to feed their families. However, they do not care about that, it is not important. What is important is to play petty politics here. On whose back? On the back of those who cannot defend themselves, those who cannot take anybody hostage.
Mr. Speaker, when there is a hostage-taking incident somewhere in Canada, we say that it is illegal. We call the RCMP and say: "Throw that person in jail immediately." However, when Mr. Bean says: "Thke the Canadian population hostage", that is okay. It is legal, and the ordinary citizen is supposed to take that without saying a word. That is not true. The government should not listen to those people. It should say: "No, let it go; there is no problem."
The Opposition says: "Appoint a mediator." But are thirty days of mediation not enough? Are sixty days of negotiations not enough? No! My colleague tells me that it is not enough. She wants the government to be irresponsible, just like the party she always- She is nodding. She is saying yes, you should be irresponsible. That is remarkable! Well I am sorry for her, but we are a responsible government. We make decisions in the interest of those people I was talking about earlier, those
who have almost nothing left, the unemployed, the people who are losing their jobs in the plants. That is what we do.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear some of the remarks made by the Tory member opposite. The member speaks very conveniently of attempting to draw money out of the unemployed of Canada. "I cannot ask," he says "these people who do not have a job to boost the pay cheques of public civil servants."
It is a very noble argument in the eyes of those who do not completely understand the issue. I think that most Canadians can see through what is most obviously a very transparent argument being made by the member opposite.
I want to remind the member opposite and those Canadians who are sitting at home who know full well the full arguments around this issue that this party he represents, this current government of the day, had the opportunity, not having to draw money out of those who are unemployed, seven years ago to do something to ensure that we did not get into a made-in-Canada recession as we have found ourselves in.
Maybe the hon. member could pick up a copy of today's Quorum and take a look at an article by The Citizen. Here is a little line in it that says: "What about the burst of fiscal generosity which preceded the 1988 election?" Those who worried about what these promises would do to the deficit were told not to worry, these were not promises but spending commitments, the government said back in the 1988 election, already allowed for in the government's fiscal plan. As soon as the election was over the government told a whole other story; that times were tough, that programs such as a national child care program were no longer spending

commitments but were now impossible because of the shortage of cash.
When did the sun dawn on this government, that suddenly there was no money in the public purse, no money to be fair? There was no money to be fair to those individuals who are sitting trying to do an honest day's work as public civil servants in this country, who are paid less than $25,000, the poverty line. Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is asking me how come there is no more money in the public treasury? He conveniently forgets, Mr. Speaker, that when we took over in 1984, his party didn't leave much in the treasury. In fact, it was empty, Mr. Speaker, when we took over!
Since 1984, we have been trying to come out of this quagmire we have been in for 20 years. If you read what has been said, you will see that all the experts say that we are doing our job. There is a reality that you don't want to face, it is the fact that you left us with an impossible debt; secondly, we are just out of the worst economic crisis that this country has ever known and you are asking us, Sir, to go on spending.
What you are not telling us and what nobody dared say is where you are going to take the money to pay for all the goodies. You know perfectly well, because you are not anymore stupid than the average man, you are sensible people, you are too partisan but you are nevertheless sensible, and you know how to add. However, you do not dare tell us what we should do to give what they are asking us; you do not dare say that we should

increase the national debt by 3.5 billion over the next five years. You don't care.
We have already mortgaged, Mr. Speaker, not only our grandchildren, but our great grandchildren. Canadians in general are asking us to live within our means, but you stick to the rhetoric which has been yours for 20 years: "Spend, spend, doesn't matter, pay later". Mr. Speaker, I find the tone of the Conservative member almost offensive. He keeps talking about Liberal mismanagement and the deficit. Why does he not take responsibility for his own problems as a Conservative government? Why does he not listen to what the Auditor General said about the need to look into all the contracting out that this government is involved in? Why has this government refused to look into that very issue?
We know right now that this government is spending approximately $5 billion on contracting out. We know that the legislation before this House is one in which a civil servant, a federal government employee with a salary of $24,000 a year or $22,000 a year, will have his or her salary frozen. The legislation specifically excludes contractors from having their arrangements frozen.
We know that it is strictly up to the government to decide how much these people will be paid. It can double the contract and expect a 50 per cent increase in the work. It could triple the contract and expect no increase in work. These people are the political friends of the government and they should not be made to suffer-$5 billion, no controls.
The Auditor General said it should be investigated. If this member is concerned about the deficit, if this member is concerned about what is happening in this country, he should look in his own back yard. He should look at the friends of the Prime Minister. He should stop the attempt at buying friends, buying votes, and show

Government Orders
some concern for Canadians. You have absolutely no credibility when it comes to the deficit. You have no credibility when it comes to fairness. You have not cleaned up your own back yard. Do that first.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is upset, but if you allow me, I would like to put a few elements back into context. He probably lost his temper and made a few mistakes.
When he says that we are not doing anything for people earning $24,000,1 would like to remind him that the offer which has been refused by Mr. Bean contained a lump sum payment of $500 for some 35,000 civil servants earning less than $27,000 a year. That is the first thing. Guaranteed employment for civil servants laid off as a result of contracting out or privatization. Try to find that in the private sector! A guarantee of a reasonable job offer to all other employees affected by workforce adjustments, provided they are mobile and can be retrained. Commitment made for all dental expenses and increase of the ceiling for orthodontic services form $2 000 to $2 500. Increase of the contribution of the employer for disability insurance premiums from 75 to 85 per cent. Increase in the number of daycare facilities in the workplace.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the 10 to 15 daycare facilities will be opened in Donnacona, at home, they are probably for the civil servants, in Ottawa.
From the 1st of April 1992, six weeks of annual leave after 29 years of service. Increase of the shift premiums from $1 to $1,10 per hour, of weekend premiums from 75 cents to $1 per hour and of lunches premiums from $6 to $7, for overtime.
Mr. Speaker, when my friend from the NDP says that we are not making any offer, that we negotiate in bad faith, I am sorry, but after what I have just read I think he put both foot in it and it is not the first time.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to participate in this debate because there is a myth which the government is attempting to sell around the country. I want to play a small role in trying to dispel that myth. That myth is that
it is okay to single out, to target, the lowest paid of the public servants of Canada for special regressive treatment. It is okay to say that the lowest paid people who work for the Government of Canada can be frozen, can have their collective bargaining rights taken away, can be held up as an example of how to pick on the weakest among us in any organization. It is okay to do all of that because out in Canada there are a great many unemployed, because out in this great wonderful country called Canada there are people who are poor, and as long as there are people who are poor and people who are unemployed, it is therefore okay to treat your own employees in any way you want.
I come from Newfoundland and Labrador. That is my province. It has the highest unemployment in Canada. It has the highest poverty in Canada. There has never existed in Newfoundland and Labrador even the slightest degree of room for what I call the politics of envy, setting up a straw man or a straw woman, feeding the fuel of that negative emotion called envy and then seeking to destroy that straw man or straw woman.
That is what the national government has done. It is the politics of division. It is the kind of instinct that if we allow it to be appealed to, it will divide the nation. It is exactly the same kind of instinct that divides French and English, the west and the east, north and south, black and white, Protestant and Catholic and Jew and Gentile. It is the same kind of appeal. It is the politics of division.
I hope Canadians who are following this debate and following this issue understand what is happening. Especially if you are unemployed and following this debate, especially if you are poor and following this debate, and especially if your job is uncertain and you are following this debate, understand the negative appeal that the government is making to you. The government is saying: "If you are uncertain, if you are poor, if you are hungry, if you are worried, if you are unhappy, then you have a right to know that some are even more unhappy, more uncertain, more unsure than you are and those people we've selected for you are the civil servants of Canada, and not only the civil servants of Canada but the lowest paid civil servants of Canada".
I am here to tell the government that those kinds of politics, the politics of division, the politics of envy, are not selling in the country this time around.

October 1, 1991

They are simply not washing. People understand as never before, having been faced with this government since 1984, the concept of fairness and balance in the public affairs of this country.
They expect the government to be fair and to be balanced in its approach to public policy. They expect the government to set an example of fiscal restraint and of being frugal, but most important of being fair. Is there any fairness? Is there one iota of fairness in saying that it is okay to give not a salary, not an increase, but a bonus of $70,000 or $80,000 for the highest paid public servants?
Many Canadians would love to have a salary of $70,000 to $80,000. Many Canadians would love to have an increase, public servants this year for example, of $700. This government gave a bonus that is over and above the $200,000 to $300,000 salary, a bonus of $70,000, $75,000 and $80,000 to the highest paid public servants in the land. It has given zero per cent to the lowest paid public servants in the land.
Whether your circumstance is that you just got a raise in the private sector or you just got laid off in the private sector, it is not hard to understand the concept of fairness as it ought to be when you look at how this government operates from day to day and when you look at the circumstances as they really are: zero per cent for a secretary and a $70,000 bonus for the hand-picked heads of corporations selected by this government.
That is not rhetoric. That is not opinion. That is not comment. That is fact. That is fact, and the same people who stand behind the administration that made that decision stand today and say: "We cannot afford to be fair. We cannot afford to be just. We cannot afford to be decent with public servants because we are really worried. We are bleeding for the unemployed."
There has been an indecent level of unemployment in Newfoundland since this government came to power and it is difficult to believe that only now is it bleeding for the unemployed of Newfoundland.
There has been an indecent level of poverty since this government came to power and suddenly this government wants to be on the side of those who live in poverty,
Government Orders
taking on those nasty, terrible civil servants making $18,000 a year.
This bill defies credibility. It is not possible to believe the government is sincere or genuine when it presents this bill.
This is one of those debates in which if a member of the opposition believed merely in political convenience, we would buy the argument that the government puts forward, that the strike is inconvenient and therefore we must slam the public back to work. That would be the easy thing to do, to say: "Yes, somebody in my constituency has been inconvenienced by those civil servants and we are going to slam them back to work."
That would be the selfish thing to do. That would be the quick, easy, convenient and cowardly thing to do. When I stopped my car on the side of the road coming back here on Monday at an airport road in Deer Lake, Newfoundland and talked to half a dozen people with picket signs in their hands, most of them making less than the minimum income of this country, I did not see a bunch of greedy, selfish civil servants. I saw people who could not really afford to be on the picket line.
They were people who could not afford to be on the picket line, whose children had just gone back to school.
They just got them ready for school. They are looking at Christmas and they want to have a few gifts under the tree. They really cannot afford to be there and they do not want to be there. They absolutely despise the fact that they are out there. Mr. Speaker, their principles are not for sale. They are prepared to pay the penalty in lost salary of being on the picket line because they want to make a point. They want the government to know that as it hauls on its jackboots and walks over them that they are not dead, that they are alive.
These public servants want to stand for their rights, Mr. Speaker, in a way they have never done before.
When the government can roll over its own, when the government can walk over the lowest paid of the public servants of Canada and not a sound is heard as it rolls over them, it sets an example for all members of our society to be rolled over by big and powerful organizations and institutions.
Members of Parliament are here not because it is the political thing to do, not because it is the easy thing to do to stand up to Bill C-29 and not because it is convenient,

Government Orders
but because it is right to oppose this bill which has wiped out the right of collective bargaining in Canada.
We acknowledge that Canadians have been inconvenienced. Of course they have. I have been inconvenienced. I do not like it and Canadians do not like it. The issue is not whether or not the Public Service strike is inconvenient for the country. Of course it is. The issue is why do we have a Public Service strike? Is it because it is unreasonable for people to seek more than zero per cent salary increases? Or is it because a government that has languished at 12 per cent to 15 per cent in the polls for the last six months finally needs somebody it can stand up and knock down.
I suggest the truth is obvious. This is a government desperate to pick a battle and win a battle, any battle with anybody. It has picked upon public servants. This is a government desperate to ride on the backs of the lowest paid public servants in this country, trying to climb back up the slippery slope of popularity.
I tell you, this government insults not so much the intelligence but the integrity of Canadians if it believes that an appeal to mob rule, an appeal to pack mentality, an appeal as I said earlier to the politics of envy, is going to result in some collective mad rush by the public at large to beat up on the public servants of this country. It will not result in that kind of mob rule.
If this government truly wants an end to the labour disruption in this country, if it truly wants to see the Public Service functioning in an efficient manner, if it is truly interested in the whole notion of pay equity, given the women in our society, equal pay for work of equal value, if this government is interested in justice at all it will back away from this disastrous course.
If the only rationale that those who would promote and who have manipulated this strike can come up with in the smoke-filled dark and dank rooms of the Tory party is the belief that somehow you are going to lift yourself out of your political misery by ganging up on civil servants, the government must know by now that that strategy has failed. That strategy has failed. The public is not buying this obvious and bare-faced and bold and brazen attempt to manipulate public opinion.
How can Canadians believe, as they desperately want to believe, as they desperately need to believe, that their government is dealing with them in a forthright fashion on something that is as fundamental as the Constitution? How can Canadians believe that all matters they need to know have been exposed, that there is no shady backroom dealing in something as fundamental as the Constitution, when the government is so obviously prepared to manipulate, to deal in the back room, to be unfair and to be unjust on something as fundamental as how you treat your own employees?
That is the issue the government ought to cotton on to. This government is in power at a time when Canada is experiencing perhaps its last opportunity to pull the nation back together. This government that is responsible and directly responsible for the current mess we are in now has responsibility to try and bridge the gap and the differences in this country, to get people pulling in one direction and to find a constitutional reconciliation.
How can the minister in charge of the Constitution, Mr. Clark, how can the Prime Minister, Mr. Mulroney, how can his lieutenants, Mr. Bouchard and Mr. Crosbie, be believed in their respective regions and in their respective responsibilities when they say: "Our only interest is Canada. We are being forthright with you. We are being honest with you. All we want is a fair and balanced deal. Trust our intentions, believe in our integrity, follow our course and come build a better Canada with us".
How can we believe that soaring rhetoric when right here in this Parliament today this same government deals with its own employees in the most deceitful and manipulative way possible. That is the issue for this government. This is not a question of batting heads with the union and winning. It is not a question of showing who is the most stubborn and it is not a question of manipulating the weakest among the federal government organization. It is a question of fairness.
Mr. Speaker, I tell you this argument that we are going to take money out of the pockets of the civil servants to feed the hungry in Newfoundland is not washing.
October 1, 1991

Let me tell you about Newfoundland. Let me tell you about the politics of envy. In 1984, when Ethiopia was suffering the worst famine it has seen to this point, when millions were starving and going to tents, Newfoundland had the highest unemployment rate in Canada, it had the highest poverty rate in Canada and on a per capita basis, it gave more than any other province of Canada to the people of Ethiopia. That is the reality of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. When they were called upon to give they gave on a per capita basis in greater measure than any other people of the country. The poorest of the country responded.
So this politics of envy that is being thrown out now as a rationale for beating up on civil servants does not find a receptive audience in Newfoundland and Labrador. I suspect it does not find a receptive audience among the newly unemployed of southern Ontario, one-quarter of a million people driven out of their jobs by this government. The politics of envy does not find a receptive audience among our native people whose treatment has been shameful in the history of this country. The politics of envy does not find a receptive, resonating core among the urban poor. It does not find a receptive audience among our farmers who are today trying to sell wheat at the lowest price since the 1930s.
The politics of envy and division in Canada do not work any more. People in this country instinctively understand that if the country is to survive, we must be fair to each other. We must care about each other. We must pull together. You cannot accomplish those goals when you accept the temptation to begin to pull apart and to beggar your neighbour and to envy your neighbour and to allow anyone to manipulate you into setting up scapegoats.
There are two political forces at work in Canada today whose success depends upon Canada's failure. The Reform Party believes in a Canada without Quebec and the Bloc Quebecois believes in a Quebec without Canada. This government has borrowed a page from both those parties when they practise the sickening politics of division and envy.
We in the Liberal Party stand opposed to Bill C-29. We do not oppose it because it is the obvious political thing to do. There are not enough civil servants in this member's riding to elect or defeat him, or that member's riding, or that member's riding. There are proportionate-
Govemment Orders
ly only a handful of civil servants in my riding and there are a hell of a lot of unemployed.
The easy thing would be to join the gang-up on those civil servants. The cowardly thing would be to say "yes, we are standing with the unemployed and the poor against those civil servants". But the right thing to do if we are going to begin to heal the wounds that have tom this country asunder, wounds inflicted by that government, is to stand against this bill. We must stand against this brand of politics and say "no" to Bill C-29, stand up for our neighbours, in this case those civil servants who have been manipulated by this government to a picket line.
Hear,, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member got to his feet and asked a question. I have just spent 20 minutes talking about that insidious poison, and obviously my words fell on deaf ears, that insidious bit of killing poison the government is squirting into the veins of the nation, called envy. That is the game here. That is the whole game. You are at 15 per cent in the polls. That means that less than two people in 10 think anything of you. You cannot get them to admire you for your virtues so you appeal to pride and prejudice. You set up the politics of envy.
I spent 15 or 20 minutes talking about that poison called envy. "If I cannot get you to like me and respect me, can I get you to rally to me, as together we shall beat up on someone else". What does the member say? What is his question? His question is: "The 234,000 people in Ontario who lost their jobs in the last 16 months,
because of the policies of the member and his government, would they not like to have these jobs?"
The answer to the question is obvious. Those people would like to have jobs. Absolutely. If the member cared about getting them jobs, the member and his party would abandon their disastrous trade policies, free trade with the United States and now free trade with Mexico. That is what led to 234,000 jobs being lost in Ontario in the last year.
This government caused 1.5 million people to be unemployed today, 1.5 million whom we know about and probably another 500,000, 600,000 or 700,000 who have given up trying because it knows that those poor, wretched, displaced unemployed souls are out there. It knows they are there. It put them there. In desperation it does not announce a job-creation policy. It does not announce an industrial policy. It does not set up some signs of hope for this economy. What does it do? It says to the unemployed worker: "We are going to put you back to work. We have a plan to put you back to work". What does it do? It sets up the civil servants as scapegoats.
That is not only so transparent as to be childish, what is worse, it is personally cowardly. It is the mark of a coward and I am ashamed to witness it.

Mr. Speaker, I hear the government saying that it cannot afford it. I would like the member to comment on just one thing, the government's handling of high interest rates and what he thinks would happen if it had reduced interest rates by just 1 per cent in this country, one additional per cent. How much would it save on the national debt?
My calculations are that out of a $400 billion debt, if interest rates dropped 1 per cent, the saving would be $4 billion. Do you think that would give the civil servants a reasonable wage increase and leave some money over to help the unemployed in Newfoundland?

Mr. Speaker, I concur with the member. What the unemployed people of Canada want is not their neighbour dragged down to share their misery in unemployment or some comfort in knowing that somebody else was slain by this government or somebody else was unemployed. What the unemployed people of Canada want is a government that, if it cannot come to grips with the reality of unemployment, at least shows some empathy, at least can bleed a little, can indicate that

there is some hope and is, at least, prepared to spend its energy creating jobs, not creating confrontation.
The government does not understand that people who are down and out do not spend their days wanting to make everybody else be down and out. What they want is a response. They want some indication that the government is listening. They want some hope.
The fishery in my province failed and failed disastrously this year. I and every other MP from Newfoundland for the last two weeks have almost daily been asking for assistance. I want assistance. speechtext:

The Ottawa Sun, "Pork and beans" says: "He was offered a job security guarantee for every member of his rank and file and what could be more important than job security in this economic climate?" What is better than job security? He was offered a $500 signing bonus for every PSAC employer earning less than $27,000. That is not a big salary, but I know a lot of people in my area who would not mind working for $27,000. That represents 35,200 people when not long ago he was calling the same people scabs because so many of them believed he could not rustle them up a dime.
That was one ball game. This is another. We hear the critics from the other side of the House, the Liberals and the NDPers. They were together, almost kissing and hugging together. It is very dangerous for the people of Canada when they get together because it is not the same party at all. One is socialist and the other one is capitalist and they like to spend money. They did spend a lot and they like taxes. We hope there will be no more tax increases, but that is the way it goes.
The NDPers want the government to haul in a mediator to solve this puzzle. A mediator is not needed here. What is needed is for Bean to get back to the negotiation table he left so quickly. Otherwise, it is an affront to his cause. That is what it is. He wants to do
something against the government because the NDP does not want to see us here.
We are doing a good job. We are doing the good job that we should do for the finances of this country. What did Mr. Bean do, big administrator? Mr. Bean did worse than what we are doing. In administration Mr. Bean is not so bad. He not a bad man. He is a good money player. He knows how to count. A lot of people here do not know how to save money.
He did his budget. He has 165 employees. What he did for his union people, his staff, is gave them a 3 per cent increase. Good guy. To give the 3 per cent increase, he cut 20 jobs and he cut his budget for $1.8 million.

I will read it to you, Mr. Speaker. It was in the April 19 edition of the Toronto Star: "The delegates at the PSAC meeting held in spring 1991 voted in favor of the abolition of 20 jobs."

The union voted to remove 20 jobs. It is unbelievable. They did it.

"Daryl Bean, the president of the union stated that employees have reason to be frustrated. But we are in a difficult situation." The Toronto Star, April 19, 1991. Daryl, poor old Daryl. We are in a difficult situation.

He is right. He did the right thing, but he is a union man. He cuts 20 jobs. We should have cut 6,000 jobs. Why did we not do it, 6,000 jobs to get 3 per cent? We did not cut the 6,000 jobs because 1 per cent equals 2,000 jobs. Anybody can count that. We did not do it, but he did it. We are the bad boys and he is the good boy. Is that true? Where is the mjhh? I will tell you where the myth is. The NDP is giving false information.

Lies, lies. They are defending the workers.

Where are they? There is not even one in this House here today, not one. There is not one. They defend the union people, the ones who do not cut the salaries, the

ones who do not freeze the salaries. They are the members of the NDP. What a farce. What a joke.
The people in my area believe them. Because I am honest they do not believe me. They want an honest politician. I am going to try to stay honest, because I tell them exactly how it is: you are lucky to have a job, you will go through this hard time, and maybe next year you will get three and the year later you will get more.
The NDP does not defend the poor workers who are losing money. The NDP defends the unions, because they finance almost totally that party. The NDP members do not have businessmen with them. They do not have people who have problems in these days. They do not have these businessmen who create jobs in their party, who have merchandise blocked at the port of Montreal which they need to sell and deliver to customers. They are not here, these guys. They are not with them; they are with me.
They call me and say: "Sir, we have to do something. Tell the minister to move", I will not tell you what because it is unparliamentary what they said to me just a few minutes ago. They have merchandise there which has to be sold, and these are the perfect boys.
I do not know. I do not know where we are going. That is the story. I hope everybody understands that, including the people watching us.

Mr. Speaker, I will now speak for the second time on the subject which is most important to me. This morning, 200 workers who have the right to be on strike and whom I respect invaded my constituency office, where I have two employees working for me, in order to scare them a bit. These employees do not belong to the union, they work for me and do not have the right to speak in my name. These employees are just doing their best. We serve the public. But those people tried to intimidate my employees in my office-it is not their office, but mine. When I have to go to their office, I have to make an appointment, and they are only public servants. How can those 200 people have the right to burst into my constituency office and ask to see me when they know I am here?
But, Mr. Speaker, I will tell these people, like I told them yesterday in my speech, that they are useful, that we need them, and that we worked with them. There are some among those who are hard workers and who give a 110 per cent of their time and of their energy to the
Government Orders
government and to Canadians. But there is one thing that I will never tolerate and I say it to all those who are listening, that is intimidation, blackmail and lies. When I worked as a volunteer-and I did that for 20 years-in my riding, and when I coached baseball teams with young kids, I used to say to children and their parents: There are two things: lies and blackmail. Keep those to yourself, because at the rate that we are getting paid, we cannot afford that. It costs too much. With baseball, people accepted that; they understood that. It was volunteer work. "If you don't let my son play, I won't do this, I won't buy gas from you." I heard that line for 20 years. "My son is good." In that mother's opinion he was good, but in my opinion he wasn't. However, we tried to let everyone play.
"I used to tell the lady: "Of course our children are always nicer and better than the others; our children are much nicer and more intelligent, but there are also other ones that are nice and intelligent". That is what parents could not accept. So they would use blackmail on me. When they did that, the little guy would not play ball anymore. I would tell the lady or the gentleman to take their son and let him play in their backyard. It is the same thing in politics. If you don't do this for me, I won't vote for you anymore. But those are the people who create problems, like Mr. Kealy.
The papers failed to talk about his past, his background. It is not the purest. It is not white as snow. We all do our best. Every one wants to help every one else. But we can go nowhere with blackmail like: "Unless you give me this, I will not do that for you." I can give everything and the moon to my people. I could give them everything they ask for, but they would be the first ones to come and see me to say: "Give us a break. We are overtaxed!" We could give them a golden Christmas tree, but, for the time being they will have to make do with a natural green one. We do not have golden ones yet. I would love to put one in each of their houses. In

any case, ray constituents, the majority of them, understand that we cannot afford such a luxury.
