speechtext: It being 5 p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 30(6), the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.

That, in the opinion of this House the Constitution Act, 1982 should be amended in order to recognize explicitly the right of Canada's aboriginal peoples to self-government, thereby making them partners in Confederation and that this House further urges the governments of Canada, the Provinces and the Territories to acknowledge that self-government requires a viable economic base and calls upon these governments to constitutionally commit themselves to negotiate with the aboriginal peoples an equitable sharing of lands and resources.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion asks the House to entrench in the Constitution the right of aboriginal people to self-government. I would reword that. It asks that we recognize the inherent right of aboriginal peoples to self-government in the Constitution. That is the first thing that it asks.
The second thing it asks is that this House further urges the governments of Canada, the provinces and territories to acknowledge that self-government requires a viable economic base. It goes on to talk about land claims and the need for settling land claims in order to complement aboriginal self-government.
When this motion was scheduled for debate I did not know what sort of constitutional proposals the government would release earlier last week, but now I am quite gratified to tell you, and you probably know it, Mr. Speaker, that the government in its constitutional proposal has accepted the principle that the right of aboriginal peoples to self-government be recognized in the Constitution. There were several provisions in the constitutional proposals of the government that deal with this matter.
The government has said that the proposals as written in its document is not written in stone, that they are subject to consultation and revision, but in any case it has accepted the principle.
Because the government has accepted the principle of the proposal I have in my private member's motion, because this party has agreed for some time to the entrenchment recognizing aboriginal self-government, and so does the New Democratic Party, I was hopeful that before this hour ends the House might agree to this motion since all parties agree to the principles lying behind it and that by doing so this House would give some impetus to the constitutional proposals already put forward by the government.
I think it would be laudatory and helpful if the House of Commons of Canada said as a body that it agreed to the recognition and entrenchment in the Constitution of the right of aboriginal people to self-government. All parties have now said that in principle.
I am hopeful, before this debate ends and when government members rise, that they will leave a few minutes at the end so we could simply accept the motion perhaps unanimously. I do not know if anybody now disagrees with this principle.
I should remind the House that similar principles were accepted and tried in the early 1980s when the government of the day, a Liberal government, agreed to call



October 1, 1991

three federal-provincial conferences to entrench the recognition of aboriginal self-government. Unfortunately the federal government was not able to obtain the agreement of enough provinces to get that matter entrenched in the Constitution. Two of those conferences took place when Mr. Trudeau's government was in power and one of them took place when Mr. Mulroney's government was in power. They all failed to get the seven out of ten provinces representing 50 per cent of the population, so the matter failed.
Now, once again, the Government of Canada has included this in its constitutional proposals, but I would hope that it would have a much greater chance of succeeding this time because a lot of water has gone under the bridge since the early 1980s. It has been about 10 years since those original proposals were made and discussed at a federal-provincial conference. We have had some very sad incidents arising from the fact that we did not recognize the rights of our aboriginal people the way they should have been recognized.
I refer to the incidents which took place at Oka last summer and at Kahnawake on the south shore of Montreal, and there are many other incidents that could be referred to.
I think that the mood today is that there is a greater recognition of the rights of aboriginal peoples. I am hopeful that the proposal that I put forward today and which is included in different words in the government's constitutional proposals will be agreed to and entrenched in the Constitution.
As far as I am concerned all of this started with me personally when I was a member of the special committee on Indian self-government which sat and worked in this country at the very beginning of the 1980s. That committee broke a lot of new ground. It was the first parliamentary committee which included as ad hoc members representatives of the national aboriginal organizations. The Assembly of First Nations appointed a member, Roberta Jamieson, who now holds a high position in the Government of Ontario. There were also representatives from the Native Council of Canada, from the Metis National Council, and from the Native Women's Association of Canada.
Private Members' Business
These aboriginal representatives appointed by their own organizations sat with our committee, had all the rights and privileges as members of the committee, except that they had no technical voting rights.
They questioned witnesses as members of the committee did. They participated in the discussions leading to the adoption of the report. Mr. Speaker, when the time came to vote on the recommendations of that report dealing with aboriginal self-government, we decided not to adhere to strict technical votes, but to adopt recommendations by consensus which included the consensus developed with the help of those representatives from the aboriginal associations.
That committee, of which I was a member, made very strong recommendations for the recognition of the right to aboriginal self-government in the Constitution. Mr. Speaker, I and others have been promoting this concept for years with, of course, the backing up of the aboriginal associations themselves, which have been first and foremost in this struggle.
Every time the matter is raised, there are members of Parliament or senators-not all-and members of the public and the press, who ask: Well, what does aboriginal self-government mean? Does it mean we are going to have 15 or 20 or 30 separate independent countries within Canada? Are they all going to have the same powers, or different powers?" And so on, and so on.
They have either voted against it or opposed the idea because they said it was not clear enough. Well, let me point this out. Although various aboriginal associations in Canada point out that they have had the right to aboriginal self-government for thousands of years, they want to exercise that right within Canada, within Confederation. I have been at many meetings where their representatives have argued that while some provinces and some groups in Canada are undertaking movements to get out of Canada, they want to be fully included but represented as groups. They want to be part of Confederation, but equally and able to maintain their inherent and historic rights.
We are not talking about, at least for most of the aboriginal groups that I have talked to, of people or associations or First Nations that want to separate totally from Canada and live independently. They want to exercise certain basic powers, often with respect to social

October 1, 1991
Private Members' Business
polity, economic development, justice, education, health care and other matters that directly touch their people and with which they have been dealing for generations.
In contrast to the concept of the policy of aboriginal self-government, we have the Indian Act, a vestige, I must say, of 19th century imperialism and paternalism. Here we have a very old Act which was passed and which was administered by governments of all stripes at the federal level, and not the NDP, because they have not formed a government, but Conservative and Liberal governments, which in fact was an act which allowed the non-Indian population of Canada, the white population, to run affairs for-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I apologize to the hon. member for this interruption, but I ask the co-operation of other members because the Chair cannot hear and understand the speech being delivered.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for that intervention. I would hope that the members of the House would give more attention to this important subject which, as I say, is not only discussed very widely with our aboriginal people, but it is also now one of the key proposals of the government's constitutional package.
I was saying that the Indian Act was an act which set up an administration basically of non-Indian people, the so-called white population of Canada, to run the affairs of the Indian people, a clear case of imperialism, of colonialism, of paternalism. It has carried on until 1991.
Now, it is true that for about the last 20 or 30 years there has been a certain devolution. The Department of Indian and Northern Affairs, of which I was a former minister, has handed over some of those powers, not legally or constitutionally, but administratively, to the bands. So there are many bands that now run their own programs of education, health and social services and so on. They in fact run those matters but their right to do so is not recognized in the Constitution, nor has the Indian Act been basically changed which takes that right away from the federal government to do so.
I think the first thing we have to recognize is that in 1991, as we near the end of the 20th century, the Indian Act is an anomaly. It is totally out of place in a modem world that one group of people should be running the
lives of other people. I can account for you the silliest and craziest examples where officials in Ottawa had to approve the widening of a road by two feet on a reserve in Saskatchewan. I mean, how ridiculous. Although passed by a certain band council in Saskatchewan, they had to come all the way to Ottawa for approval. It sat on somebody's desk for months and months before it could be done. One could tell of many, many other silly examples.
In any case, we have to get rid of the Indian Act. We have to continue for the time being transferring programs to the bands as they see fit to take them on, or to tribal councils. In many cases the bands have joined together and formed tribal councils which allow them greater scope because they are bigger, have more resources, more people. They have regional high schools and so on, with respect to these tribal councils.
I also want to mention that certain Indian nations, such as the Sechelt in British Columbia, have already had a special act passed which recognizes their right to self government. I think we should also recognize that now in the Northwest Territories, in the territorial government, the majority of people in the Northwest Territories who are aboriginal people are in control of that government, and that is a good thing as well.
Again, I want to point out that the aboriginal nations of Canada existed in this territory which is now called Canada for thousands of years. I don't know the exact period of time but anthropologists and others say it was for thousands of years. They did that as many nations. There were Cree nations, Mohawk nations, MicMac nations, Montagnais and Blackfoot and so on and so on.
They had their own languages and their own cultures, their own traditions. They had their own laws, their own systems of government, their own economies. When the Europeans came in the 16th and 17th centuries and made contact with these aboriginal nations, in some cases they signed treaties, treaties to govern the relationships between the aboriginal people and themselves. In other cases they didn't sign treaties but they simply pushed them off the land. These people who acted as their friends in many cases, when the Europeans came, were sort of pushed aside after the Europeans, both the English and the French, found their way over here. One could say the same about the Spanish in South America. They simply set them aside and treated them as second-

class citizens or not as citizens at all, or not even as human beings in many cases.
The point of the matter is that these aboriginal nations never gave up their right to self government. They never recognized in any treaty that I know of that they were ceding to the British and the French colonial powers the right to govern them, nor did they transfer in most cases their lands. That is the basis of the land claim settlements. In certain treaties there was a recognition of settlement of lands, but in many there was not, and in many parts of Canada there are no treaties whatsoever which deal with these matters.
So, the aboriginal people have retained their right to self government that they always had as nations on this continent. They retain the moral right to those lands that they occupied and now they are saying to us "We want you to recognize those rights in the Constitution". I am in this proposal today saying that we should recognize those rights in the Constitution. I understand that the government is saying the same thing in the constitutional proposals that it put forward a week ago. That is the basis of my argument with respect to the first part of my resolution.
The second part says, as I stated at the beginning of my remarks, that if you are to have self-government you must also have a viable economic basis and consequently, we should commit ourselves in this Parliament to negotiate with aboriginal peoples an equitable sharing of lands and resources, based on the lands and resources that they used and occupied before the Europeans came three or four centuries ago.
Once again, I do not want to take up too much time. As I say, I first put this motion to previous Parliaments years ago, and I have been putting this on the Order Paper year after year. That is why I am gratified to see the movement in the country and the movement among political parties. There seems to be great agreement on these principles today. I would hope that this year will not pass without the entrenchment of aboriginal selfgovernment or the recognition of aboriginal self-government in the Constitution of Canada. I would hope that
Private Members' Business
we would give impetus to that movement for entrenchment by agreeing to this resolution in this House today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to rise and speak on this very important matter as Parliamentary Secretary to the Right Hon. Joe Clark, the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
The question of aboriginal rights, in particular, a right to self-government and how it should be recognized in the Constitution, is not a new one. Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 recognizes and affirms the existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. There have been quite divergent and varied interpretations of the nature and scope of these rights.
This government is serious about constitutional change for aboriginal peoples, including the entrenchment of a justiciable right to self-government. The Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, assisted by the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and the Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, is devoting much of his time to this important matter.
This summer, at a meeting in Morley, Alberta, Mr. Clark reached agreement with the chiefs of the Assembly of First Nations on what has come to be known as the parallel process for aboriginal constitutional consultations and negotiations. Since then, the minister has met with the leaders of the Native Council of Canada, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and the Metis National Council who have established similar consultative structures to seek the views of their respective constituencies.
Section 37 of the Constitution Act, 1982 provided for a constitutional conference of first ministers, to which aboriginal representatives would be invited, to identify and define aboriginal rights to be included in the Constitution of Canada.
Two conferences were subsequently held, one in 1983 and another in 1984. By the time of the 1984 conference, the entrenchment of an aboriginal right to self-government had emerged as the primary objective of the aboriginal participants.

October 1, 1991
Private Members' Business
For aboriginal peoples, a right to self-government would reflect what is in their view the historical reality, and it would provide a secure foundation upon which a better future could be built-a future that they themselves and their children would shape.
On June 21, 1984, the section 37 process was formally extended through proclamation of the first "made in Canada" amendments under the amending formula set out in the Constitution Act, 1982. Among other things, these amendments provided for two more first ministers' conferences on aboriginal affairs-one before April 17, 1985, and another before April 17, 1987.

The Prime Minister opened the 1985 First Minister's Conference with the following remarks: "As a Canadian and as Prime Minister, I fully recognize and agree with the emphasis that the aboriginal people place on having their special rights inserted into the highest law of the land and protected from arbitrary legislative action."
Constitutional protection is an over-riding objective because it is the constitutional manifestation of a relationship and unbreakable social contract between aboriginal people and their governments. An unprecedented level of consensus was reached at the 1985 conference.
At one point, agreement appeared to be veiy close on a federal draft proposal modified by Saskatchewan which became known as the "contingent right approach".
Seven provinces appeared to be ready to support this proposal if the aboriginal association at the table agreed. The Assembly of First Nations and the Inuit Committee on National Issues however felt that they could not support the Saskatchewan proposal.
After that conference, the federal government worked hard to re-establish a positive climate for the discussion and negotiations. It stated that despite the failure to achieve consensus on the self-government amendment, it would proceed with negotiations on practical self-government initiatives within the existing constitutional framework.
It was hoped that the practical examples of self-government developed through these negotiations would help to build consensus in the constitutional forum.
Some provinces had been hesitant to agree to the entrenchment of a right to self-government without first
knowing more about what it would involve. Considerable discussion took place between the 1985 First Ministers' Conference and the 1987 conference.
Five multilateral meetings were held at the ministerial level. Seven were held at the official's level and bilateral discussions continued throughout this period.

The draft amendment that the federal government put forward at the 1987 First Ministers' Conference was a progressive proposal. It would have provided explicit recognition of a free-standing right of aboriginal peoples to self-government. The jurisdiction, legislative powers, proprietary rights, and other powers, rights and privileges of bodies or institutions exercising the right to self-government were to be defined through agreements.
This proposal would also have entrenched a commitment by the Government of Canada and provincial governments to negotiate agreements relating to selfgovernment. Such negotiations could relate to any matter respecting self-government, including, where appropriate, jurisdiction, powers, land, resources, funding and preservation and enhancement of native languages and cultures.
The 1987 federal proposal would have provided for the self-government rights set out in agreements to be deemed treaty rights for the purpose of section 35 of the Constitution, where legislatures approved. In other words, these rights would have received constitutional protection.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this proposal, or any other on the table at that time, did not secure sufficient support among provinces and aboriginal leaders to proceed with a constitutional amendment. With that conference, the formal, multilateral aboriginal constitutional negotiations provided for in section 37 of the Constitution ended.
After the 1987 conference, the federal government maintained its interest in aboriginal self-government. It continued to pursue self-government negotiations within current constitutional arrangements. Ministers also met many times with aboriginal leaders to discuss what prospects there might be for further aboriginal constitutional discussions in the future.
October 1, 1991

The companion constitutional resolution to the Meech Lake Accord would have reinstated an entrenched process of first ministers' conferences on matters of interest to the aboriginal peoples of Canada. Had the Meech Lake Accord been ratified by all provinces, the first such conference would have taken place this year.
The government acknowledged that there was an unfinished agenda with respect to aboriginal constitutional reform. Today, Mr. Speaker, we are in a period wherein we face serious challenges as a nation.
We are being called to work toward a Canada that better reflects who we are as a nation, and what we aspire to be. Consideration of Canada's future must include a review of the fundamental place and role of aboriginal peoples. As the Prime Minister stated in his address to the First Nations Congress on April 23, 1991 in Victoria, the views of aboriginal leaders, communities and individuals from across Canada will be fully considered as the government proceeds towards building a stronger Canada. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, it is the wish of the majority of Canadians, aboriginal and non-aboriginal, that this issue be resolved now.
Mr. Speaker, the proposals tabled in this House by the Prime Minister on September 24 demonstrate the commitment of this government to follow through on the extensive work which has recently been done.
The first step, of course, is to assure aboriginal peoples of participation in the current round of constitutional discussions.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace for introducing this motion at a veiy appropriate time.
I regret that the member who just spoke did not indicate that the government would be supporting this motion. I think it would have been helpful because it is basically support for a principle that is already included in the government's constitutional proposals. I believe it would have been helpful for the government and the Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs to go out
Private Members' Business
to the people of Canada with the endorsement of Parliament against this resolution, to support the constitutional proposals that have been made so that he would have Parliament's sanction for his negotiations with aboriginal people and with provinces and other interests in this country who would like to see some improvement in the relationship between Canada and its aboriginal people.
I would like to congratulate the member who presented the resolution. The key word in the resolution is the recognition of aboriginal rights to self-government. In the view of many constitutional experts aboriginal people have an inherent right, not a right to be granted by this Parliament or by this government, not a right to be delegated by this Parliament or this government to aboriginal people, but they have an inherent right. It is a right that inheres in the fact that they are the aboriginal nations who preceded European contact on this continent.
By the time Europeans arrived here they had already established organized governments based on family, tribal and clan structures. They had the power to make and enforce laws against their own people and to test those laws by whatever methods of adjudicating they had.
In the same way, like any other sovereign nation, they had the right to organize economies and to trade and become involved in trade beyond their own nations. They had the right to prosecute wars and to treat for peace. They did those things in very much the same way that other sovereign nations engage in making peace through the treaty-making system.
Of course, the treaty-making system is a system that is followed to obtain agreements between two sovereign nations. You do not sign a treaty with a group that is internal to this country. You sign a treaty with a nation that has recognized sovereign status.
It is interesting that when the first Europeans came into contact with aboriginal nations in North America, they generally approached them by signing treaties of peace which regularized the form of contact and relationship between the two nations involved.

October 1, 1991
Private Members' Business
Unfortunately, as time passed on the North American continent and as the European settlers and settlers from outside North American began to overrun the continent in terms of population, the treaties were forgotten. The aboriginal people were shifted toward the margins of society and became like any other colonized people around the world. They lost their right to be recognized as sovereign countries or, I should say, their right was ignored by the European groups that overran their societies. Those aboriginal people never ever gave up their sense of having that sovereign right and of being independent nations, having the right to enter into treaties with the European societies that overran and established their own governments in the continent of North America.
In fact, after those treaties began to be ignored by the Canadian government, we passed a racially specific Indian Act in order to designate who Indians were and who had a right to be Indians. This gave the federal government the virtual power of life or death over aboriginal people. We entered into a very shameful era of history in terms of the relationship between our nation and aboriginal nations on this continent.
I do not have to go through the recitation of events that happened in terms of the Canadian government's intent to destroy aboriginal culture either through physical extermination or through the cultural extermination of those people. The residential school system is one way where children were taken away from their parents and moved to residential schools where their parents could no longer have an influence on them. Those residential schools attempted, by a process of physical abuse and humiliation, to try to drive the culture out of those children so that they would no longer be Indian children.
When that aboriginal residential school system broke down back in the 1960s, the provincial governments, which had the right to exert child welfare legislation under the Indian Act on Indian reserves, then began to seize aboriginal children from their parents. They felt that only white middle-class parents had the proper standards and the proper norms to bring up aboriginal children in our society.
As a result of those two systems, tremendous damage was done to Indian children. Tremendous damage was done to Indian families. Tremendous damage was done to the self-esteem of aboriginal people and as a result,
many of their communities have suffered virtual collapse.
Today another situation is occurring. As my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace indicated, aboriginal people are now beginning to take over control of their own education systems. As a result, those systems are now succeeding. Aboriginal people have now begun to take over their own child welfare systems and as a result those systems are now succeeding.
Aboriginal people have begun to take over control of their own communities and have begun to enforce the law in their own communities and to establish standards of social behaviour in their own communities. As a result, they are beginning to beat the problem of substance abuse, violence and those kinds of things that have affected many aboriginal communities over the years as a result of the impact of our residential school system and the imposition of our child welfare system on aboriginal communities.
So we have two things working here. We have noted that aboriginal people have been extremely successful governing themselves. They can be successful in education, successful in child welfare, successful in running their own communities, successful in economic development, successful in post-secondaiy education when we do not try to look over their shoulder and tell them how to do it and try to set our model for how they should govern themselves.
But I think the issue here, Mr. Speaker, is the issue of the right to self-government. This is a right that we have to recognize. It is not a right that we can delegate. It is not a right that we can give to people. It is a right that they have had on this continent since time immemorial and was never taken away from them by conquest or by any legal transaction.
I support this motion. I congratulate the member for bringing it forward and I hope that the government will acknowledge that it goes along with the proposals that it has made in the constitutional proposals that came down last week. I hope that this Parliament can unanimously support this resolution so that the government will have our sanction to go out and negotiate with aboriginal people and with the other players in the constitutional debate. We can then achieve something that all Canadians can be proud of in terms of the way that we relate to aboriginal people on this continent.
October 1, 1991

Private Members' Business
In winding up I just want to quote the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs: "The failure to recognize the rights of aboriginal people to self-government weakens our whole country. Recognizing that right will make our country stronger". Let us get together in this Parliament to support the statement made by the minister responsible for the Constitution, make our country stronger, and improve our reputation around the world by supporting this motion.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opportunity to report on this government's record on aboriginal economic development is really quite timely given the recent constitutional proposals which focus largely on developing a new partnership for prosperity.
Canada has much to gain from improved aboriginal economic activity, not just in better aboriginal social conditions, but in realizing our national goal of partnership for prosperity.
A fully participating aboriginal labour force would produce a dramatic and positive effect on Canada's fiscal position as well as bringing about employment and wage parity between aboriginal and other Canadian workers, a goal which I am sure everyone in this House would support.
Economic self-reliance is an integral part of the foundation for aboriginal self-government. Economic self-reliance and self-government are two sides of the same coin. One cannot work without the other. That is why this government has strengthened the many programs and strategies to help develop strong and diversified economies in aboriginal communities and marketable skills among our aboriginal workers.
We have done this in partnership with aboriginal people by ensuring that they have the tools and decisionmaking powers over federal economic programs to manage and develop their own economies in accordance with the wishes of their communities.
First and foremost among our success stories is the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, CAEDS. This innovative program was launched just over two years ago and in this short time significant gains have been made: one, with aboriginal businesses and community leaders, a strong aboriginal controlled development capacity has been put in place through community based aboriginal capital corporations; two, more than 780 new aboriginal businesses have been launched, including gas stations, grocery stores, motels, wild rice processing plants, shopping plazas, and an airline; three, 24,000 aboriginal people have participated in federally funded skills training programs; four, significant agreements have been reached with provinces on forestry resource access and with the private sector on employment and contracting through CAEDS assisted resource access negotiations.
My colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, will shortly be tabling a full report to this House on these achievements which are being led by three departments, Indian Affairs and Northern Development; Industry, Science and Technology, Canada; and the Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission.
Indian Affairs has the lead in the community economic development and access to the resource component of CAEDS. In addition as part of its statutory responsibilities the department has prepared an inventory of available mineral resources on reserve lands to assist Indian bands in determining the feasibility of further exploration.
Similarly, Indian Oil and Gas Canada was created to optimize the royalty benefits from oil and gas resources on reserves.
It is continuing to work and to improve the services it provides to the Indian bands to help improve the reserves of oil and gas.
Through the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, that department plays the lead in the business development role by providing contributions to businesses for start-up and expansion, and by ensuring $160 million capital base is available to aboriginal capital corporations to provide a source of debt equity to aboriginal businesses.
These native-run loan companies already provide credit and related services to nearly 50 per cent of aboriginal communities. In 1990-91 Employment and Immigration spent more than $139 million as part of its Pathways to Success program to provide training and services to approximately 24,000 aboriginal clients, half of whom have turned that training into jobs.

Private Members' Business
This year target spending has increased to $200 million. With federal assistance, there are currently more than 92,000 aboriginal people with post-secondary education qualifications and more are coming onstream all the time.
All of these endeavours are providing aboriginal individuals and communities with the means to become economically self-reliant. This is being done by aboriginal people taking control of their own economic development at the grass roots level.
This bottom-up approach through CAEDS empowers aboriginal communities to build the expertise, the organization and manpower needed to solve their own problems. The federal government is also embarking on an aboriginal work force participation initiative to open up more labour market opportunities to what is rapidly becoming a highly skilled, well educated aboriginal work force.
Under this initiative, federal departments will improve the retention and the promotion of native people within the federal Public Service. It will also strengthen entiy level programs for aboriginal post-secondary graduates, improve contacts with aboriginal organizations to identify prospective job applicants, and use summer training courses and work experience more extensively with aboriginal students to introduce them into the Public Service.
It has to be clear to my hon. colleague that not only are we delivering on the promises we made one year ago with this program when the Prime Minister did unveil the native agenda, but with our new Partnership for Prosperity initiative, the government is also continuing to take action and will produce even better results to improve the socioeconomic conditions of native people.
Our Partnership for Prosperity urges all levels of government and the private sector to do their part to ensure greater economic harmony with our aboriginal people, and we all can share in that.
We are enjoying co-operation from the government of the Northwest Territories. Last summer my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, signed a $38.5 million economic development co-operation agreement with the territorial Minister of Economic Development and Tourism.
The accord provides funding for initiatives in the areas of cultural industries, community-sponsored development, minerals, agriculture, wildlife harvesting and fisheries. I know this initiative will work toward achieving a self-supporting, economically stable environment for our northern colleagues.
The key to success of all these ventures is that they are based on the advice given by aboriginal people. We consult with the aboriginal people and we will listen. We agree with them on how we can work together and follow their lead.
More skilled and more educated workers are coming onstream. Hundreds of new businesses and hundreds of new business ventures have been launched.
Aboriginal administrators are assuming greater control over their social and economic development in their communities. Here is the proof that partnerships result in real progress. This breakthrough has come about because our government is determined to develop a program. We want to take our policies and through devolution recognize that community leaders who are well versed in the needs and goals of their own members can best design and best deliver programs for their own people in their own communities.
At last count more than 72 per cent of all DIAND program dollars was being administered by Indians and Inuits through various funding arrangements. These agreements give communities the flexibility they need to apply those funds as they see fit to the priorities that they determine and their membership determines.
In the near future, Indian nations will have greater legal authority to assume authority over even more than their own affairs. Working groups of chiefs are currently developing proposals for legislative alternatives to the Indian Act which will deal with the areas of Indian moneys and taxation among other things.
The new powers accorded under this legislation will allow bands to determine their own economic destiny, and so they should.
Bill C-115 was the first Indian-led change to the Indian Act. It clearly established the authority of band councils to tax all interests in reserve lands. The new powers provided under this legislation allow bands to
October 1, 1991

establish a tax base and generate revenues which can be used in pursuit of their own community development.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is working with Indian taxation advisory boards. He is working to effect the results so that growing numbers of bands, such as the Westbank, Kamloops and the Musqueam Indian bands of British Columbia, will all have formal powers.
I must say that my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace has put forth a fine motion and it is veiy timely. I think much more needs to be done. We look forward to the discussions on the proposals over the next few months. The aboriginal people can certainly count on our support.

Mr. Speaker, I also would like to thank the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for introducing this motion tonight. It is of utmost importance because aboriginals were the first citizens, or should I say the first inhabitants, of this country. They have been here for thousands and thousands of years. They have never been recognized as such. They also have never been recognized as a founding nation. Instead they were enticed into signing treaties which created ghettos, which we prefer to call reserves.
Aboriginals never gave up their rights to self-govem. This is why the principle today has reached its maturity, but it could not be accomplished unless economic aid comes with it. One must remember that in isolated communities in particular unemployment hovers around 90 per cent. Chances for investment are not really good as most of those First Nations communities are remote and isolated. Training programs could be of some help if some permanent jobs would follow afterward.
It is a great time also because of the prejudice and the racism that exist in our justice system for First Nations communities to administer their own. One thinks readily about the Navajo nation in southwestern United States which does have its own justice system and which works extremely well according to its own values.
Tbrning to the area of health, it is a shame that upon visiting reserve after reserve the sewer and water systems are so deficient that one would think one was in a
Private Members' Business
Third World country. It is a bloody shame that Canadians do not put up the necessary funds, that this government would not put up the necessary funds to modernize the sewer and water systems in first community nations.
As paradoxical as it may sound, teachers' residences and hospital are connected to the sewer systems but not the residences of the natives. It is not unusual to see on a reserve two or three miles of sewer and water lines all around the village, but no one is connected to it except hospitals and teachers' residences.
In the area of education, the number of dropouts is unacceptable as education is the base for future self-government. The future chiefs need to be educated. They need to be educated in their own culture in their own communities, because the culture shock they face when they are studying in "white high schools" is incredible. This is why the number of dropouts is increasing dramatically, which leads to other social programs of course.
The Indian Act needs a motor job, a total overhaul: that is motor and chassis and everything. It is high time that modem rules and regulations and laws apply to the first inhabitants of our country. This includes the Prime Minister's new proposal where he suggests that Indian self-government should come within 10 years. That is far too much time. All those years of begging and pleading with successive governments for improvements are finished. It is quite understandable that aboriginal peoples all across Canada are crying for help, and it is totally justified if you see some of those reserves.
Therefore, by accepting this motion, the Government of Canada would send out a signal that the first nations are accepted as a full-fledged partner of this Confederation.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to add a few comments to what has already been said here today, but particularly to commend the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace for bringing this motion forward. I think it is a very sensitive and very critical issue at the present time. I think it is something that we as citizens of Canada have recognized. We respect the member's particular views as he has outlined them in this particular motion.

I think it is also recognizable that the government in its proposal has brought these same things forward, and I think that is very important. It is this government that has been dedicated and made a strong effort to resolve as many of these problems as can be resolved in as quick a time as possible. I do not think there is any denying that aboriginal peoples need to have their rights and their reality reflected in the Constitution of this country. No other group of Canadians has had to fight to defend rights that are as intrinsic as their heritage.
One of the most basic principles of democracy, the right and responsibility to control one's affairs, has eluded native people. It is wrong. It is unjust and frankly we must change it.
Common sense dictates that aboriginal people know best how to help themselves. That is the direction we are going to have to go in the future. The powerlessness they feel now leads to their helplessness, and that is not constructive for anyone.
There have been a number of initiatives brought forward by this government. I think it is very important that they have been outlined by different speakers here today. Because I do not have much time left, I would just like to comment on a couple of these things.
In consideration of consultations with regard to the constitutional proposal presently before the Canadian public, it ensures that aboriginal people will participate in the current constitutional deliberations. In fact, as an example, the band administrator in my riding from the Chippewas of Georgina, Mr. William McCue is sitting on my local constituency group studying the constitutional proposals. He is sitting there as a Canadian, as a person who wants to build a better place and a better country. I am very proud of that fact, and I know Bill is very proud of being involved in that process. That is why we want to continue with that kind of co-operative type of development.
There are many examples that the federal government has taken. The approach is very different and we recognize that, but the very real needs of aboriginal people in every comer of this country must be addressed on an individual basis. Each claim settlement is unique.
Each must reflect the needs and the aspirations of the unique community that it serves.
It cannot just try to use a blanket statement. That has been tried too often in the past and is not going to work in the future. This government is committed to negotiating settlements that will ensure that land and resources are managed in an orderly manner with the support of all Canada in a way that strengthens the entire nation.
This is what we can and must do. It is essential to complete the circle of Confederation so that all Canadians, whether they be native or non-native, can call this Canadian House their home.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this will be the conclusion of the speech I started earlier today.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, I would like to say that, as I said earlier on in my speech, Mr. Bean was a very good administrator. He did what he had to do. As reported in the Toronto Star, he did something he had to do, but it wasn't easy. It meant cutting 20 positions, cutting $1.8 million in his budget, and so forth. All this is good management, but he was unable to save those 20 jobs.
In fact, there is a problem with union democracy, if one can use that term. People come and tell me they want to negotiate. That is all they want. They say they want to negotiate, but they don't know Mr. Bean walked away from the bargaining table. Union members don't seem to be aware of this. We have a problem here. They want to bargain, and they wonder why we aren't bargaining. They say it's all the government's fault. As I said earlier, it is always the government's fault, whatever happens.
If the Olympic stadium in Montreal is falling to pieces, it's Brian Mulroney's fault. That is the easy way out. I say Mr. Bean is not keeping his members informed. I say that Mr. Bean may be a good administrator, but he is not the right person to keep his people informed. People simply don't know what is going on. Maybe Mr. Bean wants us to do in the public service what he did when he cut positions at union headquarters. For all I know, that
may be what he wants. If it is, well, 6,000 jobs will be lost, something we as a government cannot tolerate.
Our listeners must realize that Mr. Bean left the bargaining table without responding to our offer. He decided to give his union's response through the media, by going on strike. His members are not getting the whole story. I would like to say to our listeners that the wage freeze also applies to members of Parliament, ministers, the Prime Minister, Deputy Ministers, and senior management in the Public Service. I am sure a lot of people will be glad when they realize the salaries of politicians have been frozen as well.
Madam Speaker, in concluding, it is really too bad when 200 people barge into my office uninvited and take over my office and my staff. I have two employees who do more than is humanly possible. So these people, whose manners leave something to be desired, think they have every right to take over my office. They are on strike, so they can do anything they like. Well, I repeat, I will never give in to intimidation. I will never give in to blackmail or lies, because these are the people who asked me to be strong and honest and work very hard for their sake.
It is not always easy to say yes, and I think that the greatest gift I can give my people is honesty. And I am Sony to see, Madam Speaker, that those of my constituents who think that we are to blame were not informed of the facts by Mr. Bean. I think I have drawn an accurate picture and one as complete as possible. I hope that the people will believe that what I said is the truth and that they will shake that bloody myth of strikes being caused by our giving $80,000 in bonuses. We hear it every day. It is a myth that is being created. That is not the problem. They had bonuses before and there will always be bonuses. Bonuses are not a bad thing, but we have to freeze them. And they will be frozen because there are people earning $300,000 or $400,000- How much does the chairman of Petro-Canada make again? Five or six hundred thousand a year? Yet, he gets an $800 bonus every time he chairs the board. What do you expect! I agree with my colleague that it is too much, but in the private sector, the president of Imperial Oil earns that much and that is the way things go, that's competition. Maybe he too is getting too much!
So, here is what I tell my colleagues, my people and my constituents: we must look at both sides and avoid making the same mistake as the president of the union, Mr. Bean, i.e. cutting jobs to give a 3 per cent raise instead of zero per cent. We must be honest. These
October 1, 1991

things must be said. There is nothing better than dialogue with both sides telling the truth. I was almost intimidated into telling lies today. But I will never give in to blackmail. I will never accept to change my tune just to win a vote.
I would have preferred to do without emergency legislation. I was proud, last week that we had come to an agreement. I even put out a release. It will be remembered. Verba volant, scripta manent, as the proverb goes. Unfortunately, he quickly left the table. We cannot be blamed for that! I told our guys, our employees: "You deserve better, you are working people and you do an excellent job in members' offices. We need you. But the truth of the matter is that we are all in the same boat. There is a zero per cent increase across the board." Our financial needs are increasing. I gave the example of my son at University and others as well.
In closing, Madam Speaker, it is a fact that, whether you are a member of Parliament or a civil servant, if our salaries are frozen, our financial burden gets heavier. Children's education, transportation, fuel, everything costs more. But it might all be for the best, and I tell my people: "Bear with us. You will see that we are doing this not for the short term but for the long term."

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member for Laval East.
Maybe the constituents of Laval East do not have the full story. I want to tell the member for Laval East that Canadians are not stupid, that Canadians are well informed. They know that this government, with its high interest rates, high dollar policies and 33 new tax increases since September 1984, is the source of inflationary pressures. They know that taking purchasing power away from consumers will only deepen and prolong the recession. They know that the Tory government intends to impose a freeze on federal Public Service wage increases for 1991-92 and an annual 3 per cent limit on federal Public Service wage increases over the next two years. They know the Tory government is encouraging provincial and municipal governments to
Government Orders
impose similar wage controls. They know that wage controls in the public sector inevitably limit wage settlements for all Canadian workers. They know that there is no flexibility when a limit on wage increases is imposed on everyone, whether a clerk, a deputy minister or a president of a Crown corporation.
They know in Laval East and everywhere else in this country that the Conservative federal government is prepared to take away the collective bargaining rights of workers across this country, threaten them with job losses and contracting out, interfere with conciliation and arbitration, and legislate employees back to work. They know this government is being unfair.
I want to ask the member for Laval East: Does he think Canadians know these facts?

Madam Speaker, I do not know how to explain to this member more than the others. If they were informed, how come I asked my people to send to me in writing what they would like to have from us?
They said: "We would like to negotiate as normal human beings". I said: "Good, see Mr. Bean but you have a problem. Mr. Bean did not inform you that he quit the table". I do not think they were informed of everything.
When they got the information, because of the fact that they listened a lot to the opposition, they do not get it exactly or the phrase is cut before the end. That is what embarrasses me. I try to be honest and tell them the truth. I have nothing to lose by telling the truth. This is what I want to tell my hon. friend. We did not take away anything. The provinces got the freeze by legislation. He would not negotiate. We are not so bad. We negotiate.
Look what happened in New Brunswick. They promised an increase and after the election they pushed the legislation through and that was it. That is nice.
Canadians are not dumb, but they are not well informed. It depends on who gives them the information. As far as I am concerned on this side, I will give them the right time and I will not change my mind just to win a vote.

Government Orders
This is what is in my mind and heart. I hope people will understand that on election day. If they do not, they will regret that.

Madam Speaker, I too would like to ask a question of the member for Laval East with regard to his speech.
He seems to have identified Mr. Daryl Bean as being the problem. I want to tell the member for Laval East, as a member of Parliament from British Columbia, that British Columbians know how trade unions operate and how certification of a trade union is developed and carried through.
I want to say to the Conservative members from British Columbia that my constituents from my riding and from British Columbia will recognize that there is a very important point being left out by this government.
First of all, they are a recognized, certified union, that has the right to bargain free and collectively with this government. This government has authorized that. They have a legal strike situation on their hands and they are negotiating a package. However, when negotiations break down, people in my part of the country know that mediation is made available. The situation is taken out of the hands of the two combatants, the government and PSAC, and an independent mediator sits and tries to hear both sides.
This government denies that. It denies that mediation approach that takes it out of the hands of the adversaries, hears both sides of the problem and tries to deal with it. No, the government has decided not to allow that to happen. In other words, it is dictatorial.
For the first time in the history of the House of Commons back to work legislation is going to be invoked on workers without an independent mediation officer hearing what the two sides of these issues are.
I want to ask the member for Laval East if he thinks that is going to enhance labour relations between public servants and the Government of Canada. Mediation is a very important aspect of negotiations. This may be the first time in history that we will ever see government bring in back to work legislation without even an arbitrator at the end to look at it and bring in binding arbitration.
As a trade unionist I saw that process take place when the Liberals were in power. At least that process was followed. This is the first time in history that we have ever seen dictatorial policies of a government. When negotiations break down on either side, if either one is to blame, there is an independent mediator that should be looking at the issue.
I ask the member why we are not following that procedure before we bring about dictatorial policies of the government.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to answer immediately, no.
I will not enforce a relation with my people because of something other than the reality, that we do not want to negotiate.
I will ask the member. He can always answer me later. Why did Mr. Bean quit the table? Why did he not take the opportunity, which I thought was gold, last week? Why did Mr. Bean cut 20 people in his staff and give 3 per cent? Why did he not keep the 20 people and keep the zero?
Maybe he is a good administrator.

up to the teeth. No doubt by leaving the table and going back to the picket lines and all the troubles there have not helped the unions or the Public Service or anybody.
I would not like the hon. member for Laval East to get into all the pluses and minuses of who is right and who is wrong. However, what is wrong with the mediation procedures that are there and all the laws of Canada, both provincial and federal?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member. He knows what I feel and he knows that I always try to stand up for my people. He made a deal with someone and he cannot even respect his own deal, a golden deal which he signed and was happy with. He even called the minister uncle, uncle Tom or uncle Gilles given the opportunity. He did not respect it. Now they want to negotiate it. What do they want next?
It scares me to deal with people who have no respect and do not tell the truth to their members. That is the bad feeling I had today when I saw 200 people breaking into my office. I feel sorry for these people because I like these people. They have nice jobs and they are doing a good job.
Even if the people think that all public servants are lazy, we have the cream of the crop in Laval. We have the best people. Some of them give me 110 per cent of what they can do. When some quit we see the difference immediately. Some quit and we see a difference; we cannot get our dossier through. We give our word when we make a deal and they do not respect it. They want a mediator or an outside man. We know what we have in our pocket. We do not need an outside man to tell us what to do. We have nothing left. It is empty. There is no more, finished, that is all.
Now the outside man will tell us: "Be a nice guy". We have been nice guys. We tried to give all the other things. We went in the back pocket, in the little pocket, in the inside pocket and came up with $500 for the people who make less than $27,000. It is not a big salary and $500 is a slap in the face, but I know in my area without a job they would take two slaps in the face for $500 each. They would take it on both chins.
This is not the deal that we are going to put on the table for our people for them to tell us that they need a
Government Orders
negotiator. Then what will they need? He does not want violence or intimidation. Block the bridge, do not let people into work. I have people in my area who want to work. Do you know what they said: "If you go to work, my friend, we will remember your name. We will write it on the wall".
Is that what we want? I do not like violence. I like negotiation. I like the guy who respects his name on the piece of paper. Somebody says: "It is all Mr. Bean's fault". He signed the paper. He was here knocking on the door at eleven o'clock in the morning instead of being at the table to negotiate. Now he wants a mediator. What is he going to ask for next?

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to stand in this House today and address the bill before us, Bill C-29.
My colleague from Laval East has just spoken with a great deal of passion and he has accentuated the element of truth in this debate. I just want to remind him of the truth.

Truth is open to interpretation.

I have every intention to be as truthful as I can be. I ask Canadians who are watching us to decide which of the two sets of truths they feel is the more reliable one. I say this positively, certainly not with any kind of malice in my heart.
There is a pattern here that I think has to be noticed. This government has had a lot of difficulty in managing a number of programs in Canada since it came to power in 1984. It has botched up a lot of things. I do not say that unkindly. Governments do that.

Government Orders
If one looks for example at the F-18 contract which was awarded to a province other than Manitoba, one has to ask what kind of truth there was there. Did truth prevail?
When you look at the closing of the bases and you look at whether those bases were situated in constituencies that had certain members as opposed to others, you have to wonder what kinds of truth prevailed.
When you look at the privatization of Air Canada, you have to ask whether those 3,000 people who are without jobs are better off. Look at VIA Rail; roughly another
3,000	gone. They have no work. What about CN? About 25 per cent less employment since this government has come into power. Ask the workers what they think about that. Look at the CBC cuts. I guess that was really positive as well, was it? Ask Canadians what they think about those CBC cuts.

Ask the people in my community, ask francophones outside Quebec what they think about it. Come and talk to them, and you will see the kind of reception you will get!

There are a couple of questions here that I think are extremely important, one of which is the whole notion of legality of a strike. This is a legal strike. There are a lot of people out there who are trying to suggest that it is other than legal. This is a legal strike, but it raises certain important questions. Should the Public Service be allowed to strike? Perhaps that is the question that we ought to be debating. Under what circumstances should it be allowed to strike, or should it not be allowed to strike?
It raises another important question. My hon. colleague referred to it before. What are the appropriate strike activities when a union is in a strike position?

I do not condone acts of violence, and I believe I am not alone. I don't like the kind of intimidation that is going on when some workers are told: If you go to work, we will tell everyone. I hate this attitude, and I will do everything I can to stop it. That is a promise. People have called to tell me how upset they were because of the kind
of behaviour I just mentioned, and I think this is really too bad.

All of this raises perhaps the ultimate question. Government is using its power to override a law which contains a fundamental right. The question has to be: Who's next? There is danger obviously if you represent a cause that is not particularly popular politically. We all know that the Public Service, because it is not well known, because people do not understand it and because there are all kinds of myths that exist that are untruths, is a target that is not always a popular one.
The government can do as it pleases more or less, and it has taken advantage of the situation. As parliamentarians we have to ask the basic fundamental question: If it does it to this union, if it does it to collective bargaining, will it do it to someone else, to some other group on some other law next, some right that you and I and other Canadians have? That frightens me.

Frankly, I wonder whether other groups and individuals and, in fact, rights we all have as Canadians might be affected the same way.

Let us talk about this notion of fat cats. There is no doubt about it that there are some excellent salaries out there within the Public Service.

You really have to take a long, hard look at this question. Look at the facts! There are a lot of people who are not that well paid. Suppose we look at the various pay categories.

It is rather interesting to note that there are roughly 250 people who earn between $20,000 and $24,999. There are another almost 65,000 people who earn between $25,000 and $29,999. According to my figures, and I believe that they are the most up to date figures available, almost 18,000 earn between $30,000 and $34,999.
Already I have mentioned roughly very close to one-half of the people who are within the Public Service. It is very close to one-half of those people.
October 1, 1991

Think of this. You are living perhaps in Ottawa or in another major city, and let us remember that in Ottawa and Hull we have the majority of public servants. How would you as a father or a mother with a family be able to make a living if you are earning between $20,000 and $25,000 or between $25,000 and $30,000 in this area? You might have a better chance at it if you were between $30,000 and $35,000, but you would not be labelled a fat cat.
The other question that we have to ask is: Why this strike at this time? My hon. colleague was up on his feet with a great deal of passion and emotion. I believe that he said what he truly felt in his heart. He said: "Our pockets are empty".
I will address that very shortly. Why in the world did the government appoint a mediator in the postal strike when it had that option available here? Why le double standard? Why treat one group one way and another group another way?
I believe that this government wants this strike, that it believes that the public is on its side. What options did it have?

They had several. I asked the Library of Parliament to prepare a study so I could look at the options that were available to the government.

We talked of mediation. There is no need to define it. I think most people know what it is all about. We talked of conciliation, a very similar process in which there is a third party brought in. We can talk of fact finding: someone comes in, finds out the facts and lays them out.
We can talk about interest arbitration, another method of getting third party input but where the conclusions or the recommendations are binding. We can talk about final offer selection and mediation arbitration.
This study also indicates what kind of success this has had in the past. The government had several options available to it. It chose mediation for the postal strike, but it did not choose it in this particular case. Why, why, why?
Let me share with you what a prominent journalist, Jeffrey Simpson, said in The Globe and Mail on Septem-
Govemment Orders
ber 17: "Offering public servants a contract with no wage increase in the first year was deliberately provocative and of small consequence in the battle against the deficit".
I do not think he favours one party over the other. He is one of those individuals who tries to be honest and call the shots as he sees them. This is what he says: "Offering public servants a contract with no wage increase in the first year was deliberately provocative and of small consequence in the battle against the deficit".
It was not a Liberal or a member of the New Democratic Party who said that or a member of another party.
It was an independent journalist who said it. There have been a number of provocations. Here is another one. My colleague talks about the bonuses. You know, it is not the notion of the money involved in the bonuses that prevents people from sitting down at the negotiating table. It is the symbol of the bonuses that prevents the dialogue.
When you have 5,000 or more cabinet appointees who got bonuses in the past year that exceed the salaries of a number of civil servants, some of whom are single parents with families, then of course you get people angry. This is the point that bothers me, that people have not understood that this is provocation. This gets people angry. It gets them darned mad, and I have other words that I could use. I have other words that I could use.
Also, the increases to members of Parliament and others, senior bureaucrats, that were given prior to them. I understand what happened. I understand, in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent the day before the salary freeze was imposed. I understand. But if we had set the example, if they had set the example, do you think we would be having this kind of acrimony, this kind of difficulty right now in sitting down and trying to negotiate? I think not.
Let us not forget that an independent agency, which works for government, the Public Service Staff Relations Board said that the Treasury Board had engaged in bad faith bargaining. I did not say that. The New Democratic Party did not say that. Another political party did not say that. It was the Public Service Staff Relations Board. Treasury Board has engaged in bad faith bargaining.

Government Orders
The other thing that has never been said in this Chamber, or I have not heard it today, is that certain employees were granted a back room salary increase. They were moved up one increment in their pay scales. That is provocation. I cite ships' officers and air traffic controllers. I have no difficulty believing that they should have received increases. I believe they probably merited everything they received. But the fact that they did is an act of provocation. It sours the relationship. It prevents us from sitting down and trying to find a solution.
Several people have mentioned that we have no money.

I know that the deficit is exceeding $30 billion and that the debt is exceeding $400 billion, that is, double the one for the 1984-85 fiscal year. I know all that, but why does the government find money for other programs? I will give you some examples. I am delighted to see that it just made some announcements, because it finally transferred some corporations to Western Canada. It is time that we thought about responding to the needs of the West. We have found money to do it, and that is good. But you know, when we were talking, for example, of the 3 per cent raise for the Public Service Alliance members, $144 million, that is a lot of money! It is probably more than what my colleagues have in their bank account today, a lot more!
Also, we must not forget that the government recently made some extraordinary expenses.

For example, the bailout of the frigates. Maybe that was a good decision, but it was $260-some million. The Gulf War was another $600 million. The GST, $358.4 million to implement the program. Over 4,000 people were hired. Office space this year is at an increase of $100 million, j)lus another $38.9 million for GST offices. There is over $1 billion there, ladies and gentlemen, in case you are wondering. I could mention another $1 billion if I had the time.
The government talks about people who are breaking the law, and with justification. I indicated before that I do not agree in any way, shape or form, with violence,
with the disruption that is being carried on by the union and union members. I am trying to understand it and I have given some reasons as to why I think it is happening. It is unfortunate and I hope that we can come to grips with that as soon as this whole dispute is in fact resolved, as I hope it will be very shortly.
What about pay equity? That is the law. Yet the government is ignoring the law. I know it will say: "but you brought it in and what did you do?" Well, do two wrongs make one right? Of course not.
Why would you be denying those who should be getting this kind of financial response, most of whom are women. In our society today why would you be doing that? Why would you be denying them their just due according to law?
Let me talk about contracting out. I have a veiy interesting figure to share with this House. When this particular party formed the government in 1984, we were talking about $1.7 billion in contracting out. Where are we now? In excess of $5 billion. Big, big increase. Now why?
I do not want to be unkind, but I do wish that I could determine with precision tonight in this House where that $3.3 billion increase is going. It would be an interesting discovery and I am afraid that it would cause severe fallout.
Let us look at the employees. When the government came to power in 1984-85 in that year there were 257,013 employees; in 1990-91 there are 221,859 employees, a drop of roughly 35,000, give or take a few.
Look at that drop in employees. Look at the increase in contracting out and tell me, tell Canadians, where is the saving? Have you really saved any money for Canadian taxpayers? If so, I would like you to point it out for me.
There was a very powerful statement in an editorial in The Ottawa Citizen dated September 17, 1991, one that I would really like members of government to explain to Canadians. It said: "All the government needed to do at any time to break the costly demoralizing impasse was to offer a token raise, two, two, and two per cent.
I understand, just in case my colleague gets over-excited that two-plus-two-plus-two compounded is more

than zero-plus-three-plus-three compounded. I want to get that clear. But it is minimal over all and it could have been offset by reductions in staff if there was actually a finite limit to the funds as they claim. So why not two-plus-two-plus-two, rather than approach it from a zero per cent increase which is deliberately provocative by itself? It would not have been more expensive over time. My colleagues know that. They have never explained that away satisfactorily, and I am sorry they have not because Canadians will know that it could have been done that way.
They will know that they are being deliberately belligerent because they believe they have a cause where their sag in popularity can in fact be raised.

Looking at this situation, one wonders what is happening now. Those who have listened and read know that it is a political issue. They understand this government is not very popular. They understand this government will try to increase its popularity, which is entirely normal when you have the favour of barely 10 per cent of the Canadian people according to the opinion pools. Also, they realize there has been some dishonesty-I don't say that to be nasty-on both sides, some exaggeration. It's a little like when you apply for a job, you put forward your best assets, sometimes a little embellished, a little exaggerated. But both sides have surely exaggerated their positions.
Canadian want workers to go back to work. And workers wants to go back to work. What they want is that the government show that it is willing to negotiate and that a wage increase could very well be possible, even though minimal or barely exceeding zero, for they want to go back to the table without having an iron collar imposed on them before getting there.
If I ask you to come to the table and tell you "This is what we will do within these parameters", this is not negotiating, this is imposing one's will, which is easy when you hold all the power. You don't need much courage. When you are big and powerful and able to crush the other party, this does not require any creativity, any power, any leadership. What requires leadership however is to bring people together, talk with them and
Government Orders
try to come to solutions that are both fair and sensible, solutions that respect them.

The workers want to get back to work. The government should appoint a mediator like it did in the postal strike. It should stop playing games. It should be getting the country back to work and it should do it now.
