Madam Speaker, unfortunately, I will not be able to answer all these questions, I will leave some for other members, but when my colleague mentioned wages, he forgot to work out the average. It is easy to say some employees are not earning a lot, some are, and then there are those who earn even more.
I want to put it on record and I hope the hon. member can provide us with some answers, because I have a couple of questions for him. An average yearly salary of $33,500 is well over the national average. But that is not all. Civil servants are also entitled to a fully indexed pension, that is interesting, as well as the best job security in Canada and a dental plan totally subsidized by the employer. Do you know how much that costs? I have children who often visit the dentist, Madam Speaker, and I can tell you it costs a bundle, as you well know, since you have had to deal with many dentists. You know how much it costs when you step into a dentist office. That is part of their wages and it is worth a lot.
They have a whole range of job-related benefits, such as a subsidized health plan, a subsidized disability plan, fully-paid sick leaves, fully-paid annual leaves, family responsibility leaves, including maternity leaves. That, of course, has to be added up to their wages.
Our colleague also mentioned-

People are allowed to strike, yes he is right. People who want to work are allowed to work, too, and that works both ways. But they did not, they were not allowed. They came to my office and said: "Sir, I want to work". They had to provide these essential services in the hospitals, for example, in Montreal. Yes, they are allowed to strike. Some are allowed to work.

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
Then he spoke about the contract, dropping out, why we didn't give two, two, two. Yes, we saved 6,000 jobs with zero, three and three.

The most important thing that I want to say to my colleague-besides, I explained it in my speech and I would not want to start it over, but I invite him to read it-is that if it is the way that the government has chosen to make itself popular, I find that he gets the opposite result.
Then, my question is this: when you analyze a salary, why dont you analyze also the benefits that my people in Laval would really like to have, the fringe benefits, as they are called. Why did we put a cap of 0-3-3 to save
6,000	which Mr. Bean did not?

I said right from the beginning that I deplored violence, that one of the questions we ought to be discussing is when you are in a strike position, what are the activities that are appropriate, and which ones are inappropriate? There are inappropriate activities taking place right now. When you shout out people's names, when you say that you will remember them, when you telephone them, when you harass them, that is wrong, wrong, wrong. I will do everything in my power, with the assistance of my colleagues, to stop that kind of nonsense.
But we also ought to be discussing the whole question as to whether or not there should be additional excluded categories as well.
The question ought to be whether the Public Service should strike or not. If it is going to be able to strike, then let us respect that. We have not respected it, we have made it look as if it was illegal and what have you.
The other question my colleague addressed is the whole question of salary; average salary and benefits. It is an excellent question and I appreciate it. However, he failed to tell us, although he knows, how much more it is than the national average. He knows that by taking the average salary, he can add in all of the part-time jobs, you know, the little service jobs, and make that average salary look a lot bigger. I will let him live with his
conscience. Perhaps he can see his priest over the weekend.
Let us talk about benefits. I cannot believe how a colleague would want to try to come to grips with the problems of fellow Canadians by trying to push them down, by saying, for example, "they have dental care". Good. All Canadians should have dental care. They have pensions. Good, all Canadians should have good pensions. They have indexed pensions. Well, let me tell you, I pay a share of my pension. Do you not? Before I came here I paid a share, and if it needs to be more so that it can be indexed, then ask me for more.
But let us not trample on everyone. Let us not push everyone down. Let us try to bring them up. Let us try to define what it is that every Canadian ought to have. Surely the way to go is not to trample upon them, to push them down. The way to go is to look at those who do not have enough; enough salary, enough pension, enough medical care, enough dental care, and to make sure they have it.
Madam Speaker, this is my final point and it will be brief. My colleague should know how much he is saving on dental care because as I understand it, we get a pretty good deal as members. He could have mentioned that figure too.

Madam Speaker, I have a comment I would like to make which will lead to a question of the hon. member. The comment is with respect to the agenda that this government has in introducing this legislation.
I would like to suggest that while the government keeps talking about the need to fight inflation and the deficit through this bill and through the real reduction of wages for its public servants, the reality is that it is doing something quite different. The reality is that the government is seeking, through this legislation, to destroy the rights of collective bargaining of its own public servants and seeks to destroy the union.
The government is not trying to save money. Quite the opposite, it is trying to score a political point. First, let me say on inflation that since 1985, only in one year has the Public Service received anything more than the rate of inflation.
Second, in terms of saving money, the only cost of a 3 per cent increase in one year would be .2 of 1 per cent of the total budget of this government. The government's figures are wrong. Its agenda is hidden and it is now coming clear.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member is quite correct, there is an agenda here. I indicated that earlier on. I think they are trying to score political points and there is a propaganda war going on. There is no doubt about that.
My colleague failed to mention, for example, that if you look at the recent increases, as my colleague just did, in the private sector and the Public Service during the last few years, the public sector has not had nearly as much as the private sector. The Public Service Alliance of Canada has not. I think we have to recognize that.
The other point I wanted to make is that it is difficult working with figures, my colleague said-you know, he is seething, but I have no problems. He says now they are getting 100 per cent dental care and we are only getting 80 per cent. They would love our pension plan rather than their own, would they not? So if you are going to make some comparisons be fair.
There is a big power play going on. It is government versus the union and the government is trying to take advantage of that. You know it as well as I do. I am disappointed you would not acknowledge it.
I will move a motion at the most appropriate moment which states that the hon. member prefers their working conditions and should get them for himself. I think that would be a noble gesture on my part, in view of the fact that he believes they are better treated than we are.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to advise the House that the first five hours of debate on third reading of this bill have now expired. We will now go to 10 minute speeches without questions or comment.

Madam Speaker, I rise to oppose this bill and to speak out against it as forcefully and as strongly as I can.
My opposition to the bill springs in part from my experience over about 15 years as a labour lawyer in the province of British Columbia and the perception and perspective that has given me and also as the member of Parliament for Victoria, a community that has expressed its views very forcefully in this dispute and is very strongly in favour of the alliance and its position and of the public servants in that community.
Government Orders
Bill C-29 is at one instance a fairly innocent piece of legislation in the way it reads, until one reads very carefully into the heart of the legislation. The heart of the legislation is found in three sections.
I ask those who are watching to consider what they would do if this applied to their particular collective agreement.
Section 5 simply provides that every compensation plan for employees to whom this act applies shall be extended for a period of 24 months, beginning on the day immediately following the day on which the compensation plan would, but for this section, expire.
It should be understood that this act applies not only to members of the alliance who are now on strike, but to members and officers of the Canadian forces; members and officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; the staff of this House of Commons who are without a union and have no voice speaking for them; members of the staff of the ministers of the Crown and members of the Senate and the House of Commons, agencies, boards and hundreds and hundreds and thousands of other employees in this country, many of whom have had no voice and are not party to this particular dispute.
Section 9 then goes on to provide for zero per cent in the first 12 months and a 3 per cent increase in the second 12 months of any compensation plan covered by the act.
Finally, in section 14, the act sets out penalties, up to $500 a day. The penalties not only apply to the unions or the representatives of the unions, but to employees who are required by the act not to do anything in contravention of the act. Included in that, they are not allowed to strike.
The right to collective bargaining is a right which has developed for over 80 years and to which this country has been a proud signator through the international labour conventions. The essence of the right to collective bargaining, which evidently the government members failed to grasp or understand, is that people in a free society have the right to consent to their working conditions and the right to gather together collectively to seek bargaining and working conditions that are suitable to them.
That right of collective bargaining has, over the years, been enshrined in legislation. It has been hard-fought

October l, 1991
Government Orders
for over the decades. In the 1960s and 1970s it finally came to public servants across this country.
It has been awfully difficult for some people to understand how public servants, police officers and others can have the right of collective bargaining, including the ultimate right to withdraw one's labour if one is not satisfied with the terms and conditions. But a very fine balance developed in the legislation.
Certain employees were excluded from the right to strike, but those whose work was deemed not absolutely essential or critical in the public interest on a day to day basis were given the right which all other Canadians have, the right to band together collectively, to seek certification, to bargain collectively with its employers and only to work after they have reached agreement and working conditions to which they consent.
This Parliament gave that right to its public employees. It called on the Government of Canada over successive years to comply with that law. Over the years, from time to time back to work legislation has been deemed necessary, but this bill, Bill C-29, is a particularly Draconian historic form of back to work legislation.
Most back to work legislation will either provide for a cooling off period while mediation goes to work or will impose arbitration so that the parties go back to work and independent third parties, having heard from both sides, reach a judgment as to what are fair working conditions.
This legislation does no such thing. This legislation rejects the findings of conciliation boards and independent parties who have looked at the situation. Instead, it seeks to impose the government's view as to what are the appropriate working conditions for its employees.
The government, by this legislation, is using and confusing its role as employer and its role as the introducer of legislation into this Parliament. It is taking a power which no other employer in this country has and it is coming to this Parliament and asking it to impose the government's view as to what are the appropriate working conditions for employees of the public sector.
No other legislation coming before this Parliament has ever done such a thing. The Conservative Party, which used to think of itself as a voice for rights of Canadians,
is seeking to impose this legislation and to strip away the rights of its own public servants.
Shame on this government. We say this legislation is in conflict with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I defy the government to introduce into this House any legal opinion that suggests that this legislation does not conflict with the charter of rights.
The charter of rights gives to Canadians equality of treatment under the law. Other Canadians have the right of free collective bargaining and, if pushed to the wall, the right to strike. How come the government comes in here and takes that right away?
If it says that in the public interest this dispute must end, then it is obliged first to demonstrate overwhelmingly that the public interest calls for this strike to end and second, and even more important because a wide number of Canadians would probably agree that, at a certain point a strike in the public sector must come to an end.
If it does so, it must only do so after it has bargained in good faith for a significant period of time, it has used all the machinery available to it such as conciliation, mediation and finally, it introduces the most minimalist example of back to work legislation, that is, either a cooling off period or the imposition of arbitration.
There is simply no excuse for legislation which rips away the rights of Canadians in the fashion that this bill does.
This bill is simply bad managerial policy. It is sending thousands of Canadians back to work bitter at the government, bitter at its employers, bitter at its fellow employees across the line. Even internal disputes within the union will arise because of the difficulties that this legislation has imposed on the Public Service Alliance of Canada which fought a tremendous fight and initially won a great victory over this government. This legislation is going to leave a long-standing and bitter legacy. It is legislation which this government and this country will regret for many years.
Let me conclude by saying that out of all bad things some good may come and out of this Draconian legislation is the coming of age of the public servants of this country. I have spoken to them in Ottawa; I have spoken to them in Victoria. The message is coming loud and clear. Finally the public servants of this country have realized that they too have a stake in the kind of

government we have. They too have a stake in ensuring that they elect to Parliament people who will fight for their rights and not impose this kind of legislation upon them.
They are speaking for thousands of Canadians who now have a new vision of the kind of Canada we want, a Canada of equity, a Canada of justice, a Canada of rights. I call on this House to defeat this legislation and to launch a new day of labour relations for the public sector in this country.

Madam Speaker, being in the ten-minute rule it makes one rather focused. It is rather interesting that I follow the hon. member for Victoria who spoke very eloquently and in a professorial style with respect to the rights of the public in collective bargaining.
If I had had an opportunity to present a question to him before launching into my debate, I would have asked if he felt there was any difference between the rights of collective bargaining and the right to strike in the Public Service as against the right in the private sector. I think I know what his answer may have been.
In the few minutes I have on this very important issue I would like to go back, and I think it might bemuse the member for Victoria, and refer to the bill giving the Public Service the right to strike. In that debate on the Public Service Collective Bargaining Act of 1957, pages 13184 and following, I then, was a young pup member, against the august invincible Grit government of the day with Mr. Benson as President of the Treasury Board. I am not sure if the hon. member's father, as member for Victoria, was in the House then but he and I did serve in this House at the same time.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre at the time, the elegant statesman who is at the table, Mr. Knowles, participated very much in this debate.
At that time-unbeknownst to me that some 24 years later I would be able to read Hansard-and in a more naive approach than now I pointed out the concerns I had about extending the right to strike to members of the Public Service.
This has been a very difficult debate. No one has been, I think, happy about the situation. Certainly the public is
Government Orders
not happy about the situation. As far as I am concerned as I read the public, there is a plague on both of our houses, the House of Commons and all those involved in it, and also the house of Public Service, the PSAC, with their machinations as they try to get response to their legitimate demands. Or perhaps they have accepted some bait put out there by the government creating this confrontational situation which frankly has not helped anybody.
When this House came back after the summer recess, this bill was introduced. I must say that at that time, long before the Public Service Staff Relations Board, chaired by the former House leader of the NDP, the hon. Mr. Ian Deans, said that the Government of Canada had negotiated in bad faith-which I thought poetic justice-I also thought the Government of Canada had negotiated in bad faith. If the bill had proceeded and come to a vote at that time I must say I was prepared. Although I don't think it would have represented the collective view of my constituency which wanted the strike over, does not have a great body of public servants, and it would be very easy to side myself with the majority of good hard-working people who are my constituents, I think I would have surprised them if I had voted against the government bill and, in effect, for the PSAC. However, I honestly did not believe there had been proper bargaining procedures and that they had been bargaining in good faith. Goodness gracious, Madam Speaker, if, with all the hue and cry, we can appoint a mediator under conciliation procedures and the labour laws of Canada for the postal union and the postal problems, regardless of the physical package that the government is understandably trying to negotiate, we could have at least gone through the motions, to say the least, and might even have gone through more than the motions, to have a mediator.
I was in my window looking out at the 20,000 public servants on that lawn Monday morning and Monday noon. I must say that having seen a few sporadic displays the week before when I was here doing business, I was a little impressed and not swayed by the numbers, knowing that three-quarters of the people out there had never been politicized, radicalized. I knew that we had all had a good summer to get rested and regenerated, to come back for the fall Parliament when national building and the nation's soul searching was going to be the priority.

Government Orders
I was looking out there at these 20,000 servants of yours and mine and the millions across the country. I just could not believe that a government trying to start out with peace and good will to all, as we go through the difficult constitutional process, had either engineered or had stumbled into this situation. I am not casting blame, because as far as I am concerned, there is blame on both their houses. I thought and said to my staff: "Look, the Prime Minister has the pizzazz and the chutzpah and the street smarts, let alone his history of labour negotiation and working with tougher people than Mr. Bean on the longshore front of Montreal and other interesting places, to come out from the House of Commons and go before that crowd. And, if he had been yelled down and not given a voice and an ear, then that would have redounded to his credit". I said to my staff: "This could be the beginning of the turnaround for the low standing in the polls because there obviously has been a lot of politics in this whole business that is facing us this Monday". And I really thought that that might happen.
If it had happened and the Prime Minister of the land had come out, he perhaps did not even have to admit that he had made a mistake. He could have shown a little humility and said: "Perhaps we have made a mistake. Let's go back to the table. I am going to instruct the President of the Treasury Board to come and meet you and let us see if there is anything we can do that will fit within the physical framework. If we have to raise two and two and two then perhaps a hundred or a thousand jobs go out the window". But at least get back in there and go through the motions in a meaningful substantive way.
That did not happen, Madam Speaker. Yet we had the truce. If I had been a Tory backbencher trying to defend the government of the day on Monday and Tuesday, and then knowing that the House leader of the NDP was out being the honest broker to get the parties back to the table after I and others on the government side hypothetically had been defending the government, and knowing that he was the one to get them back to the table, that would have made me a little upset, to say the least. I would have known full well, going back to the table with the conditions they went back to the table on, that most likely there would not have been much of a
settlement and we would be faced with another situation, which we are faced with today.
That was the beginning of the week then, Madam Speaker, and my sympathies certainly were with the poor bargaining process, to say the least, in a most conservative way, of what had gone on up to that date. I knew full well that there was blame on both sides. When the bargaining procedures, no matter how sincere or whatever finally dissolved last week, the strike was resumed. There was violence. Television coverage showed public servants grappling with their own and/or the public. I must say I believe with difficulty that it is time this strike with all the problems it has caused and which are going to linger with us is over. I agree with my hon. friend from Victoria that there has not been a bill as Draconian as this Bill C-29 to put people back to work without even a hint of mediation or arbitration. In view of what is happening to the public sector, and I agree that it is getting or is out of control, that this Parliament has to act for all the injured parties, all the third parties.
You are telling me already, Madam Speaker, that my time is up and I have not even got to quote you my pearls of wisdom from 1967 when the first bill to give the strike was debated in this House, when then I said the public servants at the time knew what their perks were, they knew they did not have the right to strike. I say, with all the other rhetoric that has been said in this difficult debate, that we had better start to go back to basics to see that if in the Public Service, let alone the postal service-that is another whole issue, and they cannot have the right to strike if they have got the monopoly on the mail service-but on the right generally for the Public Service, I think we have got to go back to that basic.
In conclusion, and the sadness, Madam Speaker, is just to read a short four sentences from Lament for a Nation written by George Grant, an interesting Canadian philosopher who believed in Canada. Way back in the fifties, 1957 in particular, he felt that the last nationalist on the scene was a fellow called John Diefenbaker. He wrote this Lament for a Nation because everything else was going down the drain and perhaps the state of Canada might be preserved because of the election that man. He said many things, but the interesting thing he said about the Public Service in 1957 was this quote which is very
October 1, 1991

germane to the debate in Canada going on today and one of the problems we have here. He said this on page 18 of Lament for a Nation:
Diefenbaker's relations with the civil service invite the writing of a picaresque novel. By including these strained relations under his failures, I do not imply that the fault lay all on his side. Too many civil servants had too closely identified themselves with Liberal men and Liberal measures before 1957, and some of these did not show the proper loyalty to the elected government after 1957.
And then he goes on and says this:
Nevertheless, that Diefenbaker failed to win the respect of the civil service was a disaster. No modem state can be run without great authority in the hands of its non-elected officials. In such an uncertain nation as Canada, the civil service is perhaps the essential instrument by which nationhood is preserved. The power of Ottawa has to be skilfully used by politicians to balance the enormous anti-national forces concentrated in the economic capitals of Toronto and Montreal. If Diefenbaker was to foster nationalism, he needed to win the respect of the civil service.
Madam Speaker, he goes on to say that he did not. I am just so sad that since the present government came to power in 1984, when I shared many of its thoughts and tried to develop some of their polices, that when the history is written along with many other things, it will be that we as a government perhaps did not come to grips with our public service then, let alone what has happened today.
Therefore, this is a very sad day to have this bill before us. It is a sad day that we are going to have to most likely pass it and force back to work those who work for ourselves.

Madam Speaker, there certainly can be no question at all that you are perhaps one of the most fair chairpeople that we have had, along with the others that we have in these Chambers, given the leniency that you showed the previous speaker, perhaps no doubt given his tenure in the House of Commons, perhaps given his eloquence. I am not sure what the reason is. Nevertheless, I support what you have done. There was perhaps ample reason.
I would first like to say that this is not an issue about the quality of the work that is performed by Canada's civil service. I, as a 12-year member of Canada's civil service, would like to give a little bit of history so that I am sure I can convince you, the public and members of the House of Commons that I know of what I speak.
Government Orders
The quality of the kind of service that Canada gets from its civil servants is beyond question. Certainly, one can expect that given the numbers of people we are talking about, as in the case of perhaps a large family, large numbers of anything, there is not perfection out there. Nevertheless, I think that Canada's civil servants are a dedicated group of people and believe in Canada. I applaud them for that.
As one who worked for the federal government for some 12 years, I did run into certain circumstances that caused me some puzzlement. I distinctly recall early in my tenure with the federal government wanting to finish a job. It needed about 15 to 30 minutes. However the building I was working in was closed at five o'clock with a lock and key. It had panic hardware on it so that I could leave when my boss told me to leave. I was to get out of the building at five o'clock because the government was not going to give you any time off in lieu of work performed.
I was not looking for any time off. I simply wanted to do the job and, if that was considered to be a contribution to Canada, so be it. I think there are a lot of people out there who feel the same way.
My point is that I do not believe that in this particular case, the president of the union really is in touch with the membership.
In another example, I was transferred into British Columbia and my job was to provide for pipeline profiles for an extremely arid part of Canada. Nevertheless, I found it desirable to get back to good old Saskatchewan as soon as I could. As a result I worked without interruption until 10 or 10.30 every night, not seeking any other form of remuneration, but again making a contribution to my country and to my job. I just considered it part and parcel of having a job, of having employment.
Again, no one asked for my opinion. No one from any union asked me my opinion nor did they direct me, thank goodness, because I was probably outside their reach. Nor did they direct that I could not put in those extra hours.
There are many public servants who give that kind of dedication to the job. I have spoken to PSAC members in Regina, my home community, in the midst of this labour turmoil and I know whereof I speak. I do not believe I should relay the essence of our conversations specifically, but generally they conveyed to me that money was not the issue in this particular case. Knowing full well that 0,

Women, the majority in this country, are beginning to organize in all kinds of ways. Therefore, from the government's point of view, they must be put down, as the government is also trying to put down the native people by cutting their funding for communications, cutting their schooling, cutting their housing.
The government had to divide the working people of Canada, setting some against others, immigrants against Canadians, refugees against others, Latin American racial minorities against others. It wants to divide Canadian workers so that it is easier to force wages down in the interests of the transnational corporations.
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to ask this government and the caucus that is their automatic vote to change their minds. Their intention is very clear: They are serving the interests of the transnational corporations solely, and they are willing to wreck Canada by persecuting the working class.
Therefore, I ask those who are listening to this broadcast to consider what it is that the government is really trying to do behind the smokescreen of this deficit, which this government largely created. It is trying to bring about an undeclared war against the Canadian people on behalf of the richest people in North America. I ask all who are listening to give careful thought to that, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure and with great pride that I stand in this Chamber tonight to speak on behalf of the public servants of this country, but most particularly to speak on behalf of the public servants in my riding of Halifax.
I knew, obviously, that I had the third-largest contingent of public servants in this country, Halifax ranking third after Ottawa and Montreal. What I did not know until the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier told me was that in actual fact more public servants live in the riding of Halifax than in any of the other ridings in the country where public servants live.
I do not think the hon. member for South Shore really means that. But we will let it go for the moment.
The public servants in Halifax fall into several groups. One of those groups is the ships' crews, the crews that go out in the North Atlantic when other vessels are in trouble- "They that go down to the sea in ships", as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands has said-and rescue ships, boats, fishing vessels and so on, in the teeth of the great North Atlantic storms. These ships' crews, when they were striking over the question of regional rates of pay two years ago, downed pickets whenever a

distress call came in, went to their ships, sailed out of Halifax harbour and affected the rescue of many lives.
These workers, Mr. Speaker, are paid less, as we all know, than those ships' crews in other regions of the country. These workers, through a process that the federal government initiated when it ordered them back to work two years ago, through a mediator, had a process whereby these regional rates of pay were going to be eliminated.
The promises of this government for those workers, and I might add for other public servants in Halifax- hospital workers, also suffering under regional pay disparities- the promises of this government are writ on water, they mean nothing. These workers, among the lowest paid, who risked their lives and continue to risk their lives and dropped their pickets while they were on a legal strike to affect these rescues, instead of getting regional rates of pay alleviated as the report of the mediator, the binding report that the mediator promised and that the government agreed to, has been thrown out, are limited to 0, 3 and 3.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: The same as everybody else.

Oh, the same as everybody else, the hon. member for the South Shore says. He ought to check on some of the bonuses for some of the government's friends in the higher echelon positions. That is what the hon. member for the South Shore should do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: You are a wealth of misinformation.
But the hon. member for South Shore, who certainly can make a lot of noise, should remember that the public servants in Halifax made their presence felt on November 21, 1988-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: Stop interfering with the democratic rights of others and go to work.

Well, no, I think they were voting on November 21, 1988, as I recall. On November 21, 1988 they made their presence felt. They will make their presence felt again because they know now, as they suspected in November 1988, that trusting this government would be a waste of their time.
I have spoken many times in this House on the regional rates of pay and the absolute endemic unfairness of it. The hon. member from the South Shore knows it is unfair and knows that his constituents are
Government Orders
among the prime beneficiaries of those underpaid ships' crews that sail out of Halifax harbour.
I have spoken on those many times, as I have spoken about hospital workers who were discriminated against.
I want to get a little specific on numbers. In the Public Service of Canada, 66,000 employees earned $29,000 or less. The poverty line in 1991, for a family of three, was $25,600 and for a family of four was $28,800. Two-thirds of those earning under $30,000 in the Public Service of Canada are-guess what? Women. Is anyone surprised? No, no one is surprised. What is this government doing about pay equity?
Nothing.

Nothing. Not one thing. In reports of conciliators over the years, with relationship to the pay equity question, the following has been said and I quote:
"Apparently the government has a separate funding for pay equity adjustments and they will not come out of departmental budgets. There is room for the government to bargain pay equity adjustments in this round of collective bargaining outside the context of wage restraints".
What is this government doing about pay equity? Well let me tell you.
It is bargaining.

No, no. It is doing a little bit. One of the things that this government is doing about pay equity is fighting the right of the Human Rights Commission to deal with this issue and refusing to negotiate pay equity at the bargaining table. It refused.
Who said that?
I think it was Max Yalden.

Max Yalden has condemned the government's actions on pay equity. The commissioner for human rights has condemned the federal Government of Canada on its actions on pay equity. What a record. What a wonderful way to be. What a great thing to be able to take to the people of the country.
The government has failed to implement pay equity for female dominated groups in the Public Service. That is the truth, that is the issue and it deserves to be condemned. Instead of real pay equity, where classifications are changed to reflect new salary levels, the government gives equalization payments. Equalization payments can be removed at any time and certainly will

Government Orders
be removed if any of these groups ceases to be female dominated.
The government is playing around. We already know what the member for Calgary whatever thinks about equalization payments or any kind of gender equity for women. Heaven forfend.
What does she think?

Oh, I could tell you, but we would have to get into the question of violence against women and it is violent enough.
What else does the government do to its Public Service? We know about contracting out. We hear about downsizing. How has this downsizing been achieved? By contacting out or hiring consultants. The cost of contracting out has climbed from $1.7 billion annually to $5 billion annually, an amount greater than the entire federal Public Service payroll. The contracting out to their patronage friends is greater than the entire payroll for the Public Service of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: Prove it.

Prove it, says the hon. member for South Shore. The proof will be in the pudding and the pudding will be eaten in the next election. The public servants of Canada will not, like Oliver Twist, be prepared to go back to the table where they ask for more and be told by this Dickensian government that there is no more.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been sitting in the Chamber listening very carefully to some of my colleagues on the other side. I want to begin by asking members to let us move into the 1990s and into the 21st century. Members keep forecasting, predicting; you want more of the same and the same does not work. You had better face facts and call a spade a spade. No more taxes, cuts in programs and services, we are living beyond our means and Canada started that way back when you were in power in 1969 with a surplus of $450 million.
The Liberals want more taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
You took that $450 million surplus and you turned it into a $38.5 billion debt, by increasing program spending and increasing salaries to the tune of
13.5	per cent and 14 per cent. I tell you that we have to pay the bills. The party is over and no longer can we-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We have to pay the bills and everybody is going to participate.
On February 26, 1991, the Minister of Finance tabled his budget in this Chamber and all government employees, all MPs, cabinet ministers, RCMP officers, are treated exactly the same. Everybody will get zero, three and three over the next three years. You are. I am. Even the hon. House leader sitting up there is. He had his salary frozen as well.
Nobody likes strikes and we are not advocating a strike. There are many people within the Public Service who do not want to go on strike. There are single parents. There are families who need their salaries to feed their children, pay their mortgage, and keep a roof over their heads. But they did not have an opportunity to cast a ballot. No. It happened to be their leader, the union head, Mr. Bean who said: "Thou shalt go on strike". End of report.
Bargaining and negotiations have been taking place and the public servant has job security-do you have job security, Mr. Speaker? Mr. Speaker has job security. They have pension plans, dental plans and benefits that the free enterprise system does not have. People in my riding of Calgary South are not only losing their jobs, they are taking a decrease. People down on the south shore in Nova Scotia are losing their jobs and taking decreases. They are willing to do time sharing in order to hang on to their jobs. This is not just one sector we are zeroing in on, everybody has to help.
It has been mentioned here, and I know Mr. Speaker knows this, that six provinces have frozen the salaries of their public service: Nova Scotia is at zero for two years; Manitoba is at zero for 1990-1991; the province of Quebec has frozen its public service wages; Newfoundland; and New Brunswick has even rolled back a piece of legislation they had passed.
I sat here and listened to my colleague from Ottawa South across the way talk about money going into other
October 1, 1991

enterprises. I will tell you that by moving the National Energy Board to Calgary we are going to save millions of dollars. No longer will the oil companies have to fly back and forth, hire their lawyers, to be at the hearings here in Ottawa. They are going to hold the hearings right where the energy industry is located.
Everyone is going to participate. Everybody is going to help us to cut the budget.
I just want to make a remark about pay equity. It seems to me it was 10 years ago when the government of the day-who was in power 10 years ago?
The Liberals were.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: -when the government of the day had charges laid against it with regard to pay equity and it was taken to court. Ten years ago. You people never moved. And what government moved?
Wasn't that the Trudeau government?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That was the Trudeau government, the Trudeau government on the pay equity, and it has been 10 years in the courts. You know, Mr. Speaker, we awarded $317 million in 1989, $76 million in 1990 and $81 million this year for pay equity. Pay equity applies not only to women, but to visible minorities, aboriginal people and disabled people. You never ever, ever came out to attack that issue.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I listened to you. Now you, unfortunately, are not moving into the 21st century. One of our gentleman friends from the NDP party was talking about free trade. I will tell you, 75 per cent of our trade is done with our colleagues south of the border.
Eighty per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
All right, 80 per cent. How about 85 per cent? Now that we are going, how about 90 per cent? We need the secure market. We have to move into the global markets. We have to increase our efficiency, increase our productivity and our quality too and we have got to market smarter.
Think of the jobs that would have been lost without free trade. You should come on out and see where the petrochemical business has moved up. There are certain industries that have benefited. As we move through the 10 year period-well, Mr. Speaker, you were here during
Government Orders
that debate in December 1988. You remember all the people, the pot calling the kettle black.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Speaker likes spirited debates, but I ask for the co-operation of the two sides of the House. I recognize again the hon. member for Calgary Southwest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will only be one minute. We will not raise taxes. We will not increase the deficit. If hon. members will tell us where to cut we will all participate and we will all work on this together.
It has been a great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to be here in the House and I thank you very much.

Mr. Speaker, "we will not raise taxes"? Is that beyond the 33 times you have already raised taxes since elected in 1984? Incredible! So it has come down to this, Mr. Speaker.
Constituents in my riding of Hamilton West give me the privilege to stand in the House, rise in debate on Bill C-29, along with my colleagues, in opposition to the government's bill which not only legislates federal civil servants back to work, but imposes on them a wage freeze; 0 per cent.
Like everything else this government does, the legislation before us is the handiwork of the Prime Minister and the Tory cabinet, devised through the use of smoke and mirrors. Make no mistake about it, the government is ramming this bill through the House in the hopes that it will serve them well in the polls. Yes, well in the polls because it has become a political matter.
Is it discouraging potential converts to the Reform Party, is that what it might be about? Disgruntled Tories in all the Tory ranks across this country, it could be a little bit about that. But what is the goal of this bill, Mr. Speaker? It is to convince these groups, like the Reformers, like their Tory backbenchers, like all the Tories across this country, that the government mean business. Cut the pay cheques of federal civil servants all in the name of fiscal restraint.
The smoke and mirror illustration shows that the government is not saving money by freezing these wages and are not convincing Canadians that it is doing the right thing. The government claims to be eliminating full time public sector jobs, but let us remember, they are pushing people out through the front door and all the while contracting people through the back door, hoping Canadians will not catch them in this little charade of theirs. Not only is contracting out costing the govern-

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
ment more, but the wage freeze included in the bill does not apply to higher level public servants.
Remember the story last week, Mr. Speaker? Over
5.000	cabinet appointees received bonuses last year, some as high as 25 per cent of their salaries. One Crown corporate executive is said to have received $87,000 in his Christmas stocking, that is on top of his annual salary of $365,000. The government expects Canadians to buy this so-called wage restraint charade.
Contracting out is exempt from any budgetary restraints. How can the government say that it is saving money when its policies are clearly ruinous to the morale of the public sector, are misleading to the public, and will result in an increase in expenditures just because the government wants to take on the Public Service for the benefit of political gamesmanship? That is all it is.
I listened to the President of the Treasury Board speak in this House. He made an ironic comment. Members on this side of the House have rightly pointed out that this government is trying to pull the wool over the eyes of Canadian by contracting out public servants through the back door, capping the wages of those permanent employees and eroding any kind of job security. The President of the Treasury Board replied: "If things are as bad as the opposition claims, why then last year did over
230.000	Canadians try to gain employment in this maligned Public Service?"
The answer is painfully obvious, except to the minister and his Tory colleagues. Some 250,000 Canadians sought employment with the government because they are just a part of the 1.5 million unemployed in this country,
300.000	of whom, by the way, lost their jobs since the free trade deal was signed.
Another aspect of this debate degradates the equality afforded to women in the Public Service. The government has put pay equity on the table as a political tradeoff. It is a cold-hearted move that shows this debate is about far more than back to work legislation and the capping of wages. This government says that it is committed to paying women an equal amount for equal work done on the job but at the same time is prepared to treat the advancement of women in the Public Service as
nothing more than a bargaining chip. What this government is trading off, trading away, are its principles.
Let us also remember that the wage freezes are being rigidly applied to the lowest paid employees, thereby ensuring that higher salaried employees will receive lump sum payments, bonuses, reclassifications into higher wage brackets.
The fact is the majority of the lower paid employees are women. It has been said, and it should be repeated before we have to vote on this bill in about an hour and a half time, that two-thirds of those federal employees earning under $30,000 a year are women. That is almost 70 per cent.
One group in the lower classification of the Public Service is almost made up entirely of women, 99 per cent, whose average wage is, get this, $19,396. In 1990, just last year, the poverty line in this country for a family of three was $25,600.
What is the single mom working for the federal government to do when her employer freezes her wage at an already less than equitable level and has two children to provide for? Forget day care, this government has already reneged on that promise. It is turning its back and walking away from pay equity and the Canadian Human Rights Commissioner, Max Yalden, who also condemned this government's action on pay equity.
Let us return to the smoke and mirrors image and this analogy. As I previously mentioned the government is trying to persuade Canadians that these wage restraint measures are for the good of the country. What it is really doing is victimizing public servants and using them as scapegoats hoping to curry favour with a public which has lost confidence in it.
It has already victimized Canadians with over 33 tax increases since it came to office and has let the national debt explode to $420 billion, so there is the smoke and mirrors. The government and the member for South Shore try to blame the past governments for the present state of the deficit which they could have controlled over the past seven years in office. Cutting back on public sector wages should send a signal to the Canadian public
October 1, 1991

that the government is serious about controlling the debt, right?
The other page stolen from the Reform Party by this desperate government is a new fund that will bring the deficit down by almost half by the time of the next election when it rolls around. If this government were serious about the deficit, it would ask the former minister of financial disaster where his projections went wrong.
They went wrong time after time, projection after projection. In the six years since the government began to downsize, eradicate the Public Service, 13,000 positions have been cut and 24,000 people have been affected by downsizing. In the same six years, there are
70,000	fewer in the federal Public Service.
Much of the downsizing that has taken place has been achieved by contracting out or hiring consultants. At the bare minimum contracting out has climbed from $1.7 billion annually to $5 billion every year.
Tory waste.
This is an increase of over $3 billion a year.
They put the money into the hands of the fat cat Tories.

That is what this government has been spending on, contracting jobs to do the jobs formerly done by competent civil servants, by a full time staff. For the record the $5 billion amount the government spends on contracting out is greater than the total amount spent on the payroll for the federal Public Service.
I see I have a minute left and so I will close by saying that is the smoke and mirrors. The government would like big business and disgruntled Tories to believe that it is serious about cutting back the public sector but has spent at the same time huge sums of taxpayers' money on this public relations political exercise which has hurt the morale of the world's greatest public service and has done a disservice to the entire country through this transparency, this falsehood, this charade.
Who do I speak for? I speak for the thousands of public civil servants who work in the riding of Hamilton West, right downtown. I also speak for all those Cana-
Govemment Orders
dians who have seen through this outrageous, unfair Draconian bill, Bill C-29.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. I must say I really feel it is unfortunate that this debate is taking place. I am not sure whose interest is served by the fact that this debate is taking place.
The government brought down last March what can only be described as a very responsible budget, responding to the economic realities and the fiscal realities of this country. That included recognition of the fact that many people across this country had to participate in dealing with what this government had the courage to take on, and that is to say, the deficit and the national debt. It goes without saying that the government's own employees, including those of us in this Chamber, had to participate in that exercise.
That is unfortunate. Everyone would like a pay raise. I would like a pay raise. I could use a pay raise. I am sure everyone in the Public Service would like a pay raise. Quite frankly, I have to say in all honesty, despite the disparaging remarks that one hears from time to time, I have rarely met public servants who I do not feel give the public value for the service. They are dedicated people who want to serve Canada, just as I am sure all members of this Chamber wish to serve Canada.
The reality is that governments must act responsibly and so we had a budget that set down a wage guideline for everyone in the Public Service, everyone in the employ of the Government of Canada, including the members of Parliament in this room, the Prime Minister, and the members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, along with the members of the five bargaining units that have already settled within the zero and three.
What did we have the night of that budget? We had Mr. Daryl Bean on television saying: "There is going to be a strike". Everyone knows that the Public Service Alliance of Canada has an impeccable reputation for responsibility, a reputation that has been earned over many years of responsible actions, of negotiating in the appropriate way. I guess Mr. Daryl Bean felt that he was not high enough in the pecking order of the trade union movement or the NDP, whichever is which, I am not sure. He had to show that he was as tough as Shirley Carr and Bob White and Richard Cashin and all the

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
other union leaders in Canada and so he announced then that there was going to be a political strike and he was going to close down the Public Service of Canada.
The Government of Canada, for its part, acted in a responsible manner; it went to the bargaining table prepared, as as it remained throughout prepared, given that the zero, three and three was going to be there, to bargain other aspects like job security which when I worked for a union we felt was very important to our members. Mr. Bean does not seem to appreciate the fact that job security has been offered and put on the table by this government, and other benefits like that. He had to have his political strike. I do not know who told him he had to have that strike or whether he made that decision all by himself. Only he could give the answer to that. The months passed, the weeks passed and we got our strike. Mr. Bean got his strike.
Now how did he get his strike? It is interesting. He got his strike, from what I can see, in large measure through intimidation. It is amazing the stories that are coming out of the people who did not want to go on strike but wanted to go to work. They understood the economic reality that the government faces. They were prepared, as good citizens of this country, to take their lumps along with the rest of us and accept what was available and also many of them recognized that in these times of difficulty they were very fortunate to have jobs at their salary levels and their levels of job security.
I have got 120 fish plants in my constituency and I will tell you that there are not many people in those fish plants who make the kind of money that the people my hon. friends opposite say are so hard done by make. A lot of my fish plant workers would love to have a job at which they could make $25,000 a year, because you cannot make that kind of money working in a fish plant.
The politics of envy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: They would love to know they had the long term security that you can have within the Public Service.
Pitting Canadians against Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
It is perhaps not coincidental that in the town of Bridgewater, which is the largest town in my constituency, we have 25 people in the PSAC bargaining unit and when the strike began do you know how many of
those 25 went on strike? Twenty-two. PSAC had to bus people in from Halifax in order to man the picket lines because people on the South Shore of Nova Scotia know that when times are tough if you have got a secure job, with a dental plan and with job security and pension benefits, you could have it a heck of lot worse than you have it.
If you don't fire them first.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
They made it perfectly clear there was going to be a strike and those who did not go on strike were given the torches of hell. They were physically harassed, they were intimidated. People stayed home because they were afraid to go out of their houses. They were told that if they went to work their name would go on a list and I saw some of the lists posted up. Their democratic right to do what they wanted meant nothing in this union evidently. Their democratic rights meant nothing. Their names were put up and they were all going to be thrown out. I will be interested to see if Mr. Daryl Bean follows through on his promise to throw everybody out of his union who went to work during the strike, because he will be throwing about 60,000 of those people out of his union. I will be interested to see if he delivers on that.
It was interesting, the strike began and we were told this strike was going to go on. We were told that if back to work legislation came in it was going to be ignored. What happens nine days later? Mr. Bean comes in, with his friends I might say from the NDP, saying to the government: "I have got to get out of this situation." He went back to the table. The government made itself perfectly clear; it remained adamant that zero, three and three would be on the table and nothing else, but that it was prepared to negotiate other things.
What has Mr. Bean done? Mr. Bean, a few days later, said "we are going out again". He left the bargaining table. Now he turns around and says the government left the table. There was an unequivocal deal; he broke the deal. He left the bargaining table. What did he leave on the table? He left an average salary of $33,500 a year for public servants in his union, not a bad deal if you are a fish plant worker in Port Mouton, a pension fully indexed to the cost of living, one of the best employment security protection plans in Canada, a dental care plan funded entirely by the employer, and a full range of other
October 1, 1991

employment benefits. Mr. Bean said "No, I am leaving the table and I am leaving that there.".
There was a lot of talk when the strike was on that something needed to be done for the people who were at the lower end of the wage scale of the Public Service and the government was not doing anything. What did the government do? The government responded, the government listened, the government went to the table and offered $500 a person.
An outrage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
I understand the minister is going to make an amendment to this bill to see that they get that. Then what did we hear? For a week all we heard was about the single mothers. It is as if the whole Public Service were single mothers making less than $20,000 a year. The government responded to that. Then we heard: "Oh, that is no good, because there are not very many of them". Which way is it?
I said earlier that it is a political strike. It has obviously been a political strike from the perspective of my hon. friends opposite. We knew where the NDP were going to stand. Everybody knows, solidarity forever, the CLC, the CAW, the NDP. You get one and you get them all. Except then they realized they had a few farmers in their caucus. They had people who had responsibilities to the farmers in western Canada who are possibly having their worst year in history. What were these people doing? They were keeping a strike going that was taking money out of the pockets of the farmers of western Canada. This government is responding.
If you do not watch it, you are going to see the kind of support for farmers coming down from this government that this government under the leadership of this Prime Minister has always provided.
The NDP came in and said: "Please, we have to get out of this situation. We will give you whatever you want". So the hon. House Leader said: "Okay, you said you were going to debate this forever, you give us a House Order that says if they go out again, we will put the bill through the Commons in two days". Boy, the hon. member for Kamloops could not be quicker in saying yes and getting himself out of that little mess.
Government Orders
Then we had my hon. friends from the Liberal party, led by "me too Jean". We did not know what their position was when there was talk of back to work legislation. So we had to wait until the NDP said what they were going to do. Then we heard what the NDP were going to do-oppose the government. God forbid that the Liberal party would find themselves left out in the dark with only the NDP. So, "me too Jean" said: "We are against it too". They came up with a great idea. Their great idea was to get a mediator. That is what we heard form over there. "Let us get a mediator". It does not matter that the leader of the union said: "We have to have a strike". It does not matter that the leader of the union walked away from the table when there were valuable offers on the table for the benefits of his members. No, no, we have to do that.
My time is just about up, but I want to say one thing. The people of Canada do not support this strike. Most people in Canada recognize that public servants are people who serve Canada and deserve the opportunity to go back to work like the rest of us. Most of the people of Canada overwhelmingly, I should suspect, support the action of this government in regrettably having to put through this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, after the noise we heard from the other side, I am going to try to be a bit more low key.
I am sure you will make a lot more sense too.

The last words I heard from that member opposite was that the people of Canada do not support this strike. I think it was the only true thing he said. I should not say that. It is probably unparliamentary. But the only thing that rung true with me is that the people of Canada do not support this strike.
In fact, I do not think they support any strike. People of Canada, the same as people on this side of the House, would like to see some way of ending this strike, but in a way that respects the process of collective bargaining and the process of mediation, the process Canadians have come to associate with a democratic system in terms of the regime of labour relations. Yet, this government absolutely refuses to submit this issue to mediation because it knows it is not going to move on that one line that was printed in its budget: zero, three, three. And it will not move. As a result, there is no sensible negotiation going on. There is absolutely no sensible negoti-

Government Orders
ation that goes on at the table as long as the government has imposed that precondition on bargaining.
I have been listening to this debate for quite a while. Actually, the debate does not go back to the time that the budget was printed. I believe the government had in mind when it put that section in the budget in the first place that it was going to precipitate a Public Service strike. In fact, I would not put it past it that it had this legislation written at the time the budget came down.
This debate does not go back to the failure of the negotiations with the Public Service, it goes back much further. In fact, it goes all the way back in this Parliament to 1984 when the Prime Minister said he was going to come to Ottawa and issue pink slips and running shoes to the Public Service of Canada.
That represents an attitude on the part of that Prime Minister and an attitude on the part of the Conservative political party in this House about public servants and about public employment. This is the group that always separates the workers in Canada as to whether they work for the public sector or the private sector. They consider public sector workers as some kind of a lower form of life or a lesser form of citizen because those people have dedicated their lives to public service through employment by the government.
In some way, this party feels that that makes them a second-class standard of citizen, and that bothers me. It brings to my mind the recollection of something that happened in British Columbia back in 1983, and that was the so-called restraint program that was brought in by the William Bennett government. Everybody knows Bill Bennett, the premier before Bill Vander Zalm.
Some people might know that his chief strategist of the time was a man called Dr. Norman Spector. One of the things that Bill Bennett has bequeathed to the people of Canada, through the Prime Minister's office, is Dr. Norman Spector and the way he manages politics within a province, in the case of British Columbia, or within the country in the case of Canada.
Back during what was called the restraints era in British Columbia, the government used the excuse of a world-wide recession, declining revenues, problems with
profits in the industrial sector, problems of profits in the private sector, to take the meat axe to government programs.
He especially targeted certain programs that Conservatives do not like. For example, he targeted the Human Rights program in British Columbia and he cut the teeth out of that program. He targeted protection for tenants in British Columbia and he cut the teeth out of that program. He targeted welfare services, and in particular services to families, and he cut the resources out of that program.
He took a look at the fact that the government of the day employed family service workers and he fired those family service workers. He said the reason for this is the restraint program. The cupboard is bare, he said, to use the exact same words that were used by the President of the Treasury Board. The cupboard was bare.
He used that program to take a direct attack on employment in the Public Service in British Columbia, and that during that restraint period was when the government of British Columbia began to contract out employment in that province, began to cut the wages of civil servants in that province. It is interesting, to my memory, when I read the line in the budget that says: zero, three and three. When they get that 3 per cent, for every 3 per cent they get they are going to fire civil servants in order to keep the wage package at the same price. It is exactly the same policy that was brought forward in the government of British Columbia when Bill Bennett was premier and Dr. Norman Spector was his chief strategist. That is where we got the program. That is where this kind of restraint policy has come from. This government has been Bennetized, it has been Social Creditized and that is where the problem has come from. It is exactly the same kind of right-wing Conservative ideology that has prevailed in the province of British Columbia under Social Credit, and now this government is being Social Creditized and that is why we have this attack on the Public Service.
It is strange that the technique, Mr. Speaker, that was used by the government in British Columbia was to divide the sectors of British Columbia society and the various social economic classes in British Columbia against each other.
October 1, 1991

When I hear these members saying: "Why should the Public Service have average wages of $33,000 a year when people in my riding and people across Canada have an average of $27,000 a year", my answer to that is: "Why are these people not bringing up the level of wages in Canada so that people who are working for a living and working hard, whether they are in the public sector or in the private sector, are not being forced to live below the poverty line, have sufficient wages to make ends meet and to bring up their kids and to send them through school". Why is this government not acting to do that? This government and its members are saying: "We have got thousands of people, we have got
1.5	million people out of work in this country. They would gladly have those jobs that the Public Service Alliance are striking from and staying away from". What is this government doing to make sure that it does not have 1.5 million people out of work? Why is it not developing policies to get those people back to work instead of, as the member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte said, developing the politics of envy so that people in this country are envying each other's jobs?
We could raise the minimum wage in this country. We could improve the rights to organize and bargain collectively in the private sector so that we would have an increase in wages in those sectors and there would not be the dramatic kind of differences we have in terms of income in this country.
Mr. Speaker, you have given me the signal that I only have a few minutes left. It seems to me that this government is talking about the cupboard being bare. Whenever labour comes to the cupboard, the cupboard is bare. Whenever families come to the cupboard seeking help for child care and for family services, the cupboard is bare. Whenever pensions come to this government seeking an improvement in their pensions so that they could make ends meet, the cupboard is bare. And yet when an election is called in British Columbia and the Social Credit Party needed something to bail them out to improve their chances, suddenly $236 million appears to buy a KAON project in British Columbia.
The same thing happens when the rich are seeking tax concessions and since 1984 the rich have seen their tax burden reduced by 6 per cent in this country. Whenever
Government Orders
the rich and the powerful and the wealthy corporations come to this government, the cupboard is never bare. This government is always prepared to serve the people that it feels it represents and the people that it feels it should serve.
This is an ideological bill. This is a political battle. It is the Conservatives trying to destroy the wages and benefits of the Public Service in this country and trying to lower their wages under a general policy of lowering the wages and working conditions and standard of living of all of the people in this country other than the people that they have elected themselves to serve and that is the rich, the wealthy, the powerful and the large corporations who have been released of all of their burdens and obligations in terms of supporting this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wished to join the debate earlier in the day when the day when the member for Laval East was speaking because he was making some very good points on the hypocrisy involved in the union leadership here. He made reference to how they handled their own employees, when they faced the situation of having to deal with their own employees with regard to their own contracts, those people who work for the union leaderships themselves.
The member pointed out that in a time of restraint they too had to recognize that times were tough. What did they do, rather than have a fair system that is fair to everyone concerned, as this legislation is and as our budget was which announced the zero, three, three, not only for the Public Service, but for members of Parliament, the Prime Minister and straight across the board, everybody gets zero, three and three? Well, that was not quite the way they handled it in the unions with their own employees. In fact, there were some layoffs and reductions of salaries.
I was looking, as the member for Laval East spoke, at a column in The Sun newspaper by Ron Corbett. The business editor called it the union game. On some other union negotiations he is quoted as saying: "The feelgood phrases about workers' rights and job security seem like hollow come-ons when you look at the contracts unions give to their workers. As for the union leaders themselves, they seem a little more than tin pot ego maniacs; people driven by the hunt and the thrill of

October 1, 1991
Government Orders
victory rather than altruistic concerns for Canadian workers."
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, these union leaders always portray themselves as the altruistic ones. The morally superior ones, which would also make them hypocrites, I guess.
To these union leaders it is a game, a game played by schoolyard bullies who got addicted a long time ago to power and fame, bullies who threaten and intimidate union members and the public to incite violence and to counsel their members to provoke the police and to take part in illegal activities. I think members saw today a memo that was circulating around the Hill to strike and picket captains, Tuesday, October 1, 1991, indicating the targets for today's violence and illegal tactics. The strategy, as outlined in this memo to strike and picket captains, was to delay buses as long as possible. They would be buses used not only by union members trying to go to work but buses used by people going to work in all fields.
Again they were not just union members, but anyone who takes the morning bus: teachers, kids going to school, hospital workers and clerks. These were the people being inconvenienced by this union activity.
The memo goes on and I will quote the strategy: "Please note this is an illegal activity and will provoke police activity". These are union orders. Go out and break the law. This is a position, no doubt supported by the NDP, to go out and break the law. This is the counsel we are getting from the union leadership. These tactics will not gain the respect of Canadians nor will they affect the resolve of this government.
I cannot believe that decent, hard working public servants want to break the law, certainly not to justify the egos of game playing union leaders. I believe our public servants understand the need for restraint. They are prepared to accept the government's offer and they want to work.
The Globe and Mail quotes Jim Chorostecki, the senior Public Service union representative in Toronto:
There is a real strike fatigue setting in. People want it to be over
with and resolved and quite frankly, our members want it to be
resolved too.
That was certainly the impression I got this week in my own constituency when I spoke to union members. A young man came to my office and told me that he and his wife had just purchased their first home. They have an 18-month old baby. He is a fellow who wants to get back to work. He feels intimidated by union pressure in his
own riding. He told me that he had not had an opportunity to vote for this union leadership. He did not have an opportunity to vote for a strike.
Where was he? Asleep?
